uses Modify a decoder's weights to map new internal states to correct document identifiers for unseen documents without retraining the entire model.
why it works Retrieval works when you can tell which documents answer a query. The decoder learns a mapping from internal thought-states to document IDs. Updating only critical parameters lets you insert the right mapping for new documents without erasing old ones, solving the catastrophic forgetting problem.
Mitigating Dynamic Graph Distribution Shifts via Mixture of Variational ExpertsWWW
uses Build a mixture of experts that model different distribution shifts in dynamic graphs, producing invariant representations that work across train-test variations.
why it works Dynamic graphs change over time in ways training data doesn't fully capture. A mixture of experts handles multiple shift scenarios simultaneously, learning which one applies to each case. Invariance works because features robust across multiple shifts stay robust when the world shifts in new ways, generalizing to unseen conditions.
ShadowClone: Scalable Decentralized Identity with Cross-Domain Anonymity and Accountable TraceabilityWWW
uses Use sharding and domain-hiding signatures to let users prove membership in trusted domain sets without revealing their home domain, scaling accountability across Web3.
why it works Decentralized identity works because users must prove they belong somewhere without exposing themselves. Ring signatures hide a user in a group while preserving traceability if they misbehave. Sharding scales this by partitioning the global system, so no single authority becomes a bottleneck, yet each domain still trusts the others' accountability.
Augmented Intelligence in Technology-Assisted Review Systems (ALTARS 2026)WWW
uses This is a workshop on technology-assisted review systems that combine human judgment with AI to find and rank relevant documents at Web scale with transparency.
why it works Large-scale retrieval works when you rank by combining multiple signals: text matching, human feedback, and model confidence. Transparency means knowing why a document ranked high. Human-in-the-loop works because humans catch blind spots in pure algorithms, and algorithms scale what humans can individually review, making fair and reliable retrieval possible together.
BanditLP: Large-Scale Stochastic Optimization for Personalized RecommendationsWWW
uses Learns what each user will respond to using probabilistic sampling, then uses those learned response probabilities to solve an optimization puzzle that fairly allocates which emails to send within budget and business constraints.
why it works It works because Thompson Sampling explores efficiently—each draw from your belief about response rates explores actions that might be optimal. Once you have good probability estimates, linear optimization lets you allocate actions subject to real-world constraints without manual rule-setting, guaranteeing fairness across stakeholders.
PRISM: Personalized Recommendation via Information Synergy ModuleWWW
uses Decomposes multi-modal information about items into three types—unique to each modality, shared across modalities, and synergistic patterns visible only in combinations—then adaptively weights each type based on individual user preferences.
why it works It works because modalities interact in non-additive ways; the synergy between text and images can convey meaning neither alone captures. Information decomposition reveals what each modality contributes uniquely versus redundantly. Personalizing the weights lets users whose preferences align with synergistic combinations get those gains.
ARADD: An Automatic Real-World API Discovery and Deployment Framework for AI Guide Service in Baidu MapWWW
uses Automatically discover which APIs solve new user intents by extracting intent patterns from queries, then match them to available APIs and generate training pairs.
why it works It works because intents follow patterns—users asking similar things can be routed to the same API. Extracting and matching intents is essentially a classification task where you learn which users belong to which service. Generating labeled training data from this matching lets new models learn the pattern without humans hand-labeling thousands of examples.
RAG-GFM: Overcoming In-Memory Bottlenecks in Graph Foundation Models via Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Build a separate retrieval store of graph structure (motifs) and text descriptions, retrieve relevant ones for each query, and combine them as contextual evidence to guide graph classification.
why it works It works because storing parameters can only compress so much graph knowledge, introducing conflicts. Keeping knowledge external lets you retrieve only the relevant pieces for the task at hand. Text and structure are independent signals—text captures semantic meaning, structure captures how entities relate—so combining both gives richer context than either alone.
VL-KGE: Vision–Language Models Meet Knowledge Graph EmbeddingsWWW
uses Embed multimodal knowledge graphs (images, text, structure) into a unified space using vision-language model alignments, then link-predict with the combined representation.
why it works It works because vision-language models are already trained on millions of image-text pairs, so they know how images and words refer to similar ideas. Aligning all entities through this pre-built bridge means you inherit that knowledge without training from scratch. Combining three modalities in one space lets you predict missing links using any available information about that entity.
Octopus: Vehicle-to-Road Collaborative Perception for Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop FusionWWW
uses Merges perception data from multiple vehicles and roadside units, fusing individual views into a shared awareness with fewer blind spots.
why it works It works because each viewpoint sees obstacles the others miss. When you combine independent observations of the same scene, the overlaps confirm what is real and the gaps from one view get filled by another. The merged picture is more complete than any single view.
Enhancing Multi-Modal Entity Alignment via Multi-Grained Decision FusionWWW
uses Combines alignment scores from multiple modalities and feature granularities to match equivalent entities across different knowledge sources.
why it works It works because different modalities see different angles of the same entity. Image might see a logo while text sees the name—each is partial. Combining independent signals from different modalities makes matches more certain because multiple independent views converge on the same entity.
Unmasking Bots in Higher Dimensions: Message Passing over Simplexes for Bot DetectionWWW
uses Detects coordinated bot accounts by analyzing group patterns in networks—how accounts interact in clusters beyond just pairwise connections.
why it works It works because real bots coordinate in groups. Real humans interact independently, creating different patterns than orchestrated accounts. By looking at three-person and larger group signatures instead of just pairs, you see group coordination that pairwise methods miss.
BIND: Enabling Continuous Transaction Processing During Account Migration in Sharded BlockchainsWWW
uses Partition accounts into migration batches that maximize connections within each batch to reduce cross-shard communication.
why it works Accounts that interact frequently should migrate together; keeping them in the same batch eliminates the cross-shard overhead for those interactions. The more densely connected a batch is internally, the more communication overhead you save.
ST-LEGO: Large Language Models as Modular Architects for Traffic PredictionWWW
uses Use language models to understand task requirements and assemble modular pieces into complete traffic prediction architectures.
why it works Each module solves one aspect of traffic prediction; a language model acts as a coordinator that understands which pieces to combine based on the specific dataset. Combining weak specialists through semantic understanding produces a strong generalist.
Multi-task Inference of Diffusion NetworksWWW
uses Iteratively refine inferred network structures by sharing information across multiple similar networks, guiding each network's inference with patterns from others.
why it works When networks are similar, patterns learned from one network's sparse data constrain guesses about others. This reduces individual uncertainty by pooling weak signals; the networks essentially teach each other what shared structures should look like.
Economics Model for Federated LLM Training via BlockchainWWW
uses Use Shapley values to measure each participant's marginal contribution to model improvement and allocate training rewards proportionally.
why it works Shapley values measure each player's fair share by averaging their impact across all possible team compositions. This captures how much that player's data improved the global model compared to removing them, creating an incentive-compatible allocation.
LLMs as Orchestrators: Constraint-Compliant Multi-Agent Optimization for Recommendation SystemsWWW
uses Splits recommendation into two agents: one optimizes accuracy while keeping hard rules satisfied, the other explores diverse options; a coordinator balances the tradeoff.
why it works It works because hard constraints need dedicated handling—you cannot penalize violations, only prevent them. By separating constraint-respecting accuracy from unconstrained exploration, then coordinating between them, you guarantee correctness while still discovering good alternatives.
FCRLLM: Aligning LLM with Collaborative Filtering for Long-tailed Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Aligns semantic meaning from a language model with collaborative patterns learned from user behavior to better recommend items people rarely interact with.
why it works It works because semantic and behavioral signals come from different sources: language model text captures what items are about, user patterns capture how people behave. Aligning them via an energy-based framework ensures both signals pull toward the same answer, making predictions for rare items stronger than either alone.
No Evidence, No Problem: When Less is More for Out of Context Multimodal Misinformation DetectionWWW
uses Extracts visual entities and captions from images, combines them with text, then checks whether image and text actually describe the same situation to spot lies.
why it works It works because misinformation depends on mismatch: a real image paired with false text contradicts itself when you extract what each channel actually shows. By combining visual descriptions with textual content and checking alignment, you expose inconsistency that either modality alone might miss.
Viet Medi Species 2026: A Web-Accessible Multilingual Dataset for Vietnamese Medicinal BiodiversityWWW
uses Collects and standardizes images of medicinal plants across multiple languages and sources, linking them to global biodiversity identifiers.
why it works It works because learning from examples requires consistent data: by matching Vietnamese plant names to both scientific names and global identifiers, you create a training set that works across languages and regions. Metadata diversity strengthens learning because models see the same plants described multiple ways.
Unbiased Multimodal Reranking for Long-Tail Short-Video SearchWWW
uses Rank short videos by predicted user experience using multimodal signals and learned preference comparisons, then reorder results.
why it works AI language systems see across text, images, and metadata in ways sparse user clicks cannot; learning pairwise preferences teaches the model which signals predict real satisfaction, so ordering by that score surfaces quality content even when rare.
DTransKT: A Dual Transferable Knowledge Tracing Framework for Cross-Disciplinary Self-AdaptationWWW
uses Trace how knowledge evolves as students answer questions, using skill matching and semantic extraction to apply learning across subjects.
why it works Students transfer knowledge from one subject to another when underlying skills are the same; matching student patterns across subjects and extracting semantic skill definitions reveals the transferable core that generalizes.
VecFormer: Towards Efficient and Generalizable Graph Transformer with Graph Token AttentionWWW
uses Compress nodes and graph structure into discrete codes in a first stage, then perform focus at the level of these codes rather than individual nodes, reducing computation while improving generalization.
why it works Works because nodes within a code cluster are similar, so focus between clusters captures the essential relationships while filtering noise from individual node variation. Discrete codes create a bottleneck that forces the model to learn robust semantic groups, making predictions stable when test data differs from training.
Egocentric Co-Pilot: Web-Native Smart-Glasses Agents for Assistive Egocentric AIWWW
uses Answer questions from continuous egocentric video by compressing long context into hierarchical summaries, combining speech and gaze into structured commands, and orchestrating specialized tools via reasoning.
why it works Works because a human's first-person experience spans minutes or hours but a single reasoning step fits a much shorter window. Hierarchical compression summarizes the long past while keeping important details, and tool orchestration lets weak individual signals (noisy speech, gaze drift) combine through reasoning to yield reliable decisions.
Netting Phish in the IPFS Ocean: Real-Time Monitoring and Characterization of Decentralized Phishing CampaignsWWW
uses Clusters phishing URLs by similarity, ranks their dissemination leverage across decentralized gateways, and estimates impact of blocking small dominant clusters.
why it works It works because real-world attacks concentrate: blocking the few most-used dissemination channels removes availability for most phishing content. Clustering by behavior finds which attacks are coordinated variants of the same campaign, so you target root causes instead of chasing copies.
Linguistic Signatures for Enhanced Emotion DetectionWWW
uses Extracts measurable linguistic patterns from emotion datasets and adds them as features to neural models to boost emotion classification accuracy.
why it works It works because humans recognize emotion partly through specific word choices and grammar patterns that reliably appear together. Adding these explicit signals lets the model see what matters faster and stays robust when the neural patterns encounter new data.
CGPT: Cluster-Guided Partial Tables with LLM-Generated Supervision for Table RetrievalWWW
uses Groups table instances into clusters, generates synthetic query examples for partial tables across clusters, and adjust numeric fingerprints models using hard-negative contrastive pairs.
why it works It works because diverse training examples teach the model to handle semantic variation. Grouping tables ensures you see the full semantic range. Hard-negative pairs force the model to push apart genuinely different cases, so it learns precise, robust distance metrics for table-query matching.
VisionST: Coordinating Cross-modal Traffic Prediction with Interactive Geo-image EncodingWWW
uses Extracts visual patterns from satellite imagery and combines them with spatial and temporal patterns to jointly score traffic predictions node by node.
why it works It works because real traffic depends on overlapping factors: road layout, weather, events, congestion. Treating each modality separately loses their interactions; combining visual context with spatial neighbors and time history captures the full cause, so predictions account for all factors simultaneously.
Tabular Foundation Models are Strong Graph Anomaly DetectorsWWW
uses Converts graph anomaly detection into a tabular problem by enriching node features with structural summaries, then applies pre-trained tabular models for cross-domain generalization.
why it works It works because tabular models already solve the hard parts: handling diverse feature types and generalizing to new domains via synthetic pre-training. Structure itself is just another feature; once you express it as numbers alongside node attributes, tabular models see it naturally and transfer across graphs.
DeepSVU: Towards In-depth Security-oriented Video Understanding via Unified Physical-world Regularized MoEWWW
uses Learns multi-scale features of human behavior, objects, and background context from video, then adaptively weights them to predict threat location and explain threat causes.
why it works It works because threats arise from interactions of multiple elements: a person's action, an object involved, and the setting all matter. Modeling each scale separately captures these interactions. Adaptive weighting lets the model emphasize whichever factor most strongly signals the specific threat occurring.
Online Advertising with Spatial InteractionsWWW
uses Decide which ads to show where on screen by ranking options while accounting for how nearby ads hurt each other's effectiveness.
why it works Ad value depends on location and neighbors; treating slots as points in space and modeling interference as proximity-based lets you reason about the actual value trade-offs before assigning ads.
A Unified Framework for Context-Aware and Relation-Aware Graph Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Build hierarchical graph summaries that fuse both chunk context and entity relationships, then retrieve by searching all abstraction levels.
why it works It works because fusing context and relationships into summaries creates richer intermediate representations; searching multiple levels exploits how users reason at different scales, from details to overviews to themes.
Acting Flatterers via LLMs Sycophancy: Combating Clickbait with LLMs Opposing-Stance ReasoningWWW
uses Generate opposing reasoning pairs (agree and disagree) for headlines, then train a detector using contrastive learning on the reasoning to spot clickbait.
why it works It works because forcing the model to reason from both sides reveals cracks in the clickbait framing; comparing how agree and disagree reasoning differ highlights exaggeration and manipulation that single-sided reasoning would miss.
Anonymous Linear Bandits for Multi-User SystemsWWW
uses Eliminate arms and build a bipartite match between users and remaining arms that preserves privacy while minimizing regret.
why it works It works because successive elimination narrows choices without revealing which arms each user prefers, and greedy matching then allocates fairly; the algorithm bounds total regret because it never keeps bad arms long.
Access Controlled Website Interaction for Agentic AI with Delegated Critical TasksWWW
uses Implement fine-grained access control on websites so AI agents can be granted permissions for specific delegated tasks without exposing full account access.
why it works It works because granting capability by task rather than by account scope ensures agents can only perform actions their delegation authorizes; this separates what users allow from what agents attempt.
Foundations for the Agentic Web: Networked AI Agents in a Decentralized Architecture (NANDA)WWW
uses Design registries, protocols, and reputation systems so AI agents can discover and coordinate with each other in a decentralized network.
why it works It works because registries make agents findable, protocols enable them to communicate reliably despite differences, and reputation systems ensure agents learn whom to trust; together these create conditions where distributed agents can cooperate.
Implementation of a Metacognition Framework for Self-Awareness and Self-Regulation in Ensembles of LLMsWWW
uses Compute a metacognitive state lists of numbers measuring self-awareness across five psychology features, then route queries to system-1 or system-2 processing based on complexity.
why it works It works because the five features (emotion, correctness, experience match, conflict, importance) together reveal query difficulty; using these signals to route automatically matches processing power to need, making the ensemble more reliable.
PAMAS: Self-Adaptive Multi-Agent System with Perspective Aggregation for Misinformation DetectionWWW
uses Organize agents into auditors, coordinators, and a decision-maker that hierarchically aggregate specialized views to highlight anomaly cues in misinformation.
why it works It works because misinformation hides in noise; when agents look at different feature subsets and coordinators blend their views hierarchically rather than flooding all input to one processor, anomalies emerge from the aggregated perspectives.
Sybil Attacks on Centrality MeasuresWWW
uses Score node importance in a network, then craft fake identities to hide a true node's importance—evading detection based on network structure.
why it works It works because network importance measures rely on connection patterns; an adversary can exploit this by creating many fake identities and distributing connections in ways that obscure their true network position. The ranking algorithm cannot tell real influence from orchestrated noise.
STG-DGR: Fraud Detection on Streaming Transaction Graphs with Diffusion-based Generative ReplayWWW
uses Generate synthetic fake transaction patterns to rehearse spotting old fraud types, preventing a model from forgetting as new patterns emerge.
why it works It works because streaming fraud detection faces catastrophic forgetting—as new scams arise, models unlearn old ones. Replaying synthetic historical fraud patterns keeps the old detectors sharp without storing real data, which is impossible at scale.
MIDE: Multimodal Dialogue Emotion Recognition via Mutual Information Enhancement and Dynamic Modality SelectionWWW
uses Measure how much information each modality (text, audio, video) shares with others, then pick the best pairs for fusion and track emotion over time.
why it works It works because emotions reveal themselves differently across modalities—speech tone and facial expression sometimes disagree with words. Measuring what information each modality shares with the others tells you which pairs are trustworthy, and tracking changes over time respects that emotions evolve within a conversation.
Fairness in Opinion-Formation DynamicsWWW
uses Adjust how stubborn individuals are toward their own beliefs so that different groups end up with fair influence over the crowd's final opinion.
why it works It works because the more a person clings to their own opinion, the more weight it carries in the group consensus. By tweaking how much each person sticks to their view, you reshape who influences the crowd—targeting minimal changes that rebalance power between groups.
Rethink Web Service Resilience in Space: A Radiation-Aware and Sustainable Transmission SolutionWWW
uses Reroute satellite traffic during radiation bursts to minimize battery drain while maintaining service—balancing energy cost against uptime.
why it works It works because radiation damage and battery depletion compound over time—the energy spent rerouting now prevents larger problems later. By measuring the energy cost of different rerouting choices against the battery's remaining capacity, you optimize a tradeoff that only appears when you account for the full system.
NANDA: Resolution, Discovery, and Governance for the Agentic WebWWW
uses Builds a naming and certification system to make agents findable, trustworthy, and composable across networks.
why it works Works because DNS and certificate authorities proved that centralized trust layers enable global coordination without central control; agents need the same infrastructure.
ORKG Properties Ontology Consolidated: LLM-Driven Refinement of Crowdsourced Knowledge for Machine-ActionabilityWWW
uses Uses language models to detect and merge duplicate properties and standardize naming in a knowledge graph.
why it works Works because language understanding can recognize when different names mean the same thing; human review validates the merges.
Kleene Closure Property Path Query Optimization Based on Node Clustered IndexWWW
uses Finds all simple paths between nodes by pre-indexing representative paths and cycles.
why it works Works because while finding all paths is hard, you only need certain key ones; storing those makes queries instant.
Single-Sample Bilateral Trade with a BrokerWWW
uses Designs a trading mechanism where a broker buys from a seller and sells to a buyer using minimal information.
why it works Works because constant approximations are possible even with one sample; you don't need exact valuations, just reasonable estimates.
SEP-Attack: A Simple and Effective Paradigm for Transfer-Based Textual Adversarial AttackWWW
uses Scores word importance by combining multiple model opinions and selects the top-ranked words to create adversarial text that fools AI systems.
why it works Different models have different blindnesses; averaging their agreement reveals true vulnerabilities no single model captures. Combining weak signals this way finds robust attack patterns.
ONE-PASS: Single Forward Pass Decoding for Listwise RerankingWWW
uses Ranks items by combining probabilities from sub-rankings instead of ranking all items at once, using a structural decomposition to aggregate sub-scores.
why it works Predicting the full ranking order is costly; breaking it into smaller sub-rankings you can compute in one pass, then using algebraic decomposition to combine them, gives you ranking predictions without the exponential cost.
Beyond Single view Decoding: Dual-view Map Inference from Trajectories via Primal-Dual Graphs Co-generationWWW
uses Infers road maps from vehicle traces by encoding adjacency two ways (as rasterized images and as serialized paths) and merging both signals into unified map predictions.
why it works No single representation captures all road structure; combining rasterized density and traversability paths gives you complementary signals, so merging them yields topology more accurate than either alone.
Smart Book Seeker: Agent-Augmented Retrieval System for Metadata-Sparse LibrariesWWW
uses Refines book retrieval through dialogue-based clarification, keyword search, and multi-turn expert evaluation to pick top results.
why it works It works because retrieval fails when users lack vocabulary or experts lack metadata. Splitting the problem—clarify needs, search broadly, then evaluate with domain knowledge—solves coordination bottlenecks independently.
Enhancing Trusted Multi-View Classification via Adaptive Regularization Guided by View-Specific BiasesWWW
uses Adjusts penalties for each data view based on feature ambiguity and source reliability to balance imperfect evidence.
why it works It works because different data sources vary in quality and clarity. Weighting constraints by confidence prevents bad sources from pulling equally—reliable views drive the answer more.
Navigating Truth in Multimodal Fact-checking via Retrieval- and Reasoning-Enhanced Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Gathers image and text evidence, then refines reasoning through reinforcement learning to verify multimodal claims.
why it works It works because multimodal claims need both semantic search (find relevant proof) and logic (reason through it). Separately optimizing each improves both—better evidence makes reasoning clearer, and reasoning guides which evidence matters.
Semi-Supervised Fake News Detection with Mixture of ExpertsWWW
uses Combines GNN and AI language systems expert judgments with one-class classification and pseudo-labels to detect fake news with sparse labels.
why it works It works because two imperfect experts disagree only on borderline cases—their consensus is stronger than either alone. One-class boundaries define the normal region, and pseudo-labels amplify agreement safely.
KE-FedRS: Tackling Data Sparsity in Federated Recommendation via Knowledge EnhancementWWW
uses Enriches sparse user numeric fingerprints through sharing auxiliary representations with similar users and selecting diverse training clients.
why it works It works because inactive users and rare items need signals from neighbors. Sharing auxiliary numeric fingerprints safely pools knowledge across federated partners without exposing raw data.
ScotRec: Social Chain-of-Thought LLM Reasoning for RecommendationWWW
uses Balances user recommendations by reasoning through multiple sentiment pathways then aggregating them to counteract preference bias.
why it works It works because confirming existing preferences feels natural—it needs active opposition to resist. Explicit multi-step reasoning through contrary sentiments, then aggregating, overcomes the bias through deliberation.
MCLMR: A Model-Agnostic Causal Learning Framework for Multi-Behavior RecommendationWWW
uses Score user preferences from multiple behavior types—views, clicks, purchases—by building a causal model to untangle confounding and weighting behaviors smartly.
why it works User habits and item popularity both influence behavior, creating confounding—a click might come from discovery or habit. By modeling cause-and-effect relationships explicitly, interventions isolate true preference from noise. Adaptive weighting then fuses behavior types by learning which ones are reliable for each user-item pair.
Mixture of Sequence: Theme-Aware Mixture-of-Experts for Long-Sequence RecommendationWWW
uses Predict the next item a user will interact with from long sequences by extracting theme-specific subsequences and routing them to specialized predictors.
why it works Long sequences contain interest shifts and session hops—users care about recent trends within sessions but lose interest across sessions. Routing sequences by theme isolates coherent patterns, filtering noise, so each predictor sees only relevant history. Mixture-of-experts then blends these specialized views to forecast accurately.
1st Workshop on Applied AI and Multimodal Visualization Technologies (AAIMVT 2026)WWW
uses Integrates text, images, audio, and video into a unified visualization and decision interface, using each modality to verify and clarify signals from the others.
why it works Each modality captures different aspects of reality with different noise. Combining them so one confirms the other (e.g., speech content matches transcript tone) filters out noise specific to any single modality, surfacing the signal present in all of them.
Fed-S2: Adversarially Disentangled Federated Multimodal RAG for Safety-Critical Long-Tail Fault DiagnosisWWW
uses Builds a shared knowledge graph from text and signal numeric fingerprints that each participant shares, sanitized to hide individual patterns, then reasons over this combined graph to detect faults across different types of data.
why it works Knowledge graphs make relationships explicit, so sanitized versions preserve causal connections while hiding private signals. Multimodal numeric fingerprints aligned in a shared space mean signals reinforce across modalities, so faults visible in one domain propagate reliably to others.
LLM-GC: Advancing Granger Causal Discovery from Time Series with Multimodel Language ModelingWSDM
uses Discovers cause-effect relationships in time series by enriching raw data with semantic context from language models, aligning temporal patterns with conceptual meaning.
why it works Raw time series alone cannot distinguish true causality from spurious correlation. Adding semantic starting guess (e.g., 'when you see pattern X in the data, it means Y is happening') helps the model ignore coincidences and recognize when one variable truly drives another. Multimodal alignment ensures temporal and semantic signals reinforce rather than contradict.
Using Brand Knowledge Bases and LLM Agents to Enhance E-commerce Retailers' Catalog QualityWSDM
uses Scores and aligns product entries from an e-commerce catalog against a clean brand knowledge base to repair and match them simultaneously.
why it works Matching works because both the catalog and the knowledge base refer to the same real products; by finding which entries correspond to which references, the method can copy accurate details and fill gaps using ground truth from the brand source.
SAGERec: Sampling and Gating for Enhanced Long-Tail Item RecommendationsWSDM
uses Learns which items in a user's history are most informative, then aggregates predictions from two expert models via a learned gate that weights their agreement differently for popular versus rare items.
why it works This works because rare items need different expert knowledge than popular ones; by training gate weights specifically to recognize when each expert is trustworthy for each item type, the method puts the right expert in charge at the right time.
DGNet: Enhancing Parallel CTR Prediction Models via Decoupled Gated Network: Enhancing Parallel CTR Prediction Models via Decoupled Gated NetworkWSDM
uses Generates separate learned numeric fingerprints tailored to each sub-network in a parallel architecture, then uses a learned gate to select which layers of information from each network to combine at each step, avoiding noise buildup.
why it works Different sub-networks capture different interaction patterns; shared numeric fingerprints force compromise. By letting each sub-network learn its own representation and gating which one contributes at each step, the method ensures each interaction type uses its own optimized signal.
Image-Guided Debiasing Distillation with Preference Alignment Across Multi-News HistoriesWSDM
uses Distills image-guided debiasing knowledge from a multimodal model into a text-only model, then trains on cleaned triples using weighted preference alignment to extract objective facts for news recommendation.
why it works Images are less prone to exaggeration than text; by teaching the text-only model to match predictions a multimodal model would make while seeing both image and text, the method transfers robustness without requiring images at test time.
Adapting to Evolving Data: Test-Time Expert Aggregation for Imbalanced Tabular RegressionWSDM
uses Trains multiple expert models each specialized to a different region of the training data identified via mixture modeling, then dynamically weights their predictions at test time based on incoming features without retraining.
why it works Imbalanced data has natural sub-populations with different characteristics; training separate experts for each region gives each an easier learning task. By learning at test time which region each new point belongs to and selecting the corresponding expert, the method adapts instantly to distribution shift.
LLM-Guided Beam Search for Decision Graph Optimization with Dynamic PromptingWSDM
uses Search for a graph of conditions that predicts a number (like price or yield) with smallest error by guiding the search with language clues.
why it works It works because you're chaining two truths: (1) the search finds the structure that makes fewest mistakes, and (2) language hints prune the search space so you find good answers fast instead of exploring forever.
Forget Me, Not My Friends! Object Unlearning Based on Scene GraphsWSDM
uses Remove one specific object from an image while keeping the scene and remaining objects intact, using the scene structure to guide which parts to forget.
why it works It works because the scene structure tells you which pixels causally depend on the object and which don't. Forgetting only the causal descendants preserves everything semantically unrelated to what you're erasing.
Federated Watermarking of Deep Neural Networks with Distributed VerificationWSDM
uses Hide a secret mark inside a shared model where each client can verify ownership independently, and the mark survives removal attacks like adjust.
why it works It works because numeric fingerprints the watermark in a way that spreads across many model weights means no single attack (pruning, retraining, distilling) can erase all of it simultaneously—enough traces survive to prove ownership.
Multi-Agent System for Adversarial Robustness and Originality Attribution in Short-Form VideosWSDM
uses Detect stolen or manipulated videos by breaking the analysis into specialized tasks—one extracts visual clues, one retrieves similar videos, one weighs them together to judge if content is truly original.
why it works It works because manipulation requires coordinating across text, images, audio, and metadata. Specialists in each modality catch what a single model misses, and combining their signals reveals inconsistencies that prove theft.
Hybrid Dual-Semantics Modeling for Enhancing Large Language Model Based RecommendationWSDM
uses Improve recommendations by tuning a language model on both item IDs (collaborative signals showing what items users actually picked) and text descriptions, weighting text more but boosting it with ID signals.
why it works It works because text is semantically richer but ID signals capture real user behavior. Keeping text as primary avoids noise while letting ID patterns fill in what text misses—the two views compensate for each other's blind spots.
WSDM CUP 2026: Multilingual RetrievalWSDM
uses Retrieve relevant documents in multiple languages when given an English query, treating each language version of a document as a separate match to rank.
why it works It works because the same document in different languages encodes the same meaning but different surface words. Matching across languages finds relevance that language-specific search would miss, improving coverage for global queries.
Label-Free Contrastive Learning for Open-World Multimodal Social Event DetectionWSDM
uses Find new social events by treating similar images and text as close neighbors, learning which ones belong together without any labeled event names.
why it works It works because if you arrange multimodal data so similar ones sit near each other in a space, finding groups becomes finding clusters of nearby points; cross-modal alignment lets you compare images and text fairly.
Beyond Existing Retrievals: Cross-Scenario Incremental Sample Learning FrameworkWSDM
uses Rank items to recommend by focusing on finding new items that previous models missed, avoiding recommending the same things twice.
why it works It works because if multiple models already retrieved some items, recommending those again wastes ranking power; focusing on truly new items makes each model's contribution distinct and valuable.
Efficient Monte Carlo Algorithms for Approximating Katz Centrality on Large GraphsWSDM
uses Rank nodes by importance using random walks that approximate a weighted path count, averaging many random samples to speed up the calculation.
why it works It works because random walks converge to true importance scores given enough samples, and averaging many cheap samples is faster than exact calculation; you get ranking order right even if magnitudes are approximate.
Identify-Conceptualize-Align: A Schema-Adaptive Framework for Unified Entity Recognition and Event DetectionWSDM
uses Extract entities and events from text without seeing the specific schema by first finding spans and assigning concepts, then separately aligning concepts to different schemas.
why it works It works because general understanding (finding spans) is separate from schema-specific mapping; by splitting these tasks, each one uses only the knowledge it needs, avoiding conflicting pressures.
Large Language Model Judged Self-Training for Named Entity RecognitionWSDM
uses Label new text for named entities by training on confidence scores from a language model, combined with calibration adjustments, to find high-quality pseudo-labels.
why it works It works because language models have rich knowledge that can judge whether labels are trustworthy; combining confidence with calibration reduces both false certainty and random hallucinations.
Rigorizing Retrieval-augmented Generation with Structured Knowledge Intelligence (6 Hrs)WSDM
uses Retrieve knowledge in structured forms (tables, graphs, trees) and feed it to generation models safely by understanding how structure shapes both retrieval quality and security.
why it works It works because different knowledge structures expose different patterns and vulnerabilities; modeling structure explicitly prevents both missed context and dangerous information leaks.
Phishing Detection in Web Domains: new intelligent tool leveraging the effectiveness of emerging Generative modelsWSDM
uses Score URLs as likely phishing or legitimate using both advanced language models and traditional classification methods, then combine their outputs.
why it works It works because different methods exploit different signals: language models see semantic patterns, while traditional methods see structural features. Combining both types catches phishing attempts that would fool each approach alone.
EpicCBR: Item-Relation-Enhanced Dual-Scenario Contrastive Learning for Cold-Start Bundle RecommendationWSDM
uses Learn bundle recommendations by contrasting what users actually buy together against different view of relations (user-item, bundle-item, item-item), especially for new bundles.
why it works It works because new bundles have no history. But items within them appeared before. By learning what makes users like items and how items relate to bundles, you infer which new bundle a user will like without needing the bundle itself to exist historically.
EvioSum: An Evidence-Guided Generation Framework for Faithful and Interpretable Opinion SummarizationWSDM
uses Select evidence from multiple sources to form a summary that captures diverse opinions and explains their differences.
why it works Combining evidence from multiple viewpoints creates a more complete picture than any single perspective. When you weight and select evidence by how much it represents different opinions, you capture the full spectrum of sentiment rather than just averaging them away.
Personalization in the Era of Super(?)-intelligenceWSDM
uses Personalization is evolving from predicting what users want toward reasoning and creating recommendations that surface unexpected discoveries.
why it works Traditional recommendation works by observing past behavior. Reasoning-based systems can instead model what would actually help a user grow or learn, enabling discovery of things they never imagined wanting because the system understands the underlying intent better than habit patterns do.
When Modalities Go Missing: Early Fusion for Multimodal RecommendationWSDM
uses Fuse available modalities into a shared space early, then skip missing ones, using a collaborative filtering backbone to combine signals.
why it works Late fusion fails when pieces are missing because alignment breaks down. Early fusion leverages the fact that available modalities already sit in a shared semantic space — you can combine them directly without reconstructing missing pieces, and missing modalities simply contribute nothing rather than breaking the whole system.
Precision vs. Discovery: An Adaptive Agent Navigating the Cold-Start Trade-offWSDM
uses Route users to either a personalized ranking model or a semantic discovery model based on whether they are established or new.
why it works New users have no history, so ranking-based approaches fail. Established users have rich history that makes ranking work well. Since these two cases require opposite strategies, the key insight is simply to detect which situation you're in and apply the right tool — routing is more important than any single algorithm.
Web-Mined Hypothesis Generation for Financial Markets: An Autonomous Backtesting FrameworkWSDM
uses Extract market insights from web data, generate trading hypotheses as candidate strategies, then test and refine them against historical prices.
why it works Markets are complex and no single signal predicts perfectly. Combining signals from many sources gives a stronger prediction than any alone. Testing strategies against historical data then keeping the ones that worked best is how you find patterns that generalize — you only keep strategies that actually reduced error when measured on real data.
Assembling Your Personal AI Council in Yupp to Provide Multiple PerspectivesWSDM
uses Gather user preferences across multiple AI models in parallel, aggregate rankings from diverse user populations, and let the strongest signals emerge.
why it works No single model is best for everyone. By collecting opinions from many users across many models, patterns emerge — the models that consistently rank high across diverse preferences truly are better. Aggregating across populations filters out noise and reveals the genuine strong performers.
RankGraph-Context: Empowering Different Industrial Recommendation System StagesWSDM
uses Ranks items by learning implicit relationships between users, products, and past feedback throughout data preparation, training, and ranking stages.
why it works It works because real product relationships form patterns—items bought together, users with similar tastes, feedback signals that predict success. Capturing these patterns early and reusing them throughout the pipeline means every stage learns from the same truth.
Revisiting IPS in Recommendation Models: Unveiling Its Impact on Model PerformanceWSDM
uses Reweights training samples to reduce bias in recommendations, but shows this keeping it simple effect outweighs the bias-correction benefit when combined with multi-task learning.
why it works It works because reweighting samples forces the model to pay focus to underrepresented cases, which naturally enriches what the model learns even when bias correction alone wouldn't help. Multi-task learning amplifies this by creating diverse prediction tasks from the same reweighted data.
Beyond the Single Path: Divergent Reasoning for LLM-based RecommendationSIGIR
uses Generate many different reasoning paths inside the model using controlled randomness, then select and combine the highest-quality paths to produce diverse, accurate recommendations.
why it works It works because a single reasoning path risks missing better alternatives. By generating multiple paths in parallel and picking the best ones, you explore the model's reasoning space more thoroughly, then aggregating them balances diversity and accuracy.
GIGP+: A CPU-GPU Co-Processing Engine for Multi-Vector RetrievalSIGIR
uses Retrieve top candidates on CPU using exact filtering, then score and rerank them on GPU in parallel, coordinating work to hide synchronization delays.
why it works It works because filtering is sequential and CPU-friendly while scoring is parallelizable and GPU-friendly. By doing filtering on CPU and scoring on GPU in a pipeline, neither waits idle; CPU filters while GPU scores, and overlapping hides latency.
Advantage-Conditioned Flow Policy for Offline Reinforcement Learning in RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learn what actions users prefer by studying their real logs, then score actions by how much they improve future reward, filtering out actions that lead nowhere.
why it works User logs show which actions worked in the past. By scoring actions by their future payoff (learned from logs), you get guidance without needing to try risky new actions live.
Tool-Star: Empowering Multi-Tool Collaborative Web Agent via Reinforcement LearningSIGIR
uses Train a model to call the right tools in the right order by practicing on generated examples, starting with easy cases, then learning from its own mistakes with rewards.
why it works Practice on many examples builds muscle memory for tool reasoning. Starting easy and progressing hard ensures the model learns stable patterns before tackling edge cases.
Corpus-Centric Learning for Zero-Shot Table RetrievalSIGIR
uses Represent tables as hybrid structures linking semantic and structural information, then blend dense semantic search, sparse keyword matching, and graph traversal to find relevant tables without labeled query data.
why it works It works because table semantics hide in structure: column order, relationships, and entities all encode meaning. By fusing multiple weak signals—each captures different aspects of relevance—the system avoids over-reliance on any one signal and generalizes to unseen queries.
MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity LinkingSIGIR
uses Disambiguate entity mentions in multimodal text by learning separate expert models for different features, then weighting and merging them hierarchically across semantic levels.
why it works It works because entity identity depends on multiple factors—text, image, and semantic context—each expert model learns one perspective, avoiding dominance by any single signal. Hierarchical weighting lets coarse context guide fine details, so the model integrates evidence systematically rather than hoping one signal alone suffices.
HiRA: Decoupling Planning and Execution with Hierarchical Reasoning in Deep SearchSIGIR
uses Decompose complex search queries into subtasks, assign each to a specialized agent with tools, reason and integrate results hierarchically to synthesize information across sources.
why it works It works because complex reasoning has structure: high-level planning (what questions to ask) is distinct from low-level execution (how to answer each). Separating them prevents execution details from confusing the plan. Specialized agents exploit domain-specific tools and knowledge, so each step reaps expertise gains rather than one model spreading itself thin.
MCP-Focus: Leveraging Function-Oriented Document Enhancement for MCP Server RetrievalSIGIR
uses Find the right tool servers by analyzing their code automatically, generating clear function-focused documentation, and ranking candidate servers by match to user requirements.
why it works It works because unstructured documentation hides function semantics: you cannot rank what you cannot understand. Extracting tool inventory from code and refining descriptions with implementation context produces retrieval-ready documents that capture actual capabilities. Clear function-level documents fuse multiple signals—tool names, descriptions, and expected behaviors—into a strong relevance signal.
MVIGER: Multi-View Variational Integration of Complementary Knowledge for Generative RecommenderSIGIR
uses Treat conflicting recommendations from different prompts and indices as samples from a hidden choice, and learn a starting guess over which to trust.
why it works It works because different prompts reveal different facets of true preferences; modeling their disagreement as stemming from a hidden source lets you adaptively weight each facet by how relevant it is.
Seeing the Whole Through the Parts: Discovering Objects through Semantic Part Mining in Weak SupervisionSIGIR
uses Detect objects by first identifying semantic parts, then assembling those parts into structurally consistent wholes instead of classifying objects directly.
why it works It works because humans see objects as collections of meaningful pieces, and fitting those pieces together enforces that the final detection actually looks like a real object. This structural constraint eliminates confusion between part fragments and complete instances.
Cross-Domain Interest Representation Learning for Scenario- and Task-Aware RecommendationSIGIR
uses Route recommendations through task-specific experts weighted by domain and scenario, then combine their outputs using a learned gating function that aligns multimodal features.
why it works It works because each domain and task has different priorities—what matters in video differs from gaming. By learning which experts to trust for each situation and weighting their votes accordingly, you capture cross-domain patterns without forcing one model to do everything equally well.
Fourier Kolmogorov-Arnold Network and Hypergraph Enhanced Contrastive Learning for RecommendationSIGIR
uses Recommend items by decomposing user-item interactions using a special function approximator, then contrasting multiple views of the graph to find the strongest patterns.
why it works It works because user preferences are complex functions of many weak signals—one graph view emphasizes structure, another emphasizes denoising. By learning complementary representations and comparing them, you extract the durable preference patterns that appear across multiple perspectives, filtering out noise.
Think, But Don't Tell: Implicit Reasoning for LLM-based Sequential Recommendation via Multi-Teacher DistillationSIGIR
uses Transfer what big models learned about reasoning into a smaller model by showing it many reasoning examples and training it step-by-step.
why it works It works because good reasoning can be decomposed into patterns. Once you show a small model which reasoning steps are correct via examples, it learns to recognize and repeat those patterns internally, getting the accuracy benefits without needing the big model at runtime.
SRAG: A Lightweight and Specialized Retrieval-augmented Generation System at the EdgeSIGIR
uses Store knowledge on separate edge devices, route queries to the best-matched device using compact summaries, and move knowledge between devices to fit their specialties.
why it works It works because specialized knowledge bases beat generic ones under compute limits. By routing queries smartly and migrating content to well-matched devices, you get high accuracy without replicating everything everywhere or needing central coordination.
Verbalizing LightGCN: Direct Learning of Textual Representations from User-Item Interaction Graph via LLMsSIGIR
uses Learn user and item profiles from interaction graphs by having a language model simulate message-passing, combining graph structure with semantic text.
why it works It works because collaboration and semantics are complementary signals. By letting language models mimic graph aggregation in natural language, you unify two sources of preference information without needing to bridge learned spaces and text.
Mixture-of-Retrieval Experts for Reasoning-Guided Multimodal Knowledge ExploitationSIGIR
uses Select which knowledge source to retrieve from by learning which one the model needs most at each reasoning step, training via fine-grained rewards across steps.
why it works It works because different experts shine at different moments. By rewarding the model for using the right expert at each step rather than just the final answer, you teach it to route intelligently; diverse experts then cover more ground.
Consensus-Anchored Expansion for Noise-Resilient Re-rankingSIGIR
uses Re-ranks search results by identifying documents that both keyword and semantic search agree on, then expands the query through those trusted anchors while suppressing drift from the original intent.
why it works It works because keyword search and semantic search make complementary errors—one misses paraphrases, the other catches false topical matches. Where both agree, they've confirmed relevance; expanding through those proven anchors adds coverage while rejecting the errors each makes alone.
ProEchoMem: Enhancing Long Video Understanding via Multi-Trace Probe-Echo MemorySIGIR
uses The system builds a knowledge structure from video, then responds to queries by simultaneously activating all related memories and blending them into a coherent answer.
why it works It works because videos contain many overlapping scenes and ideas. By treating memories like parallel traces that all activate together and then integrating them—rather than picking just the top-ranked clip—you capture richer context without exceeding words limits.
Question-Adaptive Graph Learning for Multi-hop Retrieval Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses The system builds a multi-level graph from facts, then uses a graph learning model that aggregates information level-by-level, guided by the question, to find all relevant knowledge chunks.
why it works It works because complex questions need facts at different scales—entities, relations, passages. By explicitly modeling these levels and letting the question guide which information to combine at each level, the system filters noise and gathers richer context than single-level retrieval.
Mitigating Bias in Large Language Model Based Question Answering through Causal Front Door PromptingSIGIR
uses The method samples multiple reasoning paths from a language model, identifies which intermediate thoughts actually cause the answer, then averages answers weighted by valid reasoning.
why it works It works because language models pick up demographic shortcuts during training (e.g., 'nurse' often follows female pronouns). By intervening on intermediate reasoning as the causal step and selecting only paths with valid logic, you block spurious associations while letting genuine inference flow through.
Good Ranks Follow Good Answers: Unsupervised Answer-Driven Reranking for Multimodal Document QASIGIR
uses Rerank search results by checking which ones lead to correct answers, then optimize the ranker to reward results that produce right answers downstream.
why it works It works because direct feedback from answer correctness is far more aligned with what we actually care about than proxy scores from annotation or language models. The method steers toward strategies that improve the end goal, not intermediate proxies.
Evaluation of Agents under Simulated AI Marketplace DynamicsSIGIR
uses Simulate how users switch between systems, how systems compete for focus, and measure which one wins market share over repeated interactions.
why it works It works because realistic outcomes depend not just on accuracy but on competitive effects: early advantage, lock-in, and switching costs. Lab benchmarks on isolated systems miss these forces, but simulating them reveals which systems truly survive in practice.
Towards a Relevance Posterior in Neural Information AccessSIGIR
uses Score documents using both a learned estimate of relevance given the query and a learned starting guess belief about quality regardless of query.
why it works It works because query-independent starting guess capture persistent document value that query scores alone miss. Combining them through fusion lets you shift expensive computation offline while keeping accuracy by balancing both signals at rank time.
Towards a General Intelligent Information Agent: Framework, Models, and EvaluationSIGIR
uses Build a single agent that learns four models of situation, content, tasks, and user preferences to route people to search, recommendations, or conversation.
why it works It works because combining all four models lets the agent choose the mode that minimizes both the user's effort and its own work. Each model captures a different force shaping what the user needs; together they guide the agent to the right interaction for each moment.
A Reproducibility Study of Bundle Editing and Bundle RecommendationSIGIR
uses Test eight ways to edit bundle content and nine ways to recommend bundles, measuring how replacing items creates the biggest bottleneck.
why it works It works because reproducibility across many methods on real data reveals which obstacles are universal, not method-specific. When nearly all approaches fail at one step like replacement, that step must be the key to improving the whole pipeline.
A Reproducibility Study of LLM-Based Query ReformulationSIGIR
uses Test ten language model query rewriting methods on many data sets to see which results replicate across different retrieval types and model sizes.
why it works It works because heterogeneous starting guess studies bury the real dependencies: rewriting gains depend heavily on the retrieval method (word-based versus learned) and model size. Controlling all variables reveals which improvements are robust versus artifacts of specific setup choices.
Lighting the Way for BRIGHT: Reproducible Baselines with Anserini, Pyserini, and RankLLMSIGIR
uses Rank documents by combining term weights with fusion methods; BM25Q applies statistical word importance to queries themselves, not just documents.
why it works It works because ranking only needs to get the order right, not exact scores. Weighting by how much a word matters to distinguish topics automatically surfaces the most relevant documents first. Fusion combines independent signals so their weaknesses cancel out while agreement amplifies.
Auto-Judge: A Cross-Task Benchmark for Comparing LLM Judges for Citation-Grounded RAG SystemsSIGIR
uses Evaluate automated AI language systems judges by comparing their scores to human judgments; measure correlation across diverse evaluation tasks and diagnose failure modes.
why it works It works because human judgment is the ground truth we can measure against. Comparing judge predictions to human ratings reveals both accuracy and systematic biases. Testing across multiple tasks and known vulnerabilities isolates which types of evaluation a judge handles well.
Orcheo: A Modular Full-Stack Platform for Conversational SearchSIGIR
uses Integrate query reformulation, ranking, and response generation as modular components; combine component outputs to produce end-to-end conversational search results.
why it works It works because conversational search is a pipeline where each stage refines or reweights the previous one: reformulation clarifies intent, ranking surfaces relevant information, generation shapes it for the user. Modularity lets researchers contribute better stages independently while reusing others' work.
Refairmulate: A Large-Scale Dataset for Gender-Fair Query ReformulationsSIGIR
uses Rewrite queries to simultaneously improve retrieval ranking and reduce gender bias in results.
why it works It works because query reformulation changes what you ask for, and by optimizing for both relevance and fairness together, you disentangle bias in the training data from bias in the retrieval ranking, making both improve at once.
Beyond Maintenance: A Benchmark and Multi-Agent Framework for Repository-Usage Code GenerationSIGIR
uses Retrieve correct APIs from a repository, then score and refine multi-step code that calls them correctly to build applications.
why it works It works because code generation is a scoring and refinement loop: retrieval finds which functions exist, scoring validates if they fit together, and iteration learns which combinations lead to working programs.
OpeNTF2: Fairness-aware Graph Neural Team FormationSIGIR
uses Score teams of experts by modeling skill-sharing collaborations as a graph, predicting which experts work well together while removing bias toward popularity and gender.
why it works It works because expert teamwork is relational—success flows through connections—and by mapping those connections as a network, you can score teams by their relational position rather than only individual skill, while debiasing which connections get highlighted.
WebMall - A Multi-Shop Benchmark for Evaluating Web AgentsSIGIR
uses Score web agent success on complex shopping tasks across multiple simulated stores with heterogeneous product data, including price comparison and product substitution.
why it works It works because real shopping requires agents to find and rank across many stores, so a benchmark must simulate realistic product complexity and conflicts in pricing, exposing whether agents can match needs to options across many sources.
Mitigating Collaborative Semantic ID Staleness in Generative RetrievalSIGIR
uses Updates the unique labels assigned to products as user preferences shift over time, keeping them consistent with the old system while reflecting new behavior.
why it works It works because identifiers only matter if they capture current meaning; aligning new identifiers to old ones preserves a working system while updating what those identifiers actually mean.
Booking Funnel and Substitution-Aware User Behavior Modeling for Demand Prediction and Joint Room PricingSIGIR
uses Predict hotel and room demand by modeling the two-stage booking funnel and how price changes for one room type shift demand to others.
why it works It works because booking is two-stage (hotel then room type) and room choices affect each other. By decomposing into stages and explicitly modeling substitution—when a price rises, some customers switch to competing rooms—the model captures real causal structure instead of treating all interactions the same.
EviRAG: Evidence-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Vision-Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Retrieve medical reports by first matching structured clinical facts exactly (presence and side of findings), then refining with semantic similarity for description details.
why it works Dense similarity alone retrieves reports that sound similar but are clinically wrong. Using hard constraints on facts first narrows to clinically safe options, then semantic matching picks the best description within that safe set. Two-level filtering prevents nonsense while staying specific.
MuPP: Multi-Preference Padding for Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses When a user has few interactions, generate multiple diverse facets of each item's appeal and use those to fill gaps, so the recommendation model sees richer behavior patterns.
why it works Repeating the same item many times wastes capacity; creating diverse sub-preferences from real items trains the model on meaningful variations without adding artificial noise.
Improving Ad-hoc Search Effectiveness for Conversational Information Retrieval via Model MergingSIGIR
uses Merge the weights of a single-query search model and a conversation-aware search model so one model does both tasks without retraining.
why it works Two trained models each captured patterns the other missed; blending their weights preserves both because the shared foundation makes their parameters complementary.
REMICA: Reflective Memory and Interventional Context Alignment with Multi-Agent LLMs for Inappropriate Utterance DetectionSIGIR
uses Store past decisions and their reasoning, retrieve similar cases at test time, and verify consistency between retrieved reasoning and new predictions to catch errors.
why it works Earlier decisions contain valid reasoning you can reuse; checking consistency between memory and current verdict catches when the model contradicts itself, signaling error.
ZoRRO: A Zero-Weight Personalized Recommender System for Scalable News RecommendationSIGIR
uses Rank news articles by combining simple signals (user history, article popularity, topic) with fixed weights, no model training required.
why it works Fixed simple rules can outrank learned models when they capture the dominant signals; rules scale faster and are easier to deploy than updating trained models constantly.
GeoSearch: Augmenting Worldwide Geolocalization with Web-Scale Reverse Image Search and Image MatchingSIGIR
uses For a query photo, combine results from database lookup, web search, and image matching to retrieve candidate locations, then use a language model to vote on the most likely GPS coordinates.
why it works Different search methods find different clues; voting on the result lets methods specialize: web search finds text context, database finds visually similar photos, matching verifies alignment.
LUMI: Unsupervised Intent Clustering with Multiple Pseudo-LabelsSIGIR
uses Groups texts by computing shared pseudo-labels for each, then pooling text numeric fingerprints with the average of labels that describe it, weighting by overlap.
why it works When many texts share the same thematic label, averaging their label numeric fingerprints creates a stable centroid. Texts close to that centroid are likely similar. Pooling each text's numeric fingerprints toward shared labels amplifies the signal from labels many texts agree on, drowning out noise.
Revisiting Poison Pills for Neural Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Identifies documents whose inclusion in feedback sets degrades retrieval results, analyzing interactions showing that harmful documents can combine to form helpful sets.
why it works Feedback documents act as a system: each reweights what's important, and their combined effect depends on how they steer together. Some documents hurt alone but help in combination because their weaknesses cancel or their signals reinforce differently than in isolation.
Context Convergence Improves Answering Inferential QuestionsSIGIR
uses Selects passages by measuring how much each sentence eliminates wrong answers, then orders sentences by elimination power, improving reasoning over cosine-similarity selection.
why it works A sentence that strongly rules out many bad answers is more informative for reasoning than a sentence merely similar to the question. By measuring elimination power (how much narrower the possibility space becomes), you select and order evidence by its actual reasoning value, not surface similarity.
StAR: Adaptive Structure-Aware Reranking for Semantic-Structural Alignment in GraphRAGSIGIR
uses Ranks retrieval candidates by blending semantic closeness with hyperbolic structural similarity, using query-level hierarchy alignment to adjust structural weight.
why it works Semantic closeness alone misleads on multi-hop questions by ranking semantically similar but structurally irrelevant results first. Hyperbolic distance captures hierarchical structure naturally. Combining both and adapting the mix per query lets structural evidence override semantics when the query needs multi-hop reasoning.
L2Rec: Towards Dual-View Understanding of LLMs for Personalized RecommendationSIGIR
uses Applies personalized compact changes to a language model's parameters for each user, producing separate behavioral and semantic adaptations that fuse into unified recommendations.
why it works A single model backbone can learn to behave differently per user if you route through user-specific tweaks. Small per-user perturbations are efficient (compact, quick updates) yet powerful because they operate in the full learned feature space. Two separate adaptations fused together capture both user history and meaning.
Better than Dense? Investigating the Natural Backward Compatibility of Learned Sparse RepresentationsSIGIR
uses Combine term-based and learned scores through ranking fusion so older indexes stay useful when query encoders change.
why it works When you shift to a new query encoder, the old index was built from a different scoring method. By blending the word-matching scores (which don't change) with new learned scores, you anchor to something stable and preserve the old ranking information, letting it guide decisions even as the encoder improves.
BANANA: Bounded Adaptive Navigation Architecture for Nested ArchivesSIGIR
uses Search through nested document sections iteratively, deepening only when current evidence is insufficient, with a bound that guarantees coverage.
why it works Dense lists of numbers lose entity names and numbers—facts get buried. Plain text preserves identity signals. By searching shallowly first and only drilling deeper when needed, you find answers fast. The deterministic contraction bound ensures you won't miss information—you progress through progressively wider contexts until evidence appears.
Automating Generation of Long-Form QueriesSIGIR
uses Group short queries into clusters that represent coherent search sessions, then combine them into a single long narrative that mimics human search behavior.
why it works People's actual searches form natural clusters where one question triggers the next. By discovering those clusters and synthesizing them into a single narrative, you get a representative query that a human might write.
CSyMR: Benchmarking Compositional Music Information Retrieval in Symbolic Music ReasoningSIGIR
uses Answer music questions by chaining multiple symbolic analysis operators together to extract evidence from sheet music, aggregating results into a single answer.
why it works A single musical fact requires looking at multiple features of the score—note pitch, timing, harmonic context. By combining multiple independent analyses, each weak in isolation, into one reasoned path, you extract implicit meaning.
Towards Unified Affective Reasoning via In-Context Reinforcement LearningSIGIR
uses A language model learns to reason about emotions and sentiments across multiple related tasks simultaneously, using examples in context to handle different labeling styles from different datasets.
why it works It works because emotional reasoning follows shared underlying patterns across tasks, so learning them together lets the model borrow strength from related problems, and seeing examples helps it map different annotation styles to the same underlying concept.
CRED: Calibrated Relational Enhanced Distillation for LLM-Based Pointwise RerankingSIGIR
uses A smaller model learns from a larger one how to rank documents by matching not just the absolute score each document gets but the pattern of score differences between candidates, with special care for the hardest negatives.
why it works It works because ranking only needs the right ordering, not the exact scores; by copying the score patterns between documents rather than raw scores, the smaller model learns the essential structure; focusing on hard negatives matters because those are where false rankings create problems.
Exploring and Improving Cross- and Multi-Domain Personalized Question Answering via a Dual Retrieval Augmentation ApproachSIGIR
uses For personalizing answers, search both the user's profile and a general knowledge source, then combine results to handle cases where the user's profile comes from a different topic area than their question.
why it works It works because user profiles are noisy indicators of their true interests, so when the profile comes from a different area, the general source fills the gap; combining two weak signals is stronger than either alone because each compensates for the other's blind spots.
GATHER: Convergence-Centric Hyper-Entity Retrieval for Zero-Shot Cell-Type AnnotationSIGIR
uses For finding cell types from a list of genes, find genes that act as hubs in a knowledge network: places where many input genes converge, revealing which cell types they collectively point toward.
why it works It works because individual genes are noisy, but when many genes all reach the same cell-type node through the network, that convergence is a strong signal of identity; thinking about network paths lets you find consensus without asking the language model to pick the answer.
Simulating the Lateral Reader for News Trustworthiness Reports with an Iterative Multi-Agent RAG SystemSIGIR
uses To fact-check a news article, generate investigative questions, search for evidence multiple ways, filter and rank that evidence, and decide when you have enough before writing a trustworthiness report with citations.
why it works It works because systematic questioning mirrors how humans check facts: ask what to look for, search in multiple ways to avoid missing true information, and rank by reliability; stopping when you have enough prevents wasting effort chasing ever more distant clues.
M-DaQ: Retrieving Samples with Multilingual Diversity and Quality for Instruction Fine-Tuning DatasetsSIGIR
uses To build training data in many languages, pick examples that score well for quality and that are spread out in meaning-space so you capture the range of things the model should learn.
why it works It works because a model learns best from examples that cover the full range of the problem space; by deliberately spacing examples far apart in meaning, you ensure coverage; by checking quality, you avoid learning from wrong examples.
Calibrating Uncertainty with Cross-Model Consistency for LLM Hallucination MitigationSIGIR
uses When multiple language models give answers to a question, trust an answer more if other models agree on it, and less if they disagree, using this agreement as a signal to adjust each model's confidence.
why it works It works because agreement among independent models is a strong signal of truth: if multiple systems that learned differently all reach the same conclusion, something real is driving them; disagreement means at least one is wrong, so staying cautious is wise.
Agentic Multi-Source Grounding for Enhanced Query Intent Understanding: A DoorDash Case StudySIGIR
uses Score and order multiple intents for an ambiguous query by grounding predictions in available inventory and web evidence, then applying business rules.
why it works It works because resolving ambiguity requires anchoring to real-world facts. By checking what's actually available in the catalog and what the web confirms exists, you prevent the model from hallucinating answers. The business rules then pick the best real option for each user context.
HybridSparse: An End-to-End Hybrid Framework for Efficient Large-Scale RetrievalSIGIR
uses Score items using both exact-word matching and semantic similarity together, training them jointly so each signal strengthens the other.
why it works It works because exact matches miss paraphrases and synonyms while semantics alone miss precise terminology. Training both jointly teaches them to agree about what matters—when keyword importance and semantic similarity both rank something high, it's more reliable than either alone.
Meituan Merchant Business Diagnosis via Policy-Guided Dual-Process User SimulationSIGIR
uses Simulate group behavior by extracting decision policies from histories, then using those policies to align both reasoning and statistical models.
why it works It works because real behavior is both intentional and habitual—people follow learned patterns they don't articulate. By discovering shared policies in the data, you anchor the reasoning model (prevents over-explaining) and guide the fitting model (prevents pure statistics). Fusion corrects for biases in either approach alone.
Joint Optimization of Relevance and Engagement in Multi-Task Ranking for E-Commerce with Efficient LLM SupervisionSIGIR
uses The ranker scores items on a scale from irrelevant to highly relevant, then balances this against user engagement signals to return items people both want and will click.
why it works Engagement alone can promote mediocre popular items. By scoring true relevance separately—even with a lightweight language model—and then combining both signals, the system can favor items that genuinely match intent while still rewarding engagement. The ordering of relevance levels is crucial: the relative ranks matter more than exact scores.
Full Retraining, Incremental Fine-tuning, and Hybrid Serving: Model Updating and Serving for Industrial Generative Recommender SystemsSIGIR
uses The system maintains a stable base model trained on old data and a fresh model trained on new data, routing active users to the fresh model and others to the stable one.
why it works Full retraining on every new batch is expensive and can flip old patterns that still matter. adjust on recent data alone forgets the old patterns. By running both in parallel and routing smartly, active users get fresh understanding while stable users stay grounded in proven knowledge—lower cost, no catastrophic forgetting.
RedGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Recommendation in REDnoteSIGIR
uses The model generates recommendations by learning a mapping from users and their intents to item codes, using a single model to predict clicks, dwell time, and engagement all at once.
