why it works Works because real-world knowledge graphs contain spurious connections that add noise and mislead the recommendation model. Denoising removes false correlations, and task-specific reweighting emphasizes edges that distinguish good recommendations from bad ones, focusing signal on what matters for predicting user preferences.
How Social Media Peer Comments Influence Privacy Decisions in Photo Sharing: Context and Individual Differences Cause Comments to BackfireWWW
uses Measures how peer comments change the likelihood that a user shares a sensitive photo, separately for different user types and comment mixes.
why it works It works because randomized comment variants isolate what caused the sharing decision. Comparing outcomes when only the comment changes reveals which factors actually drive behavior versus what merely appears correlated.
Towards Fair Large Language Model-based Recommender Systems without Costly RetrainingWWW
uses Identifies which training examples cause bias in recommendations, then removes their influence on the model to improve fairness without full retraining.
why it works It works because removing the true bias-causing examples fixes the model at its core. You don't need to retrain from scratch; small adjustments that undo the influence of those few examples efficiently flip wrong predictions back to fair ones.
When to Invoke: Refining LLM Fairness with Toxicity AssessmentWWW
uses Detects when demographic-related variation in toxicity judgments is likely to occur, then applies targeted refinement to reduce group-level disparities in model outputs.
why it works It works because unfairness concentrates: certain inputs consistently produce biased outputs. Identifying these risky cases and applying corrective scrutiny at inference time stops bias before it propagates, without needing expensive retraining or model changes.
HGSA: Heterogeneity-Guided Sarcasm Adaptation for Video Sentiment Analysis via Polarity DisentanglementWWW
uses Separate sarcasm signals from straightforward signals by tracking how sentiment flips across different types of content—text, audio, video.
why it works Sarcasm flips the meaning but only certain parts of the input carry this flip. By keeping sentiment signals separate instead of mixing them, you can see which parts genuinely oppose each other, revealing where sarcasm hides.
From Representation to Clusters: A Contrastive Learning Approach for Attributed Hypergraph ClusteringWWW
uses Learn what nodes belong in the same group by comparing which nodes look alike to each other and which hyperedges hold them together.
why it works When you learn from comparisons—nodes that should cluster together sit near each other—the geometry of similarity directly guides where the clusters form, so clustering becomes reading off natural gaps in that learned space.
Trustworthy Foundation Models for Web Intelligence: Causal Perspectives and ChallengesWWW
uses Foundation models used on the web need causal reasoning to separate real cause-and-effect from coincidental patterns, ensuring they act trustworthy.
why it works Causal reasoning reveals which relationships are real versus accidental; this distinguishes genuine insights from spurious correlations that can mislead the system into unfair or fragile decisions.
Proactive Misinformation Forecasting via Incremental Topic Detection and Sentiment PolarizationWWW
uses Forecast misinformation by tracking how sentiment diverges rapidly within emerging topics, using that divergence as an early warning signal.
why it works Polarization creates an echo chamber where misinformation spreads; high divergence means opposing camps, which correlates with how unverified claims propagate, so measuring divergence gives you a predictive edge before false claims take hold.
Fine-Grained Traceability for Transparent ML PipelinesWWW
uses Compute a score showing how much each sample contributed to the model's decisions, anchored to verifiable checkpoints.
why it works It works because when you track how each data point flows through the system and compute its specific contribution score at known checkpoints, you can later verify whether the data was used and was unchanged, making the flow auditable rather than opaque.
From Manipulation to Mistrust: Explaining Diverse Micro-Video Misinformation for Robust Debunking in the WildWWW
uses Classify videos by analyzing both content and external evidence to determine whether manipulation, AI-generation, or out-of-context reuse caused the misinformation.
why it works It works because cross-checking video features against retrieved evidence reveals gaps and contradictions that unmask specific types of deception; different deception types leave distinct fingerprints in content and context.
Does This Button Work? Investigating YouTube's Ineffective User ControlsWWW
uses Quantify how similar unwanted recommendations are to content users explicitly rejected, measuring whether feedback controls actually prevent similar items.
why it works It works because similarity is a meaningful proxy for whether a recommendation actually honors user feedback; if controls fail to prevent similar content reappearing, the gap between user expectation and platform behavior is quantifiable.
From Native Memes to Global Moderation: Cross-Cultural Evaluation of Vision–Language Models for Hateful Meme DetectionWWW
uses Test how well hate-detection models work across different cultures and languages, revealing bias toward Western interpretations.
why it works It works because models trained on Western data absorb Western meanings. By measuring performance separately per culture and prompting in native languages, you expose how much detection relies on cultural cues the model never saw, revealing when translation erases meaning.
Verifiable Federated Representation Learning for Cross-domain Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Learn user representations that separate what behavior is shared across platforms from what is unique to each, preserving privacy while enabling transfer.
why it works It works because users behave consistently across platforms in some ways and consistently differently in others. Teasing apart shared patterns from domain-specific ones lets you transfer knowledge—cross-platform insights—without leaking domain-specific data or trusting dishonest servers.
Concept-Grounded Detection of Vaccine Misinformation in Multimodal Content Using Interpretable Vision-Language ModelsWWW
uses Extract structured concepts (symbols representing visual and rhetorical ideas) from images, then train a transparent model on those concepts to detect vaccine misinfo.
why it works It works because concepts are interpretable—you can see exactly which visual cues (a syringe plus angry face plus text warning) triggered a detection. By grounding detection in human-understandable concepts rather than opaque scores, you get decisions you can audit and explain, making mistakes obvious and correctable.
Emergence of Structural Disparities in the Web of Scientific CitationsWWW
uses Models how biases in who cites whom compound over time, concentrating recognition among some authors.
why it works Works because homophily and preferential attachment are well-established mechanisms; their combination explains present inequality and why representation alone won't fix it.
Re-understanding Graph Unlearning through MemorizationWWW
uses Assesses how hard it is to unlearn each piece of data, then adjusts the removal strategy based on difficulty.
why it works Works because memorization difficulty varies; easy-to-forget items need less effort, hard ones need special techniques.
Enhancing Domain-Adaptive Hashing via Evidential Learning and Progressive AlignmentWWW
uses Handles noisy labels by assigning uncertainty scores, then gradually aligns cross-domain data by trustiness.
why it works Works because uncertainty scores reveal which labels are likely wrong; progressively trusting aligned samples avoids compounding errors.
KEGOD: Kernel-enhanced Latent Substructure Learning for Graph Out-Of-Distribution DetectionWWW
uses Detects unusual graphs by finding inconsistency between what neural and similarity function methods say about structure.
why it works Works because in-distribution graphs show consistent structure from multiple angles; out-of-distribution breaks that agreement.
Blockchain-Enabled, W3C Standards-Compliant Decentralized Zero-Knowledge Proof Framework for Mobile Identity AuthenticationWWW
uses Proves user identity by checking a mathematical signature without revealing the user's secret key, using discrete logarithm hard problems.
why it works If only the user knows the secret key, only they can generate signatures that pass the mathematical check; the check's security rests on a problem so hard it can't be inverted, making forgery impossible.
How Human Experts Educate Specialized LLMs: Filling Knowledge Gaps in KG-Augmented Generation through Hallucination DetectionWWW
uses Trains a specialized model on expert knowledge while detecting when the model makes up false facts, accepting expert answers for uncertain cases and model answers when confident.
why it works Models sometimes hallucinate; if you can detect when the model is guessing versus confident, you can trust its confident answers and fall back to experts only when needed, minimizing costly expert involvement while keeping quality high.
SecureSplit: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Split LearningWWW
uses Defends against poisoned data by transforming numeric fingerprints to make poisoned samples stick out, then voting to remove them based on majority agreement.
why it works Poisoned samples are rare and different; transforming to make those differences obvious, then using majority voting as a robustness check, filters them out because a single poison can't outweigh the majority of clean data.
Can LLMs Fool Graph Learning? Exploring Universal Adversarial Attacks on Text-Attributed GraphsWWW
uses Crafts graph and text perturbations that fool both systems that learn from examples and language model detectors simultaneously.
why it works It works because shared reasoning patterns exist between different architectures. Finding perturbations that exploit those shared patterns breaks multiple models at once by targeting their common knowledge.
FairGU: Fairness-aware Graph Unlearning in Social NetworksWWW
uses Remove a person's influence from a network graph while ensuring protected characteristics stay fair and accurate.
why it works When you delete someone from a graph, their connections vanish—the method works by carefully rewiring what remains so that sensitive attributes don't accidentally become over-represented or exposed. Fairness protection requires identifying what would have happened naturally versus what shifted only because they left, then adjusting for that difference.
SemFuzz: A Semantics-Aware Fuzzing Framework for Network Protocol ImplementationsWWW
uses Test network protocols by finding rule-breaking test cases and checking if responses match what the rules say should happen.
why it works Protocol rules are written in language; when you extract rules precisely and then generate test cases that break them on purpose, violations become obvious—you spot bugs because expected output mismatches actual output. The method works because deep semantic flaws show up as discrepancies, not just crashes.
Shift-Resilient Diffusive Imputation for Variable Subset ForecastingWWW
uses Predict future time series values from incomplete data by decomposing patterns into steady parts and changing parts, then handling each separately.
why it works Real time series split into two layers: correlations between sensors that stay stable over months, and sudden shifts within each sensor across windows. By decomposing these, you can impute the stable part reliably while treating volatility honestly—the steady correlations guide missing values, and the volatile parts adjust for shifts independently.
DAPWeb: Construct-Aligned Evaluation of MLLMs for Web-Based Child Mental ScreeningWWW
uses Evaluate whether AI systems can reliably interpret children's drawings as mental health screening by testing consistency across psychological constructs and drawing samples.
why it works Construct validity means the system measures what it claims to measure—if an AI says a drawing shows anxiety, that conclusion should hold across different drawings of the same child and match human experts. Testing consistency and construct alignment reveals whether the system has learned real psychological patterns or just surface correlations.
Audit?of?Audits for the Web: Bayesian Meta?Evaluation that Yields Interval?Valued, Threshold?Aligned Fairness ClaimsWWW
uses Pool multiple fairness audits using Bayesian inference to produce interval-based fairness claims that express uncertainty and align with regulatory thresholds.
why it works Different audits disagree due to sampling noise and metric choice—Bayesian pooling treats each audit as an imperfect measurement and combines them into a updated chance distribution, which gives intervals capturing true uncertainty. Soft constraints ensure that fine-grained and coarse-grained audits stay consistent, and uncertainty quantifies the auditor's collective confidence.
Matrix as Plan: Structured Logical Reasoning with Feedback-Driven ReplanningWWW
uses Improve logical reasoning in language models by representing reasoning as a grid of numbers plan that can be verified and repaired when steps are wrong.
why it works Chain-of-thought reasoning is fragile—parsing breaks when wording shifts slightly. A grid of numbers representation makes dependencies explicit and queryable, so verification can spot missing or circular steps. Feedback-driven replanning then rewrites the grid of numbers to fix errors, replacing brittle parsing with editable structure.
Real or Rogue? Detecting Malicious Miniapps with Deceptive Reporting InterfaceWWW
uses Detect malicious miniapps that fake the report interface to prevent users from reporting them by learning what legitimate reporting interfaces look like.
why it works A legitimate report interface has consistent visual and behavioral patterns that differ from fakes; malicious ones either discard reports silently or redirect them. Identifying these patterns from millions of interface examples lets the system score and flag lookalikes before they deceive users.
LLM and AI Agent: Golden Rule is All We NeedWWW
uses Derive ethical principles for autonomous systems and human behavior by formalizing the Golden Rule—treating others as you wish to be treated—in game theory.
why it works The Golden Rule works because reciprocity creates stable equilibria: if everyone treats others as they wish to be treated, betrayal becomes costly and cooperation thrives. Game theory formalizes this—mutual fairness and honesty emerge as solutions that maximize collective welfare while respecting individual preferences.
Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Detects anomalous text at the word level by learning to assign each word an anomaly score, locating the specific parts of a text that deviate from expected patterns.
why it works Anomalies are words that appear in combinations or contexts the model learned are rare or wrong. Scoring each word independently lets you find exactly which parts break the learned pattern, whereas document-level scoring obscures which words caused the signal.
Beyond Denial-of-Service: The Puppeteer's Attack for Fine-Grained Control in Ranking-Based Federated LearningWWW
uses Manipulates rankings submitted by a corrupted participant to steer a global ranking system toward attacker-chosen outcomes while preserving the statistical appearance of normal convergence.
why it works Ranking systems aggregate discrete orderings, which appear opaque to change detection. By strategically flipping which items rank above or below others, an attacker can shift the aggregate consensus without changing the magnitude of any single update, evading statistical guardrails.
Unsupervised Dense Retrieval with Conterfactual Contrastive LearningWSDM
uses Trains retrieval models to be robust by comparing documents where relevant passages are altered against versions where irrelevant passages are altered, measuring sensitivity to changes in what actually matters.
why it works Causality says relevant passages cause the relevance judgment. If a model's output barely changes when you alter irrelevant passages but shifts dramatically when you alter key passages, the model has learned which parts actually matter. This causality-grounded robustness resists tricks that fake relevance.
Causality with Knowledge Graphs: Semantics and InferenceWSDM
uses Discovers and reasons about cause-effect relationships directly from knowledge graphs by respecting their ontological structure and handling incomplete information.
why it works Knowledge graphs encode what entities are known to be related. Causal reasoning requires knowing what was actually measured versus what is simply missing. Ontologies clarify semantic categories, so causal inference respects real distinctions (a 'side effect' is different from an 'unrelated symptom') instead of treating all relationships alike.
Can LLMs Uphold Research Integrity? Evaluating the Role of LLMs in Peer Review QualityWSDM
uses Evaluates whether language models can assess the quality and factual accuracy of peer reviews by checking if reviewer claims are actually supported by the paper being reviewed.
why it works Review quality depends on whether a reviewer's criticisms point to real claims in the paper. Verification requires checking which statements in the review are grounded in the paper versus which are unsupported opinions. Models succeed when they distinguish what the paper actually says from what a reviewer claimed it says.
DagFC: Dependency-Aware Fact-Checking via Claim-Constructed Knowledge Graphs and Large Language ModelsWSDM
uses Decomposes a complex claim into simpler sub-claims, maps their dependencies as a graph, then verifies each sub-claim while propagating results through the dependency structure to catch reasoning that spans multiple steps.
why it works Complex claims have sub-claims that build on each other; isolating and verifying each one alone misses how earlier conclusions enable later ones. By tracking the flow of reasoning through dependencies, the method captures multi-step logic that a single claim cannot.
From Perception to Share: Understanding Misinformation Through User Believability and Linguistic AmbivalenceWSDM
uses Measures how believable users find news claims, models the linguistic conflicts and mixed emotions in text, then uses both as signals in a graph model to separate false claims from true ones.
why it works Misinformation often contains tension between incompatible frames or emotions that signal deception; by capturing both human credibility judgments and the presence of linguistic conflict, the model exploits two independent truths that both point toward falsehood.
From Data to Model in Bias: A Statistical Analysis of Political Bias in the C4 Corpus and Its Impact on LLMsWSDM
uses Analyzes the political slant in a large web corpus using persona-based annotation and statistical tests, then measures whether the bias in the data propagates into model outputs through training.
why it works If bias enters models only through the data they learn from, then corpus bias and model bias should correlate; by checking this correlation and testing statistical equivalence, the method proves that the training data is the cause.
Explaining the 'Unexplainable' Large Language ModelsWSDM
uses Show which concepts inside a language model actually drive its answers, instead of pointing to correlations that happen to co-occur but don't cause output.
why it works It works because intervening on true causal concepts (changing what the model thinks, not just its activation patterns) proves what actually steers the answer. Correlations vanish under intervention but causes remain.
Design and Evaluation of Whole-Page Experience Optimization for E-commerce SearchWSDM
uses Rank items on complex 2D search layouts by learning which combinations of position and item features lead to long-term user satisfaction, not just clicks.
why it works It works because causal frameworks separate correlation from actual influence; by using quasi-experiments, you avoid false signals like confounding that short-term clicks might hide.
Identifiable Disentangled Representation Learning for Causal Inference under Network InterferenceWSDM
uses Estimate individual treatment effects on a network by learning three types of hidden factors: which help assign treatment, which confuse treatment with outcome, and which adjust for networks.
why it works It works because treatment effects are biased by confounders and spillover; separating hidden factors lets you identify which are true confounders versus which are just network side effects.
ChorusCVR: Chorus Supervision for Entire Space Post-Click Conversion Rate ModelingWSDM
uses Estimate whether a user will convert after clicking by treating un-clicked items and clicked-but-not-converted items differently, since they have different meanings.
why it works It works because un-clicked items are merely unknown while clicked-non-conversions are true negatives, so treating them as the same misleads the model into thinking absence of action means the same thing as action-followed-by-rejection.
Risk-Aware Utility Re-Ranking for Financial Asset RecommendationWSDM
uses Rank financial assets by expected value accounting for risk and how likely a user is to take each recommendation, then adjust to trade a little ranking quality for better real-world returns.
why it works It works because a perfect ranking that users ignore is worthless and a ranking that delivers losses is harmful—balancing adoption probability and risk tolerance yields real value, not theoretical rank order.
Debias Once for All: A Data-Centric Strategy for Fair Machine LearningWSDM
uses Make a machine learning model fair by rewriting its training data to come from a synthetic fair dataset instead of changing the model itself.
why it works It works because unfairness lives in the data—historical bias encoded in patterns—so fixing data upstream of any model makes all downstream models fair by default, whereas model-specific fixes break portability.
On Causal and Anticausal LLM-based Data SynthesisWSDM
uses Generate raw diverse data first, then label it, versus the reversed approach of baking labels into generation prompts.
why it works The causal order mirrors real data creation: facts exist first, then we label them. This avoids the backward approach where labels distort generation, which makes the model overfit to label-specific patterns instead of learning genuine variety.
KnowFC: Navigating Knowledge Conflicts in Large Language Model-based Fact-CheckingWSDM
uses Learn when a language model should trust its built-in knowledge versus external evidence, then build reasoning chains that prevent conflicting knowledge from derailing fact-checking.
why it works It works because confidence is not truth. By identifying where a model's internal knowledge is reliable versus where it's overconfident, you can rely on evidence when the model is weak and trust itself when the evidence is weak, rather than always fighting between them.
Joint Graph Learning for Robust Causal Inference over Knowledge GraphsWSDM
uses Fill in missing attributes and estimate treatment effects by modeling how entities influence each other in the knowledge graph structure.
why it works It works because missing data and causal effects are not independent problems. Using the relational structure to infer missing attributes helps the model understand connections between entities, which then allows it to account for how one entity's treatment ripples through related entities.
CelebCaption: A Benchmark Dataset for Identity-Sensitive Unlearning in Image CaptioningWSDM
uses Measure whether unlearning methods actually remove a specific person's influence from image captions or just hide it with false information.
why it works It works because true unlearning is different from obfuscation. If you test with varied captions, controlled presence and absence of names, and measure both generation quality and susceptibility to membership attacks, you can tell if the model genuinely forgot versus just learned to deny.
Planning Before Retrieval: A Constrained Planner–Executor Framework for Reliable and Efficient KG-Augmented ReasoningWSDM
uses Plan structured queries over a knowledge graph by reasoning about which constraints and connections matter for answering a question.
why it works Real-world knowledge is connected through relationships — knowing which relationships matter and in what order to follow them turns a chaotic search into a directed path. Planning first ensures you only retrieve what actually answers the question, filtering out coincidental connections.
Geo-Personalization Bias in News Search: Analyzing Filter Bubbles in Search Engine Results with Multi-Perspective LLM AnnotationWSDM
uses Analyze search results across locations and time to measure how geographic personalization, local events, and topic traits shape filter bubbles.
why it works Filter bubbles aren't random — they're systematic patterns caused by specific factors. By controlling which factors vary (location one time, topic another time) and measuring the result each time, you isolate what actually causes each bubble, separating real effects from coincidence.
Constructing Commonsense Knowledge Graph for Persona ConsistencyWSDM
uses Builds a commonsense graph encoding which statements agree or conflict with a persona, then identifies and rewrites AI responses that contradict the established persona.
why it works It works because persona conflicts are rooted in semantic meaning, not just surface text. A knowledge graph captures which ideas logically belong together; checking responses against it catches indirect contradictions that keyword matching misses.
Bridge Breaking for Graph Neural NetworksWSDM
uses Identifies bridge nodes that connect unlike classes in networks, then aggregates their neighborhoods differently to prevent the smoothing that causes misclassification.
why it works It works because bridge nodes sit at boundaries where smoothing is wrong—averaging across different classes doesn't help. By detecting these critical nodes and treating them specially, you preserve the sharp distinctions that matter for classification.
Enhanced Cold-Start Sequential Recommendation with Causal Diffusion Preference ModelingWSDM
uses Generates preference patterns for new users by identifying causal interactions in historical sequences, then using those patterns to initialize sequential recommendation models.
why it works It works because not all past interactions drive future behavior equally—some are noise. Causal analysis isolates the interactions that truly shape preference; generating representations from only those signals gives new users a head start grounded in real drivers.
Uncertainty Quantification for Dynamical NetworksWSDM
uses Quantify uncertainty in network predictions by estimating how much unknown structure, noisy parameters, and random fluctuations change the system's future behavior.
why it works It works because real networks have hidden pieces and noise; uncertainty quantification asks 'how wrong could we be?' By measuring how sensitive predictions are to what we don't know, we learn which unknowns actually matter and build stronger forecasts.
Credibility Drift Attacks: LLM Crafted Adversarial Manipulations That Flip News BelievabilityWSDM
uses Make minimal, targeted edits to news stories that subtly change causal claims and qualifying facts, shifting perceived credibility while avoiding obvious tampering.
why it works It works because humans evaluate credibility through causal reasoning—does the evidence support the claim? Removing a qualifier or reversing causality breaks that chain invisibly. Small changes fool readers because they alter the logical structure beneath the surface, not the words themselves.
Self-Paced Fair Ranking with Loss as a Proxy for BiasWSDM
uses Score items to rank them, but learn to prioritize examples with low errors while gradually introducing harder cases, reducing gender bias without explicit demographic labels.
why it works It works because easier examples teach the model the right patterns first, and gradually adding harder cases prevents it from memorizing biased shortcuts. By filtering through how confidently the model scores each example, you can detect when gender bias is causing errors and correct it.
Confounder-Aware Causal Graph Learning Framework for Multivariate Time Series AnalysisWSDM
uses Build causal relationships between time-series variables at two scales (whole sequences and local segments), modeling hidden confounders with dedicated variables rather than assuming all causes are observed.
why it works It works because real data has unmeasured causes affecting multiple variables at once. By explicitly representing these hidden causes with special variables, then solving for what they must be from the patterns you see, you can untangle which relationships are truly causal versus merely correlated.
Improving Interpretability of Cognitive Diagnosis Models with LLM-based Semantic AugmentationSIGIR
uses Predict student mastery by analyzing not just right or wrong, but which specific answer students chose, using language models to infer what misconception each wrong answer represents.
why it works It works because different wrong answers reveal different misconceptions. By mapping each answer to the specific idea gap it represents, you move from a crude right/wrong signal to precise diagnosis, enabling targeted teaching rather than generic feedback.
Mitigating Adversarial Attacks by Transferring LLM-generated Narrative Reasoning for Robust Fake News DetectionSIGIR
uses Use a language model to spot consistent stories in how fake news spreads, then teach a graph algorithm to ignore isolated conflicting information and weight the coherent thread.
why it works Fake news attacks introduce noise meant to confuse the aggregator. By aligning everything to a consistent global narrative first, you make the aggregator robust to random noise.
Diagnosing Identifiability in Two-Tower Models for Unbiased Learning to RankSIGIR
uses Test whether a model's ability to distinguish relevance from position bias is actually coming from the data by perturbing the parameters and checking if performance drops.
why it works A parameter that can be moved without hurting prediction is not constrained by the data; you cannot identify it. Measuring sensitivity reveals which parameters the data actually pins down.
FollowTable: A Benchmark for Instruction-Following Table RetrievalSIGIR
uses Rank tables by relevance when users include both topic constraints and fine-grained schema requirements like column semantics and value ranges, not topic alone.
why it works It works because relevance is multidimensional: a table may be topically perfect but structurally wrong (wrong columns, wrong granularity). By ranking jointly on topic and schema satisfaction, the model distinguishes topical matches that are useless from those that actually fit the user's intent. Instructions reveal causal constraints, not coincidental patterns.
Multi-Perspective Driven Expected Location Preferences for Next POI RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Predict next POI by modeling real preferences separately from contextual behaviors, and inferring where users actually intended versus settled for.
why it works It works because visit data mixes genuine preference with circumstance — work locations skew behavior — so filtering out external causes leaves true preferences to predict future choices accurately.
Beyond Semantic Relevance: Counterfactual Risk Minimization for Robust Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Score retrieved documents by how well they steer a model toward correct answers even when queries are adversarially biased, using causal intervention to identify true evidence.
why it works It works because causal intervention reveals which documents genuinely cause correct answers versus which only happen to be similar. By testing documents against perturbed queries that contain cognitive biases, you identify evidence that works for the right reasons, not just cases where the bias and truth align.
Decoding Multimodal Cues: Unveiling the Implicit Meaning Behind Hateful VideosSIGIR
uses Identify hateful content by weighing different harmful elements (images, words, sounds) together and explaining which parts caused the decision.
why it works It works because hate content is multimodal—harmful elements in different forms reinforce each other. By learning which elements matter and why, you separate genuine reasons for flagging from noise, and humans can verify your reasoning is sound.
OntoEL: Neuro-Symbolic Biomedical Entity Linking with Differentiable Fuzzy EL&#8869; ReasoningSIGIR
uses Match medical entity names to their true identities using learned nearness in a space, then recheck each match against logical rules that describe what's valid.
why it works It works because entity synonyms cluster together when you measure them as nearness; soft rule-checking then filters out candidates that logically contradict the context, eliminating ambiguity that pure similarity alone would miss.
Hierarchical Denoising Entire Space Multi-Task Model for Post-Click Conversion Rate Prediction with Noisy LabelsSIGIR
uses Predict if a user will convert after clicking by fixing the mistakes that arise when training data is corrupted by noise from multiple stages.
why it works It works because noise compounds across stages: noisy clicks plus noisy conversions create a mess. Explicitly modeling and correcting for this hierarchical noise makes loss estimates honest again, so the model learns true patterns instead of noise.
Do Simulated Users Need to Remember? Analyzing the Impact of Memory Models in Conversational Search EvaluationSIGIR
uses Simulate users during multi-turn search to test systems, varying whether the simulator remembers past interactions or forgets them.
why it works It works because simulated user behavior must match real patterns to produce trustworthy rankings. Memory affects how queries change across turns; capturing the right memory model makes simulation predictions match what real users would do.
SciCheck: Reasoning Distillation for Biomedical Claim VerificationSIGIR
uses Verify medical claims by adjust a small model on reasoning examples from a large model, trained to mimic correct reasoning paths only.
why it works It works because reasoning can be distilled. If you capture the reasoning steps that lead to correct verdicts and filter out wrong ones, a smaller model learns the decision rules without needing the original large model or perfect evidence.
An Epistemic Position-Based Click Model: From Interactions to Epistemic Distributions of Relevance and BiasSIGIR
uses Estimates ranges of uncertainty around click probabilities by modeling how strongly relevance and screen position each influence whether a user clicks.
why it works It works because observed clicks are shaped by two separate forces: how good the item really is and where it appeared on screen. Uncertainty ranges reveal which factors are well-understood versus which are guesses, making predictions more trustworthy.
Tokens to Types: Context Editing with Selective Entity Abstraction for Grounded GenerationSIGIR
uses Silences misleading background knowledge in language models by replacing entity names with abstract type labels before generation, so the model must rely on provided context rather than learned starting guess associations.
why it works It works because language models have strong learned associations between names and facts from training data, which can overpower new information. Replacing names with generic labels blocks those spurious lexical paths while preserving the relational structure needed to reason about the new scenario.
Mining Informative Interests via Latent Cross Reasoning for Search Enhanced RecommendationSIGIR
uses Identifies which past searches genuinely reveal recommendation intent by filtering noisy signals in a learned hidden space, then using only those reliable searches to recommend items.
why it works It works because users search for many things—some show true preference for item types, others are outdated or off-topic. By learning to recognize which signals align with genuine recommendation needs, it avoids spurious correlations that would degrade predictions.
Mitigating Structural Overfitting: A Distribution-Aware Rectification Framework for Missing Feature ImputationSIGIR
uses Fills missing user features using learned feature patterns and graph structure, then corrects distribution shift at test time by projecting distorted features back onto the true learned pattern.
why it works It works because missing values can be inferred from neighbors and learned patterns, but the model may overfit to structural peculiarities during training. By learning the true underlying feature surface and realigning at test time, you recover natural semantic diversity and handle new graph structures correctly.
Looking for the Bottleneck in Fine-grained Temporal Relation ClassificationSIGIR
uses Classifies relationships between events in text by first determining point relationships between time boundaries, then decoding those point relationships into interval relationships.
why it works It works because interval relationships are complex and rare in data, making direct learning hard. Point relationships between endpoints are simpler and more frequent, so learning those first provides reliable intermediate structure that combines naturally into the final answer.
RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learns drug recommendations by reasoning through patient cases, then adjusts to balance cure likelihood against each person's individual drug risks.
why it works It works because showing the reasoning path grounds recommendations in clinical logic, and personalizing safety tolerances respects that different patients have different risk profiles that affect what counts as safe.
Inductive Subgraphs as Shortcuts: Causal Disentanglement for Heterophilic Graph LearningSIGIR
uses Identifies which connections between nodes in a graph are real causal relationships versus accidental correlations caused by misleading subpatterns.
why it works It works because some subgraph patterns appear frequently but mislead the model; explicitly tracing causal paths versus spurious paths lets you ignore the false correlations and learn only from genuine signal.
HCPRA: A Hierarchical Cognition-Perception-Reasoning Agent Framework for Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in ConversationsSIGIR
uses Reconstructs why someone feels an emotion in conversation by tracking what the speaker knows, perceives, and reasons through.
why it works It works because emotions don't come from nowhere; modeling the speaker's knowledge and mental steps lets you trace the actual causal chain from situation to feeling.
PurifAI: Detecting and Fixing Search-Induced Distortions in Web-Augmented LLMsSIGIR
uses Detects web search results that conflict with trusted internal knowledge and prevents them from overriding the verified facts.
why it works It works because truth has a source; when web content contradicts known-good internal sources, the contradiction itself signals danger, and blocking those results preserves accuracy.
Exploration-and-Thinking: Agentic Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs via an LLM-RL Synergized FrameworkSIGIR
uses The system learns to explore knowledge graph paths efficiently while scoring which paths lead to correct answers, then discards paths that look right but actually contradict the facts.
why it works It works because reasoning is a search through possibilities. By coupling path exploration with learning what real evidence looks like and penalizing false leads, the system avoids following coincidental patterns and focuses on genuinely valid reasoning chains.
Debiased Recommendation Beyond the Positive Propensity AssumptionSIGIR
uses The method estimates how likely each product-user pair is to interact, then corrects for the fact that some pairs (like distant restaurants) were never shown to users and thus never clicked—deriving bounds on correct answer probabilities.
why it works It works because selection bias—the data only shows what was chosen to show—breaks standard probability estimates. By identifying unrealistic pairs and deriving upper bounds on what their true interaction rates could be, you can debiase the learning without complete information.
Unified Entity Matching under Scarce Supervision via Meta-Rule Induction and RetrievalSIGIR
uses Extract matching rules from limited labeled examples, cluster rules into reusable patterns, then retrieve the most relevant pattern for each new entity pair to guide scoring.
why it works It works because explicit rules are more transferable than learned weights alone. Grouping rules by pattern lets you identify which rule actually applies to a new case, and rule-guided scoring is more robust than hoping adjust captured the right behavior from scarce data.
CoMCo: Consistency-Aware Multi-Agent Coordination for Zero-Shot Cross-Modal Entity MatchingSIGIR
uses Iteratively rank image-entity matches using multiple scoring signals, enforce that related entities get consistent matches, and only call expensive reasoning for ambiguous pairs.
why it works It works because global consistency (enforcing that related items match coherently) catches mistakes that local ranking would miss. The system exploits the constraint that if item A matches product X and item B is related to A, then B should relate to X too.
FairSpec: Expert Specialization for Fair LLM-based RecommendationSIGIR
uses Train separate expert models for recommendation quality and fairness, route each input to the appropriate expert via a learned router, and optimize both objectives jointly.
why it works It works because fairness and utility compete when baked into a single model, but separate experts let you suppress sensitive attributes in one expert without corrupting preference learning in the other. The router learns when to trust each expert.
How Far Are We from Automatically Identifying Violations of the Data Minimization Principle in Privacy Policies?SIGIR
uses Extract privacy practices from policy text, classify violations into types (inherent vs. contextual), then compare practices against patterns mined from compliant policies to flag anomalies.
why it works It works because compliance patterns from many compliant policies form a baseline of what practices typically match a stated purpose. Violations are contexts where a practice deviates significantly from the baseline or contradicts what the service needs, which becomes detectable when you have the pattern.
Towards Conflict-aware Selective Knowledge Unlearning for Continual Few-shot Knowledge Graph CompletionSIGIR
uses Forget which old facts conflict with new ones in a growing knowledge base, then update entity relationships by learning what changed.
why it works It works because removing contradictory knowledge lets the model update its internal state of what entities are like without getting stuck in old, wrong assumptions. The progressive unlearning prevents the model from averaging together conflicting beliefs.
Privacy Preserving Information Retrieval: Defining Privacy Research Pillars for a Future Research AgendaSIGIR
uses Define the research questions and safeguards needed so information access systems do not leak personal data when users search and retrieve.
why it works It works because thinking clearly about what each privacy threat means and where data flows makes interventions concrete and measurable rather than vague. The framework exposes gaps between what we think we're protecting and what we actually are.
Deletion Isn't Enough: Auditing RAG for Selective ForgettingSIGIR
uses Test whether removed facts still leak into generated answers even though the documents containing them were deleted from the retrieval system.
why it works It works because compliance looks at two separate channels: whether forbidden documents are retrieved, and whether their facts appear in answers anyway. Checking both reveals that deleting records is not enough if the model learned the fact during training.
Evaluation Validity in Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Decide whether metric improvements on benchmarks actually mean users experience better results in the real world.
why it works It works because not all measurement is valid: you can improve a metric while degrading the real experience if the metric measures the wrong thing. Checking that the metric correlates with what users actually want ensures progress is real, not statistical.
The Relevance of (Relevant) Entity PresenceSIGIR
uses Learn to rank documents by scoring how relevant entities are to the query, but detect when the model is secretly using knowledge it shouldn't have.
why it works Ranking by relevance score works because good scores put matching items first. But the deeper issue here is telling whether the score comes from the document text itself or from seeing which entities appear in known-relevant examples—separating the real signal from data leakage.
Mind the Metric: Reproducibility and Fair Benchmarking of Spectral Graph Models for Collaborative FilteringSIGIR
uses Use frequency-space filtering to separate true preferences from noise in user-item histories, then test if those improvements really hold under fair conditions.
why it works Frequency filtering works because user preferences and random noise occupy different frequency bands—high frequency = noise, low frequency = true preference patterns. But the study reveals some published results inflated this benefit through metric errors, showing the method only truly works in certain conditions.
The Powerless Noise: How Experimental Settings Shape the Reported Power of NoiseSIGIR
uses Test whether adding random irrelevant text to retrieval-augmented generation actually helps question-answering, or whether the effect vanishes under different settings and model versions.
why it works The claimed benefit of noise hinges on specific prompt formats and decoding constraints in older models. Changing prompts or allowing longer outputs makes the effect disappear, showing the benefit wasn't a deep property of the retrieval-generation interaction but an artifact of those particular experimental choices.
From Top-1 to Top-K: A Reproducibility Study and Benchmarking of Counterfactual Explanations for Recommender SystemsSIGIR
uses Explain a recommendation by finding the smallest changes to user-item history that would flip the recommendation, testing if these explanations hold across different recommender models.
why it works Counterfactual explanations work because they isolate causation: if changing X flips the outcome, then X is causal. Finding minimal changes avoids spurious correlations. Testing across model types reveals whether the explanation truly points to causes or just artifacts of one model's quirks.
KCC: Korean Civil Case Dataset for Legal Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Rank legal cases by combining factual similarity to the query case with legal reasoning principles, using expert-annotated relevance judgments.
why it works It works because legal relevance depends on two separable things: does this case involve similar facts, and does the legal reasoning apply? Scoring each independently then combining them captures both the similarity that matters and the reasoning connection.
GONets: A First-Look Into GitHub Organisation NetworksSIGIR
uses Represent open-source collaboration as a network of users connected to repositories; analyze patterns of contribution and code reuse diffusion through the network structure.
why it works It works because contribution patterns form a network where proximity (users in the same organization or sharing repos) predicts future collaboration. Information and code spread along edges; analyzing the network structure reveals how influence and reuse propagate.
The Alignment Gap: A Benchmark Demonstrating the Lack of Cross-Lingual Mapping in Dialect-Specialized Language Models - The Case of EhugboSIGIR
uses Measure how well language models align meanings across languages by placing Ehugbo queries and English documents in a shared space; compare global vs. regional models.
why it works It works because if two meanings are equivalent across languages, they should occupy the same region in a carefully trained space. Models trained on diverse language pairs learn this alignment; regional models, despite understanding each language well, lack the translation bridges to map between them.
A Dataset of Cultural Heritage Manipulation on English Wikipedia in the Russo-Ukrainian ContextSIGIR
uses Analyze Wikipedia edit pairs to detect subtle narrative shifts in cultural attribution and agency; identify cumulative patterns of framing change.
why it works It works because comparing before-and-after text reveals intentional changes: what words were added, removed, or reframed. Subtle manipulation appears as consistent directional changes across many edits. Aggregating patterns across revisions exposes coordinated narrative shifts that individual edits might hide.
RRE-GTC: A Geo-Temporal Cluster Dataset for Real-Estate Price Estimation and Market-Aware SearchSIGIR
uses Rank real-estate listings using geo-temporal price clusters combined with transport accessibility; use linear attribution to separate location value from intrinsic property quality.
why it works It works because real-estate price depends on separable factors: intrinsic property features and location premium. A linear model that explains price variation via these factors lets you isolate how much value comes from each. Ranking by combined features surfaces listings matching buyer preferences.
A Sensitivity-Aware Test Collection for Search Among Personal InformationSIGIR
uses Retrieve relevant emails while withholding ones marked as containing sensitive personal information.
why it works It works because relevance and sensitivity are two separate properties that must both be scored independently, and only returning results that rank high on relevance AND low on sensitivity lets you deliver useful information without exposing privacy.
PeerPrism: Peer Evaluation Expertise vs Review-writing AISIGIR
uses Detect whether peer review text was written by a human, an AI, or came from a hybrid collaboration where ideas are human but writing is AI.
why it works It works because authorship has two sources—intellectual ideas and surface writing—and by treating them as separate features rather than a binary, detectors can score each independently and reveal when ideas are sound but expression is alien.
From Single- to Cross-Document: Benchmarking Multi-Granularity Event Analysis of Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Predicts what event comes next in a story and infers which events cause which, tracing the path of one incident across multiple documents.
why it works It works because causality has structure: causes come before effects and appear in related documents, so showing how one event reliably triggers others reveals the true causal chain.
EVADE-Bench: Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating and Enhancing Evasive Content DetectionSIGIR
uses Learns to detect when product text or images are trying to hide rule violations through disguise, scoring how likely each piece is hiding something.
why it works It works because intent leaves traces: words chosen to deceive follow patterns, and images cropped to hide things show consistent cropping marks; these patterns reveal what is intentionally obscured.
SimEval-IR: A Unified Toolkit and Benchmark Suite for Evaluating User Simulators and Search SessionsSIGIR
uses Tests fake users by how realistically they click on results and how accurately their behavior predicts which search system is better.
why it works It works because realistic behavior and valid system rankings are separate properties; resemblance to real clicks is only useful if it actually identifies which system truly works better.
Scalable K-Means Guided Partitioning for Block-based Sparse Document RetrievalSIGIR
uses Cluster sparse documents efficiently using a balanced K-means-guided bisection that groups similar lists of numbers together.
why it works It works because similar lists of numbers (measured by proximity in the sparse space) tend to be relevant for the same queries. Clustering groups these naturally-similar documents so retrieval only needs to search a few clusters instead of all documents, cutting search time dramatically.
ExODRec: An Explainable Framework for Outlier Detection Model RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learn to predict how well each candidate model will perform on a new dataset by training on past datasets where we know both the model's success and the dataset's characteristics.
why it works This works because if different datasets have patterns in what makes them hard or easy, and models have consistent strengths and weaknesses, then studying past successes teaches you which model traits match which dataset traits. You never need to run the models—just predict from the patterns you've seen.
Attend to Fragments: How Key Information Affects Large Language Models for Factual Inconsistency DetectionSIGIR
uses Detect when a language model is checking a claim by identifying whether it's actually reading the relevant evidence or just fixating on repeated words, filtering unreliable detections.
why it works Language models often rely on keywords instead of logic. If shuffling sentence order breaks the model but the answer stays the same, it proves the model isn't reasoning from content. Filtering those cases improves accuracy because you eliminate decisions made for wrong reasons.
Towards Emotional Intelligence in Conversational AI: How Well Can LLMs Recognise Emotion in Conversations?SIGIR
uses Compare language model emotion labels to human annotations across conversation contexts, measuring agreement and studying which cases the model handles well or poorly.
why it works If language models are to replace annotators, they must match human judgment reliably. Measuring disagreement reveals whether the model is learning emotion recognition or just mimicking surface patterns. Context tests show whether the model understands emotional flow or treats each turn alone.
Failing Forward: Understanding Query Failure in Retrieval, Judgment, and GenerationSIGIR
uses Measure which queries are hard to retrieve, hard to generate answers for, and hard to judge as correct, finding that the three difficulties are mostly independent.
why it works If difficulty came from just query semantics, the same queries would fail everywhere. But they don't—retrieval struggles with different queries than generation, and judgment struggles differently still. This tells you each task has its own biases, so you can't fix one by fixing another.
Answer First, Evidence Second? Uncovering Hidden Risks in Well-Structured AI Search SummariesSIGIR
uses Measures when summaries match or contradict their cited sources by scoring agreement between summary content and source text similarities.
why it works If evidence truly supports a summary, the main ideas in both should be saying the same things and appearing in the same order. When you measure how much summaries and sources align point-by-point, mismatches reveal where claims drift from what the sources actually say.
Is a Busy Search Agent a Good One? Overthinking and Overretrieval at ScaleSIGIR
uses Counts excessive retrieval and reasoning steps in agent trajectories, then assigns penalty scores to discourage wasteful patterns and guide trajectories toward efficiency.
why it works By measuring exactly what kinds of steps lead to waste (redundant documents, circular reasoning), you can assign a cost that makes those choices less attractive. Agents optimize what you measure; measuring waste directly makes them optimize it away.
Pretraining Exposure Explains Popularity Judgments in Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Measures how many times entities appear in training data (exposure) and compares it to both real-world popularity and the model's stated preferences, showing they align more with exposure than ground truth.
why it works Models learn what the training data emphasizes. If an entity appears frequently in pretraining, the model learns strong associations with it regardless of reality. Exposure captures what's statistically regular in data; aligning to exposure means the model is doing exactly what training shaped it to do.
When RAG Disagrees: Detecting Latent Epistemic Conflict via Logit InteractionsSIGIR
uses Compute a score from model's internal confidence and semantic overlap with retrieved context to predict whether retrieval will help or hurt output.
why it works A model's internal raw scores reveal true confidence separate from text it produces. When retrieved context aligns semantically with raw scores confidence, the model genuinely trusts the context. When they diverge, the model is torn—a sign that retrieval contradicts its learned knowledge. This internal signal detects conflict faster than checking the output.
Numerical Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Detection and AnalysisSIGIR
uses Detect when retrieval-augmented answers invent numbers by checking if generated numbers appear in retrieved documents, flagging fabrications.
why it works Numbers are discrete and traceable—either they're in the source or they're made up. This is different from text hallucinations, which can be paraphrases or rephrasing. A simple check for number presence catches pure fabrication with perfect recall because a made-up number leaves no shadow in the source.
uses Use historical pre-promotion behavior to predict which customers will buy during a promotion, accounting for the fact that pre-purchase browsing shifts to buying later.
why it works Pre-promotion and promotion periods have different user behaviors—before the sale, people add to carts but don't buy. On sale day, they convert. This is a distribution shift that previous models ignore. By learning from historical pre-promotion data that captures this exact shift pattern, the model learns when cart-adding signals future conversion, not immediate purchase.
Separating Wheat from Chaff: Fine-Grained Defenses Against Poisoning in Multi-Perspective RAGSIGIR
uses When retrieving for multi-perspective generation, model how different opinions relate as clusters of agreement so you can tell the difference between a real disagreement and an attack designed to bias the system.
why it works It works because real perspectives on an issue form clusters where many documents agree, while an attack tries to inject a document with hidden bias that stands alone; seeing which documents naturally cluster together reveals the true topology of legitimate disagreement.
CSMAD: Hallucination Detection via Multi-Agent Debate with NLI-Verified Contradictory StatementsSIGIR
uses Multiple independent judges evaluate both a claim and a deliberately constructed opposite claim, then compare their reasoning to decide what is actually true.
why it works It works because disagreement forces each judge to defend their position against direct contradictions, revealing which arguments hold up under scrutiny. When both versions are rejected or both accepted, exchanging reasoning uncovers flawed shared assumptions that isolated judges would miss.
Effective Offline LLM and DNN based Matching, Filtering and Ranking for Search Ads Retrieval in E-CommerceSIGIR
uses Ads are ranked offline using language models to filter by relevance and systems that learn from examples to rank by conversion, ensuring only high-quality candidates reach online systems.
why it works It works because online systems have strict latency limits, so only a tiny fraction of candidates can be scored; offline scoring with powerful models has no speed constraint and can eliminate irrelevant noise beforehand. This frees online systems to focus ranking effort on the best candidates.
Constraint Persistence in Conversational Product SearchSIGIR
uses Constraints users state in conversation are classified (identity, contextual, session) and their relevance is scored when users switch product categories, preserving only the ones that still apply.
why it works It works because not all constraints are equally sticky; an ingredient preference (identity) transfers across product changes, but a temporal one (needed today) doesn't. Scoring relevance per constraint type prevents over-constrained queries (zero results) while respecting user intent.
LLM-Click Agreement: Harmonizing Implicit Feedback and Semantic Judgments for Enterprise SearchSIGIR
uses Supervision for search ranking only uses query-result pairs where both click signals and language model judgments agree, filtering out pairs where they disagree.
why it works It works because clicks are behavioral (people are biased, multitasking) while language model judgments are semantic (pure relevance); agreement means the pair is genuinely good by both lenses. Disagreement often signals label noise, so keeping only agreements trains cleaner models despite having fewer examples.
SID-Coord: Coordinating Semantic IDs for ID-based Ranking in Short-Video SearchSIGIR
uses Scores videos using both exact ID memorization and semantic meaning, with a learned gate that decides which to trust based on whether the item is popular or rare.
why it works It works because memorization excels on frequent items (you've seen them often) while semantic similarity helps on rare items (you see patterns instead). The gate learns when each approach is trustworthy. For rare items, semantic patterns are reliable; for common ones, exact history is.
Enhancing Multi-Valued Treatment Uplift Modeling with Knowledge Sharing and RCT DataSIGIR
uses Learns how treatments affect different people by sharing knowledge across treatment groups and anchoring the representations to stabilize learning.
why it works It works because sharing signals between treatment groups borrows strength when data is sparse. Anchoring representations prevents them from drifting differently per mini-batch. Using RCT data adds unbiased ground truth, which pulls the model toward correct causal effects.
Bridging the Topology-Semantic Gap: A Benchmark and Framework for Power Grid Work Ticket GenerationSIGIR
uses Combines semantic search with power-grid topology: uses semantic retrieval but constrains it to respect electrical system physical laws, with explicit reasoning chains.
why it works It works because power grids have rigid physical constraints that pure semantic matching misses. Symbolic patterns match abstract intentions to technical entities, while subgraph encoding ensures physical feasibility. The two together prevent hallucinations that violate safety rules.
TRACE: A Conversational Framework for Sustainable Tourism Recommendation with Agentic Counterfactual ExplanationsSIGIR
uses Recommendations balance relevance with environmental impact by eliciting user sustainability preferences through conversation and generating counterfactual explanations showing greener alternatives.
why it works Users often default to popular choices without considering impact. By extracting hidden sustainability preferences through conversation, the system learns what users actually value, not just what they initially ask for. Counterfactual explanations show what would change if they chose greener alternatives, helping users see the causal link between choices and outcomes.
Peerispect: Claim Verification in Scientific Peer ReviewsSIGIR
uses Extract claims from reviews, find evidence in the paper, and check if the evidence supports each claim using natural language reasoning.
why it works It works because written claims and supporting evidence, when found, should align in meaning; failing to align signals the claim is unsupported or incorrect, isolating reviewers' subjective opinions from factual statements.
MuseKG: An Interactive Knowledge Graph Over Museum CollectionsSIGIR
uses Organize museum objects and metadata into a typed network, then answer questions by finding entities related to the question and retrieving their connected evidence.
why it works It works because museum data is inherently relational—objects connect through people, events, and places; representing these connections explicitly lets similarity become reachability, so finding related objects becomes following edges in the graph.
SLeDoC: System for Legal Document ComparisonSIGIR
uses Compare legal document paragraphs by semantic meaning rather than word-level matching to detect inconsistencies, rewrites, and paraphrased contradictions.
why it works It works because paraphrased text has the same meaning even with different words; semantic comparison groups paragraphs by what they actually say, so contradictions that survive paraphrasing become detectable without character-level fragility.
FactOWL: A Cost-Efficient Tool for Long-Form Factuality EvaluationSIGIR
uses Extract atomic facts from long text, search multiple sources to find supporting evidence, aggregate evidence across sources, then estimate what fraction of facts are correct.
why it works It works because hallucinations stand out when facts are broken into small claims checked against real sources; multi-source aggregation amplifies signals from true facts while errors in one source are contradicted by others, revealing the true factuality rate.
PatentMerit: A Holistic System for In-depth Technology UnderstandingSIGIR
uses Score patents by disruptive potential and evolution using network citation patterns and clustering to surface high-impact technologies.
why it works Citation networks reveal which patents influence others; grouping patents by topic shows where breakthroughs cluster. Combining these separates genuinely transformative work from one-off contributions.
Detectability and Evaluation Risks of LLM-Generated Answers in Low-Resource Swahili Agricultural Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Score text patterns to distinguish AI language systems-generated agricultural answers from human-authored ones.
why it works AI language systems produce consistent patterns (length, diversity, similarity) that differ from human text; scoring and classification separate true signal from noise, revealing detectability as a diagnostic for evaluating generated content.
Towards Evidence-Aware Retrieval and Verification for Scientific Fact-CheckingSIGIR
uses Rank scientific papers by whether they actually support or refute a claim, not just by word similarity; distinguish supporting evidence from coincidental mentions.
why it works It works because simply finding papers with overlapping words misses the distinction between papers that actually address the claim versus papers that mention related terms by chance. Scoring based on evidence structure—whether the paper's logic actually connects to the claim—separates true support from false positives.
Faithful LLM-Assisted Question Answering for Technical and Academic SearchSIGIR
uses Ground AI answers in retrieved evidence and learn to distinguish citations that actually support the answer from fabricated or unsupported claims.
why it works It works because models learn spurious correlations when trained on data containing hallucinations. By explicitly training on task of separating supported claims from unsupported ones, the model learns the structure of genuine logical support versus plausible-sounding fabrication.
Characterising the Effects of Social Conformity on Information Seeking in Mixed Human-AI EnvironmentsSIGIR
uses Learn how human information-seeking changes when AI agents participate in discussions; distinguish AI influence from natural social conformity effects.
why it works It works because social conformity and AI effects both influence behavior, but untangling them requires controlled observation. By measuring behavior in mixed and unmixed settings and modeling the interaction, you isolate AI's true causal effect from confounding social mechanisms.
MANILA26: SIGIR 2026 Tutorial on Information Retrieval for Climate Change ImpactSIGIR
uses Finding relevant documents from scientific literature by ranking them by how closely their content matches climate evidence, accounting for geographic and temporal context.
why it works It works because when you treat documents as locations in a space where similar topics sit near each other, you can find what you need by measuring distance. Adding weights for geography and time ensures the most relevant evidence ranks first, filtering out noise and bias.
Verifiable User Simulation for Search and Recommendation SystemsSIGIR
uses Simulating user behavior by learning structured profiles and checking whether simulated choices match the real people they represent, to test if search and recommendation systems are fair.
why it works A simulator is only trustworthy if you can trace why it made each choice and verify that choice reflects the user it claims to represent, not the model's hidden biases. Auditing each component—profile, contract, execution, feedback—catches bias before it harms real users.
Second Workshop on Explainability in Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Explaining why a search result or recommendation was shown by identifying which input features influenced the score most and measuring whether the explanation helps humans trust the system.
why it works An explanation is trustworthy only if it points to the real reasons, not post-hoc rationalizations. Measuring cause—which features actually moved the score—requires methods that isolate each feature's effect. Information theory measures how much the explanation reduces uncertainty about the system's decision.
SynthIR: The First Workshop on Synthetic Content in Information Retrieval EcosystemsSIGIR
uses Evaluating search and recommendation systems in an environment where some content is made by AI, distinguishing real information from generated content, and measuring whether users can tell the difference.
why it works Mixed environments of real and synthetic content break traditional metrics because a system might rank generated garbage highly if it happens to match keywords. Measuring whether users trust the result requires auditing whether retrieved content is verifiable. When you know which content is synthetic, you can catch ranking failures.
Justice, Emancipation, Democracy, and Information Access (JEDI): The SIGIR Workshop on Resisting Corporate and Authoritarian Capture of Information Access PlatformsSIGIR
uses Designing search systems that resist corporate control and support democracy by auditing whose voices get amplified, which information sources are suppressed, and how ranking choices entrench or reduce power imbalances.
why it works Search is political because ranking chooses whose information reaches whom. Separating truth from manipulation requires auditing the choices: which stories rise, which stay buried. Weighting voices fairly—by merit, not profit—is a design choice, not an accident. Measuring whose interests a system serves exposes whose freedom it supports or restricts.
VulGen: Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Identifying and measuring failure modes in generative systems used for information retrieval.
why it works It works because vulnerabilities are patterns that emerge when you actually run the system against adversarial or biased inputs—testing whether the system's behavior matches its intended function reveals when it fails.
59 papers

Measuring surprise and information

Underneath search and compression sits a way to measure how surprising an outcome is, and therefore how much information it carries — a rare event tells you a lot, a certain one tells you nothing.

Why it works — the principle

It works because information has a natural, hard-to-cheat measure: the more unlikely a message, the more it narrows down the possibilities, and the fewer bits you need on average to send common things and more for rare ones. Systems that spend effort in proportion to surprise put their attention exactly where the uncertainty — and the payoff — actually is.

D-Models and E-Models: Diversity-Stability Trade-offs in the Sampling Behavior of Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Measure whether a language model's next-word probabilities match the true probabilities that matter for a task, revealing a trade-off between variety and stability.
why it works When a model samples the next word, it uses learned probabilities. If those probabilities are stable (don't bounce around) they match task requirements better. If they vary wildly, the model produces diverse outputs but unreliable ones. The math works because sampling is controlled by these probabilities, so their accuracy directly controls output quality.
MoE-LC: General-Purpose Lossless Compression for Multi-modal Data via Entropy-Aware Multi-ExpertsWWW
uses Estimate how hard each batch of data is to compress, then assign more experts to hard batches and simpler experts to easy ones, routing each piece to the expert best suited to it.
why it works It works because different data has different complexity (one video is simple, another is intricate). Matching expert capacity to complexity improves efficiency: simple data doesn't waste resources, hard data gets the focus it needs. Surprise (how much surprise) measures complexity directly, so it naturally tells you which expert to use.
Digital Skin, Digital Bias: Uncovering Tone-Based Biases in LLMs and Emoji EmbeddingsWWW
uses Measure whether emojis with different skin tones sit close together in the model's inner representation space, and whether they carry different sentiment scores even when the base emoji is identical.
why it works It works because if a model truly treats a smiling face emoji equally regardless of skin tone, they should sit at equal distances in the model's learned space and carry the same sentiment. Large distances or sentiment gaps reveal the model has learned to encode skin tone as distinct and meaningful in ways that shouldn't matter, exposing where bias is baked in.
Rhythm of Opinion: Interpretable Hawkes-Graph Networks for Hierarchical Opinion PropagationWWW
uses Model opinion propagation as a point process where opinions flow at rates determined by emotional context and hierarchical position.
why it works Opinion spreads in bursts when emotions align, modeled as time-clustered events; the rates reveal how hierarchy and feeling drive adoption. This captures that propagation speed depends on both content and audience readiness.
Do You Think What I Think? A Qualitative Study for Maximising User Engagement through Latent Visual PropertiesWWW
uses Identify visual design choices—color, layout, symbolic encoding—that do not directly represent data yet improve insight and engagement.
why it works Visual properties work because they exploit how humans process information: color evokes emotion, layout guides focus, symbols encode meaning. These channels communicate beyond the numbers alone.
Toward Graph-Tokenizing Large Language Models with Reconstructive Graph Instruction TuningWWW
uses An AI language systems learns graph-to-text alignment by reconstructing graph structure from its internal words outputs, adding explicit graph supervision to language-only instruction tuning.
why it works It works because text-only supervision creates asymmetry where language dominates and graph context is underutilized; by requiring reconstruction of the original graph, you force the model to preserve all information, making alignment bidirectional rather than text-biased.
Early Recall Estimation and Stopping in Technology-Assisted Reviews via Ranker-Sampler FusionWWW
uses Combines a ranking model's scores with a probability sample of documents to estimate true recall without judging the entire corpus, enabling early stopping decisions.
why it works It works because the ranker's scores act as an informative starting guess about which documents are likely relevant; updating that starting guess with random samples gives unbiased estimates, and confidence bounds tell you when additional sampling won't substantially improve the estimate.
Spectral Disentanglement and Enhancement: A Dual-domain Contrastive Framework for Representation LearningWWW
uses Partition high-dimensional features into strong signals, weak signals, and noise using decomposition, then amplify the strong signals that carry task-relevant meaning.
why it works It works because features collapse into narrow cones, wasting features. By sorting features by importance (how much they vary), you focus on the true pattern and ignore noise, which improves generalization because real knowledge fits simpler than noise does.
Evaluating LLM Recommendations Under StressWWW
uses Test models on five tasks of rising difficulty and measure how much their accuracy drops, then compute a sensitivity score to rank robustness under stress.
why it works It works because stress reveals true robustness: a model that works on easy tasks but fails on hard ones is fragile. The drop in performance is the right signal—you're seeing what breaks first, which tells you where the model is weakest and most likely to fail in deployment.
Towards Better Evaluation Metrics for Text-to-Motion GenerationWWW
uses Match text descriptions to motion using optimal transport, then measure discrepancy without assuming a fixed shape of distribution, to evaluate generation quality.
why it works It works because optimal transport finds the most efficient coupling between text and motion—the minimum cost to transform one into the other. This captures global matching better than local methods. And avoiding the Gaussian assumption catches real data that's spiky or multimodal.
A Prompt-Aware Structuring Framework for Reliable Reuse of AI-Generated Content in the Agentic WebWWW
uses Attaches confidence scores and metadata recording how the content was generated, with verifiable credentials to estimate reliability when the same content is reused.
why it works It works because reusing untracked content causes errors to compound and spread. By measuring and recording confidence at generation, any downstream user can estimate the true reliability of what they're reusing, stopping bad information before it chains into hallucinations.
Blind-QEM: A Privacy-Preserving Framework for Quantum Error Mitigation via Zero-Knowledge ProofsWWW
uses The system verifies quantum computation results using zero-knowledge proof protocols that confirm correctness without revealing the circuit's structure or proprietary noise models.
why it works Zero-knowledge proofs work because the verifier can check a commitment matches an execution without ever seeing the secret. Here, the quantum provider can prove the result follows from the submitted circuit without exposing that circuit, protecting intellectual property on both sides.
Active Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Conflict-Fused Uncertainty QuantificationWWW
uses Combine three uncertainty signals at each step to decide when to fetch external information, triggering retrieval for multi-hop reasoning.
