why it works It works because uncertainty has multiple sources: the model's internal confusion, disagreement across multiple runs, and conflict between different signals. Fusing all three captures the true ambiguity better than any single signal, so retrieval triggers precisely when needed.
Trust in One Round: Confidence Estimation for Large Language Models via Structural SignalsWWW
uses Score model confidence by analyzing patterns in the internal hidden states across multiple scales, without needing extra computations.
why it works It works because a model's internal layers show stability and coherence patterns before the model produces its final answer. These patterns correlate with correctness better than surface-level signals like likelihood or similarity, and they cost nothing extra to compute.
Data Degrades with UseWWW
uses Measure how much information each data use leaks and account for cumulative privacy loss across repeated queries.
why it works Privacy loss is proportional to information revealed; repeated uses amplify individual leaks because each query constrains future possibilities. Aggregating these bounds prevents privacy guarantees from degrading as data is reused.
SMART: A Social Movement Analysis & Reasoning Tool with Case Studies on #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatterWWW
uses Extract emotion distributions from social media posts and forecast their intensity and volume in future posts.
why it works Emotions have inertia and respond predictably to external events; modeling past sequences as a mixture of emotions lets you forecast when sentiment will shift, enabling early detection of discourse changes.
Understanding the Consequences of VTuber ReincarnationWWW
uses Measure the quantitative impact of reincarnation on audience size, revenue, harassment, and industry ripple effects using 728K livestream sessions.
why it works Aggregate statistics across many events reveal patterns that single cases cannot. The volume of data allows real effects to emerge from noise, showing how individual career transitions translate into measurable shifts in audience behavior and creator welfare.
Prediction Guardian: A Distribution-based Real-time Anomaly Detection and Mitigation Framework for Online AdvertisingWWW
uses Monitor the shape of ad-ranking prediction scores over time; when the distribution shifts (fewer high bids, more low bids, or suddenly extreme values), flag it and smooth outliers.
why it works Healthy systems produce predictable, repeatable distributions of predictions; a sudden shift means the training data or real-world behavior has changed. By comparing today's distribution to historical baselines using divergence metrics, you catch silent failures before they ripple downstream into billing or user experience.
RobustReviewAI: A Robustness Evaluation System for AI-Powered Peer ReviewWWW
uses Measures how a review system's decisions change when text, tables, and formulas are altered, revealing weak points.
why it works It works because small changes that don't affect true meaning (perturbations) expose whether the model is truly understanding the paper or relying on brittle patterns. If decisions flip under these changes, the system isn't robust.
Additively Competitive SecretariesWWW
uses Minimize the worst-case gap between what an optimal decision-maker in hindsight could have achieved and what a decision-making policy achieves on average when hiring from a random-order stream.
why it works This works because the regret metric penalizes both being too conservative and too aggressive in the right way: policies that miss good candidates (high regret) and policies that hire bad ones (high regret) must balance the two, which naturally finds strategies that capture most of what's possible without requiring perfect timing. The additive gap is also robust—it scales fairly across different problem sizes.
AMID: Model-Agnostic Dataset Distillation by Adversarial Mutual Information MinimizationWWW
uses Create a shrunk dataset by minimizing mutual information between the synthetic data and the specific architecture used to build it, turning it into a two-player game where one side erases architecture-specific bias.
why it works This works because when you reduce information shared between the dataset and the model's identity (CNN vs ViT shape), you force the synthetic data to encode only the problem's true structure, not just shortcuts that one architecture happened to exploit. A dataset with minimal architecture-specific signal must rely on genuine patterns, so it trains any architecture well without re-distillation.
Beyond Engagement: A Human-Centered Evaluation Framework for LLM-Powered Recommender SystemsWWW
uses Evaluate recommendation systems not by engagement metrics alone, but by human-centered outcomes—trust, transparency, agency, satisfaction—to align ranking strategies with what users actually value.
why it works It works because engagement metrics optimize what's observable but not what matters: clicking a misleading result 'works' for engagement but harms users. Grounding evaluation in human values like transparency and trust creates accountability to actual user welfare, not just platform goals.
Explaining Synergistic Effects in Social RecommendationsWWW
uses Explain social recommendations by identifying subgraphs where pieces of information amplify each other—parts that together tell you more than they would separately—and tracing paths through those subgraphs.
why it works It works because synergy means the information-gain is real: when two signals together predict better than either alone, it reveals actual interaction in the data. Maximizing information gain finds genuine coordination rather than coincidence, so explanations ground in what actually drives the recommendation.
Struggling at the Start: Structural Causes of Decoding Difficulty in Code GenerationWWW
uses Measures how uncertain the model is about which words comes next, especially at line starts, then refines predictions by reducing that uncertainty.
why it works At decision points where structure matters most, high uncertainty signals the model has competing plausible next words. Reducing that uncertainty there sharpens the model's choice and improves correctness, because the model itself already contains the knowledge—it just needs less divided focus.
ULoR: Uncertainty-Aware Leave-One-Out Refinement Framework for Diagnosis PredictionWWW
uses Quantifies the model's uncertainty about each diagnosis, then for high-uncertainty ones, uses multiple-choice reasoning to confirm or replace the prediction.
why it works High uncertainty means the model's top guess might be wrong. By quantifying that doubt and drilling down on uncertain cases with structured reasoning, you catch corrections you'd miss by trusting a confident wrong answer. Uncertainty itself is information about when to scrutinize more.
SoftHateBench: Evaluating Moderation Models Against Reasoning-Driven, Policy-Compliant HostilityWWW
uses Generate hostile text variants that keep the harmful stance constant but soften the language, then measure how many detectors miss the reframed version versus the overt one.
why it works Detectors trained only on explicit hostility learn surface patterns, not underlying intent. By controlling what changes and what stays fixed, you isolate whether the detector catches reasoning-based hostility or only crude slurs. Systematic reframing exposes this gap.
On the Effectiveness of Mempool-based Transaction AuditingWWW
uses Compute the false-positive rate of detecting censorship by measuring when independent observers disagree on transaction presence; show that timing (transactions separated by 30+ seconds) dramatically reduces false alarms.
why it works If a transaction exists, all observers should eventually see it; discrepancies are evidence of blocking. But network delays cause false alarms. Waiting longer ensures propagation is complete, so discrepancies become rare unless true censorship occurs. Time-separation filters out transient delays.
SoK: Zero-Knowledge Proof Systems — An Empirical and Theoretical Comparison of SNARKs and STARKsWWW
uses Compares how fast two types of proofs (SNARKs and STARKs) generate, verify, and shrink themselves on real hardware, measuring which trade-offs suit which use cases.
why it works Proof systems make different architectural choices: SNARKs assume a trusted setup and optimize for speed and size; STARKs skip trusted setup but are larger and slower. Measuring both on the same platform with the same workload reveals which choice costs more for each real-world constraint (speed, size, trust, security).
NERdME: A Named Entity Recognition Dataset for Indexing Research Artifacts in Code RepositoriesWWW
uses Label named entities in README files to teach models to recognize artifact names, dataset descriptions, and code implementation details.
why it works Information extraction works because specific patterns mark where important entities appear. Marking examples trains a model to recognize that same pattern elsewhere. Named entity recognition works because once you see ''dataset X was stored at location Y'' repeated across examples, the model learns that pattern signals an entity boundary.
Towards Automating Articles Screening Processes Using Chain-of-Thought Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Use a reasoning-enabled AI language systems on structured text chunks, measure complexity via information rank, and filter multiple candidate summaries by voting to extract patient-intervention-outcome elements reliably.
why it works It works because expert papers share predictable structure and the model can reason through it step-by-step, catching subtleties a quick classifier would miss. Measuring information content of each chunk tells you when to apply reasoning versus simple extraction. Consensus across multiple independent model runs filters out hallucinations—if three runs agree on a fact, it's more likely real than any single answer.
(Everything You Never Knew You Needed To Know About) Rank-Biased Measurement For Web SearchWWW
uses Measure search result quality using a geometric decay down the ranked list, where top positions are much more important, quantifying the measurement's own uncertainty.
why it works It works because users rarely scroll past a few results, so the top three matter vastly more than position fifteen. A geometric decay (each rank worth a fraction of the last) matches this behavior exactly. Uncertainty quantifies how much your measurement could change if the hidden qrels beyond what you annotated were different—bounded rather than infinite.
Multi-modal Bipartite Graph Structure Learning with Information Bottleneck for Micro-video RecommendationWWW
uses Minimize information bottleneck within each modality and across modalities to extract minimal sufficient representations for recommendations.
why it works Bottleneck forces each modality to discard everything except what predicts recommendations, and forces different modalities to agree only on what matters. This squeezes out modality-specific noise and redundancy between modalities.
Spiking Graph Predictive Coding for Reliable OOD GeneralizationWWW
uses Detect when a graph model becomes unreliable by iteratively comparing predictions to actual graph behavior and exposing the internal errors that signal a distribution shift.
why it works Works because out-of-distribution examples create mismatches between what the model expects and what it observes in the graph. Spiking error signals reveal these mismatches before bad predictions happen, and iterative correction exposes uncertainty in the mismatch itself, making reliability interpretable.
TRACE: Trajectory-Aware Comprehensive Evaluation for Deep Research AgentsWWW
uses Evaluate research agents not just by whether they got the answer right, but by measuring the quality and efficiency of their reasoning steps, with adjustable difficulty.
why it works A right answer with bad reasoning may fail on harder variants or in new contexts; weighing the reasoning process itself—how grounded the evidence is, how many steps were wasted—reveals true capability.
Smart Eye: LLM-Guided Proposer-Verifier Framework for Industrial-Scale Log Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Select the most informative log patterns under a false-alarm budget, then grind them into rules that catch anomalies with minimal false alarms.
why it works It works because anomalies are rare and distinctive—the patterns that help you catch them are also the ones that reduce confusion. By optimizing which patterns matter most while keeping false positives bounded, you trade recall against reliability in a controlled way.
Predicting Expectancy Violations Using Eye-Tracking Features: A Machine Learning ApproachWWW
uses Predicts when users are surprised by search results using eye-movement patterns like how long they look and how often they refocus.
why it works Surprise changes focus behavior in measurable ways; looking longer at unexpected content is statistically higher than at expected content, so sustained eye metrics capture the mismatch signal reliably.
JitterSketch: Finding Jittery Flows in Network StreamsWWW
uses Identifies network flows with high variability in packet timing by filtering stable flows and reporting unstable ones.
why it works It works because flows with bad timing stand out statistically from normal flows. The variability itself is the signal—large deviations from steady patterns directly measure timing problems.
Identification of Influential Node Group in Attributed Graph through Explaining Graph Neural NetworkWWW
uses Identifies influential node groups by measuring how much model output drops when each node is removed.
why it works It works because truly important nodes break the model when removed—the performance damage quantifies importance. Graph structure and node attributes together determine which nodes matter most.
16th Temporal Web Analytics Workshop (TempWeb)WWW
uses Analyzes how the web evolves over time by tracking changes to content, structure, and relationships at temporal scales ranging from hours to years.
why it works Temporal analysis reveals causality and impact—which changes led to which outcomes. Information gain increases when you know not just what changed but when, because timing patterns disambiguate correlation from causation.
Dynamic Metrics to Validate the Use of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential for Dynamic SamplingWSDM
uses Track how much error a chemistry prediction model makes as it forecasts material behavior step-by-step through a simulation.
why it works It works because watching errors accumulate over time reveals whether a trained model truly understands the underlying physics or merely fits patterns that break when conditions change, separating real knowledge from overfitting.
A Comprehensive Guide to Time-Series Anomaly DetectionWSDM
uses Detect anomalies by measuring when data points deviate most from expected patterns in time series.
why it works An anomaly is simply something that deviates from what you'd expect to see. By measuring how surprising or unusual each point is compared to normal behavior patterns, you identify things that don't fit the pattern, making detection a direct measurement of deviation.
Continual Learning on Evolving Graphs via Mutual Information Maximization across Dynamic Node EmbeddingsWSDM
uses Maximizes shared information between node representations from consecutive time steps, preventing knowledge of past connections from being erased when learning new ones.
why it works It works because node roles persist—the same nodes remain central or peripheral as the graph evolves. By forcing new representations to preserve information about old ones, you anchor learning to stable patterns rather than overwriting them entirely.
DiffNBR: Spatio-Temporal Diffusion with Information Bottleneck for Next-Basket RecommendationWSDM
uses Uses paired denoising models to predict users' next purchases by separately learning repetitive buying patterns and exploratory new-item desires, with information flow controls.
why it works It works because purchases come from two distinct impulses—habit and curiosity. By splitting these signals and controlling information flow between them, you let habit patterns strengthen through repetition while exploratory patterns explore freely, matching how real shopping actually works.
Code LLMs Still Fall Short of Top Programmers: Evaluating Algorithmic Code Generation Through Computational ThinkingWSDM
uses Evaluate code generation in four phases—understanding examples, choosing algorithms, describing solutions, and writing code—measuring how well models perform at each step, then correlate performance across steps.
why it works It works because coding is sequential reasoning: you cannot write correct code without understanding the problem and picking the right algorithm first. By measuring each phase, you reveal where models actually fail. Correlation shows that earlier reasoning directly enables later success, exposing the true bottleneck.
FACE: A Fine-Grained Reference-Free Evaluator for Conversational Information AccessSIGIR
uses Select the best instructions to score each atomic unit of a conversation, then aggregate scores into one overall rating.
why it works It works because the atomic units capture concrete details of what happened, and choosing instructions that matter most for each aspect ensures those details influence the final score proportionally to their importance.
Inferring Targets from Calibrated Hesitations via Mutual Information Maximization in Multi-Behavior RecommendationSIGIR
uses Maximize the shared information between learned user intent patterns and actual conversion events to infer when a user was interested but hesitated.
why it works It works because high mutual information means the intent patterns genuinely capture what makes conversions happen. When intent is high but conversion didn't occur, that gap reveals hesitation rather than genuine disinterest, letting you recover the true signal hidden in missing conversions.
NuggetIndex: Governed Atomic Retrieval for Maintainable RAGSIGIR
uses Store individual atomic facts with validity timestamps and confidence, then rank them by freshness and conflict-free status before returning them as retrieval results.
why it works It works because you're separating the signal (individual facts) from noise (contradictions and stale information). By tracking each fact's lifetime and filtering expired ones before ranking, you prevent the system from returning answers that are outdated or contradict themselves.
Information Seeking Behavior in LLM-Based RAG: Mental Models and Missing InformationSIGIR
uses Study how people think chat systems work versus what they actually do: do they assume the system read everything or only searched parts.
why it works It works because users bring mental models from old interfaces. When a new interface hides the search and ranking stages, people assume exhaustive work and stop verifying, leading them astray. Revealing the true stages in the interface would let users calibrate their trust.
Towards Inclusive Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Challenges and Opportunities for Cognitively Impaired UsersSIGIR
uses Design systems that adapt query handling and answer clarity to each user's current cognitive level, with caregivers able to verify what was retrieved.
why it works It works because a single query-answer flow assumes stable comprehension, but dementia cognition fluctuates. Tracking that change over time and showing caregivers the evidence prevents misunderstanding and maintains informed oversight as the user's needs shift.
Stop Using the Wilcoxon Test: Myth, Misconception and Misuse in IR ResearchSIGIR
uses Test whether the Wilcoxon statistical test correctly identifies true differences between ranking systems, or if it makes false claims too often.
why it works It works because the Wilcoxon test makes assumptions that do not hold in ranking metrics: the test breaks down when applied to highly discrete scores, leading it to declare false discoveries. Switching to better tests like permutation methods preserves the real false-positive rate.
Too Many Questions: Deriving Concise and Effective Nugget BanksSIGIR
uses Build evaluation question banks by extracting contrastive differences between good and bad system responses, focusing on what actually separates winners.
why it works It works because generic questions don't reveal which systems are better; contrastive questions do. By grounding nuggets in actual response pairs and examining what distinguishes winners from losers—topicality, detail, evidence—you extract questions that strongly correlate with actual system quality.
Confidence-Based Stopping Methods for Systematic ReviewsSIGIR
uses Stop searching documents when the information gathered is confident enough to make a decision, rather than searching until a target recall number is hit.
why it works It works because decision-making doesn't actually require finding every relevant document—it requires enough evidence to choose with confidence. Once you've seen enough contradictory or confirming signals, more searching wastes time without changing the answer.
Query Performance Prediction under Corpus Growth in Dense RetrievalSIGIR
uses Predict how a retrieval system's quality will drop as the database grows larger, using the distances between top results and background results.
why it works When a database is small, top results stand out clearly from the rest. As it grows, more similar items enter the background, pushing the good ones down. Measuring this 'distance gap' between tops and background tells you whether the ranking will hold up.
Humans, LLMs, and Measures Do Not Align in Attributed Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Compare whether language models, humans, and automatic scoring methods all agree on which system output is better, finding major mismatches in evaluation.
why it works It works because alignment breaks reveal what each evaluator actually cares about. If language models and humans agree, the scoring method is probably right. If they differ, one group is using information the other ignores, which means you can't trust single-method evaluation.
An Analysis of Attribute Utilization in Side Information-integrated Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses Measure how much each recommendation model relies on item attributes by randomizing those attributes and observing how much the predictions change.
why it works If predictions change dramatically when attributes are scrambled, the model is using them; if predictions stay the same, the model ignores them. The change size reveals true dependence.
Semantic Recall for Vector SearchSIGIR
uses When evaluating if a search method retrieved the best results, only count misses where the missed result was actually relevant to the query, ignoring irrelevant nearby results.
why it works Search databases often contain irrelevant items close to relevant ones; penalizing all misses overstates failure. Only penalizing semantic misses shows true retrieval quality.
CoCo: Conformal Confidence Suppression to Optimize Search ResultsSIGIR
uses Estimate how showing versus hiding content changes customer revenue, then suppress content only when uncertainty is small enough.
why it works Showing bad content hurts revenue; suppressing good content also hurts it. You need to know both the effect size and how confident you are. Only suppress when the prediction is sure, because uncertain predictions are likely wrong and hiding based on a guess is worse than taking the risk.
When Context Bites: Detecting RAG Poisoning via Document-Level Attention CollapseSIGIR
uses Detect poisoned documents by watching how focus spreads—benign answers have scattered focus while attacked answers concentrate it on the poisoned doc.
why it works When a model is genuinely uncertain, it spreads focus across many relevant pieces. When an attack tricks it into trusting a poisoned doc, focus collapses onto that doc because it confidently follows the manipulation. The internal focus betrays the attack even when the output looks confident.
Generative Enhanced Modeling: A Collaborative Framework for Enhancing User Representations via Semantic IDSIGIR
uses Uses language models to create clean user interest profiles, then removes noise while preserving signal about what each person really wants to watch.
why it works It works because language models capture semantic meaning that raw click sequences miss. By explicitly denoising at both user and item levels, you keep true preferences while discarding random clicks. This is grounded in information theory—you maximize signal while suppressing noise.
58 papers

Spreading information across a network

When the data is a web of connections — who follows whom, what's bought with what, which fact links to which — a thing's meaning comes largely from its neighbours, so you let evidence flow along the links.

Why it works — the principle

It works because in real networks connected things tend to be alike — friends share tastes, linked pages share topics — so a node can borrow evidence from its neighbours, and letting that evidence spread a few steps sharpens every guess using the crowd around it. It only fails when the links carry no real signal.

Social Event Prediction via Fourier Graph LearningWWW
uses Predict future events in a social network by storing events as complex numbers that encode both what happened and when, then spreading that information across edges.
why it works Encoding semantic meaning in the real part and temporal patterns in the imaginary part lets you handle both at once. Multiplication in frequency space is cheaper than convolution in time, so you can process large event streams fast. Nearness in this complex space means events that are semantically similar and temporally aligned.
Concordia: Enabling Low-Conflict Distributed Transaction Scheduling in Sharding Blockchain via Cooperative PerceptionWWW
uses Each shard predicts future cross-shard interactions using a graph algorithm, broadcasts low-dimensional signals, then prioritizes transactions by popularity.
why it works Conflicts happen when shards make decisions independently. By predicting what other shards will do and sharing compact signals, each shard learns its neighbors' likely moves without full data. Popularity-driven packing exploits the fact that hot items create predictable patterns; handling them first stabilizes the rest.
How Graphs Can Help You Stay Informed in an Evolving WorldWWW
uses Decide which web pages to recrawl using graph structure and learned probabilities, prioritizing updates that cascade to many downstream pages.
why it works When one page changes, its outbound links matter more than random updates because information flows through those connections, so prioritizing them keeps the graph fresher with fewer crawls.
Cross-Type Semantic Alignment for Multi-Type Anomaly Detection in Heterogeneous GraphsWWW
uses Detect anomalies in graphs with multiple node types by aligning semantic features across types and weighting their contributions to balance sparse and rich nodes.
why it works Nodes of different types carry unequal anomaly signals; weighting by reliability spreads discriminative cues from informative nodes to sparse ones, surfacing anomalies that cross type boundaries.
DA-RAG: Dynamic Attributed Community Search for Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Dynamically extracts query-relevant subgraphs by finding attributed communities that match the question, then passes these self-complementary subgraphs to the AI language systems.
why it works It works because knowledge bases have natural clusters of related facts; retrieving an entire community around query-relevant nodes captures implicit context and connections that single-node or low-order retrieval would miss, enriching the AI language systems's grounding.
Heterophily-Agnostic Hypergraph Neural Networks with Riemannian Local ExchangerWWW
uses Pass information through hypergraph bottlenecks using curved space geometry that locally adapts how tightly or loosely to let signals flow, so nearby nodes stay distinguishable even after many rounds of sharing.
why it works Curved geometry lets you expand space where signals need breathing room and contract it where they should squeeze together; this prevents the blurring that flat geometry causes, so each node's learned fingerprint remains unique and meaningful across many passes.
Securing Your Place in the Review Network: A Dynamic Embeddedness-aware Graph Neural Network for Restaurant Survival PredictionWWW
uses Predict restaurant survival by measuring how deeply each restaurant sits in its network of customers and peer restaurants, then track how that position changes over time.
why it works Well-connected restaurants that sit at the center of customer and peer networks get more support and word-of-mouth; tracking this position over time shows whether a restaurant is gaining or losing ground, making survival predictable.
Unsupervised Subgraph Anomaly Detection Based on Pattern CollaborationWWW
uses Identifies suspicious groups in networks by learning which patterns appear repeatedly in normal subgraphs versus abnormal ones, using paths and cycles to sample candidate groups.
why it works Anomalous groups differ structurally from normal ones. By seeing which pattern combinations appear together in normal graphs, you learn what 'collaboration' looks like, so subgraphs that deviate from those learned patterns stand out as anomalies.
Using Psycholinguistic Features for Multiplex Community Detection in Temporal Social NetworksWWW
uses Detects communities in social networks by treating emotional language (grievances, moral framing) as separate communication channels layered atop who interacts with whom.
why it works People cluster around shared beliefs and emotions, not just direct interactions. Adding emotional language as a separate layer reveals which groups form around common grievances or values, so communities defined by what people care about emerge more coherently.
FS_GPlib: Breaking the Web-Scale Barrier — A Unified Acceleration Framework for Graph Propagation ModelsWWW
uses Simulate how information or epidemics spread across a graph by batch-updating many nodes in parallel, partition the graph strategically to minimize data shuffling between computers, and run many independent random simulations to average results.
why it works It works because spreading is a local process—each node only talks to neighbors—so you can update thousands in parallel without talking to each other. Partitioning by target node keeps the graph pieces independent and reduces network traffic, while averaging many random runs recovers the true expected outcome.
Towards Robust Detection of Chinese Toxic Variants via Dynamic Knowledge Graph–LLM ReasoningWWW
uses Build a knowledge graph linking canonical toxic words to their obfuscated variants using phonetic and visual similarity; traverse the graph to recognize hidden toxic expressions.
why it works Toxicity hides through transformation—phonetic abbreviations, symbol swaps, homoglyphs—but these transformations leave traces (similar sounds, similar shapes). By encoding variant relationships as a navigable graph, you turn variant recognition into path-following: find the transformation that connects what you see to known toxic terms.
Line Graphs Are Here! Unlock a Simple Solution for Data Sparsity and Class Imbalance in Recommender SystemWWW
uses Transform user-item recommendations into a line graph (where each node is an edge in the original graph), apply graph learning techniques to generate synthetic training examples, and feed augmented data back to the recommender.
why it works The line graph transformation turns the data-scarcity problem into a node-scarcity problem where mature imbalance-correction techniques apply. Generating augmented nodes in line-graph space and projecting back to user-item space creates synthetic training pairs that respect the original graph structure, boosting signal without introducing noise.
Consensus Stability of Community Notes on XWWW
uses Measure how shared-opinion contributors rate a fact-check note differently from opposite-opinion contributors after the note becomes visible, and predict note disappearance from polarization patterns.
why it works This works because fact-check systems survive only if their communities can reach rough agreement across viewpoint divides. When viewpoint-similar raters cluster toward approval and dissimilar raters cluster toward rejection, the ratings become a proxy for the fundamental disagreement—if the note can't bridge the gap once exposed to both sides, it fails. Measuring this post-display shift predicts which notes lack real consensus.
Unicoon: Hypergraph-based Multi-Agent Simulation of Information CocoonsWWW
uses Models how information and recommendations spread through social networks and user groups, tracking which content reaches which people and creating cohesive clusters.
why it works It works because people naturally form groups where they see similar content, and once you map out who connects to whom and what they receive, you can predict where information pools and where it gets cut off. Hypergraphs capture the fact that one piece of content can reach many people at once, not just pairs.
SemaReg: Semantic Service Registry for Resilient IoTWorkflow Orchestration in Edge Computing EnvironmentsWWW
uses Discovers services in distributed edge networks by matching a requested type against available semantic types using ontology rules, replicating that registry across devices.
why it works It works because exact matching fails when a needed service is down but a compatible one exists. Semantic subsumption—understanding that a subtype can always do what a supertype does—lets you find substitutes. Spreading the registry across multiple copies ensures services stay discoverable even when some copies vanish.
Source Localization in Continuous-Time Propagation via Spectral ODE ModelingWWW
uses Find the source of information spread by solving an inverse equation: given how information flowed over time in a network, learn what initial state and rates would produce that observed flow.
why it works It works because information flow follows deterministic patterns (like heat diffusion); if you know the pattern, solving backward reveals the source. Filtering network noise lets the model focus on real structure, and treating time continuously captures the actual dynamics—discrete steps miss gradual spreading.
From Criteria to Ranking: Targeting-Aware Tripartite Graph Learning for Multi-Criteria RecommendationWWW
uses Score items by spreading user preferences and criterion signals across a three-way graph of users, items, and evaluation criteria.
why it works Works because spreading respect the structure—information about what users value for each criterion flows through the graph and accumulates at items that match, producing the score.
EIAN: Explicit Interaction-aware Attention Network for Interpretable Event ModelingWWW
uses Predict the next event in a time sequence by explicitly modeling how each event type influences others, using separate channels for within-type patterns and cross-type influences.
why it works It works because real event sequences have two hidden forces: regular rhythms within each type and unexpected cascades between types; exposing both lets the model capture the true drivers of what happens next.
Mining Citywide Dengue Spread Patterns in Singapore Through Hotspot Dynamics from Open Web DataWWW
uses Learns how dengue transmissions spread between city neighborhoods by modeling how infection hotspots in one area influence neighboring regions over weeks.
why it works It works because infections spread through networks—locally between nearby mosquito habitats, and long-distance through people commuting. Learning this network from case data reveals the hidden transmission paths.
DREAMS: A Social Exchange Theory-Informed Modeling of Misinformation Engagement on Social MediaWWW
uses Predicts how many people will engage with misinformation by treating each action as part of an evolving sequence shaped by emotional rewards and platform design.
why it works When you model a person's choices as a sequence of negotiated exchanges (effort given for reward received), past actions reveal the pattern of what will come next. Platform design and emotions shift this pattern over time, so tracking how that evolution unfolds predicts the next engagement.
Boltzmann Interaction Models with Gibbs Decision Policies in Multi-Agent Delivery SystemsWWW
uses Treats each drone as making probabilistic decisions based on local energy (cost, service balance, interference), with a temperature parameter tuning exploration.
why it works In physics, temperature controls how particles explore; low temperature locks in coordinated states, high temperature allows escape. This principle transfers to agents naturally balancing individual efficiency against collective goals.

uses Retrieve answers from huge graph structures by filtering down from broad communities to specific entities, scoring each stage to keep the best candidates.
why it works It works because large graphs have hierarchical structure: related entities cluster into communities, communities cluster into regions. By searching levels from coarse to fine and re-ranking at each stage, you prune dead ends early and focus compute on promising paths.
DSTAG: A Semantic Tag-Enhanced Dual-Graph Convolutional Network for Temporal Knowledge Graph CompletionWWW
uses Enrich entities and relations with semantic tags, then spread information across connected graphs to fill missing facts about evolving relationships.
why it works Knowledge graphs work because relationships follow patterns in connected structures. Passing information between neighbors captures how entities interact indirectly. Multi-Source Information Driven Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph Learning for Traffic ForecastingWWW
uses Model traffic flow by building hypergraphs capturing high-order spatial groupings and temporal correlations, then pass information through to predict future counts.
why it works Traffic patterns repeat because roads and time have structure. Organizing data so similar roads cluster together and similar times group together lets you spot what influences a location's future. Hypergraphs capture how one road's flow affects many neighbors at once, not just pairs, revealing how congestion spreads.
FraudShield: Knowledge Graph Empowered Defense for LLMs against Fraud AttacksWWW
uses Build a knowledge graph linking fraudulent keywords to fraud tactics, then use it to highlight suspicious patterns and guide language models toward secure responses.
why it works Fraud defense works because fraudulent text shares recognizable patterns with known deception tactics. Structuring those patterns in a graph lets you spot when new text resembles fraud you've seen before. Showing the model those similarities forces it to acknowledge the danger before responding, triggering more careful output.
PIGCN: Physics-Inspired Graph Convolution Networks for Heterogeneous Social Event DetectionWWW

why it works Real events form because messages reinforce and interfere with each other, like waves. Using wave equations captures how information bounces between similar messages. Force-based attraction pulls related messages together while repulsion pushes unrelated ones apart, so the model naturally clusters messages from the same event.
Dual History Enhancement with Hybrid Hypergraph-Graph Networks for Temporal Knowledge Graph ReasoningWWW
uses Captures both nearby relationships and distant multi-step connections between entities in a knowledge graph, then predicts future events by weighting the contribution of each type of connection based on a gating mechanism.
why it works It works because future events depend on both immediate neighbors and distant entities reachable through multiple hops. Gating mechanisms let the model learn which connection distance matters most for each entity pair, balancing local details against global context to forecast accurately.
Credit and Power Co-evolution Modeling with Dynamic Graph LearningWWW
uses Jointly predicts power consumption and credit risk by modeling how credit changes and power anomalies influence each other bidirectionally.
why it works It works because credit and power are entangled—credit changes affect financing strategies which affect power consumption, and power anomalies signal operational stress that affects creditworthiness. Modeling both together captures this mutual causation, making each prediction better than modeling them separately.
Federated Latent Factor Learning for Privacy-Preserving Spatio-Temporal Signal RecoveryWWW

HyperDetector: Advanced Persistent Threat Detection via Hypergraph Neural Networks with Enhanced Global PerceptionWWW
uses Detects attacks by scoring how multi-entity events spread and connect across system records, paying focus to distant relationships.
why it works Attacks spread signals across multiple entities in patterns; by weighting connections based on their relevance to the attack signature and linking distant parts of the system together, you can spot coordinated behaviors that isolated local analysis would miss.
The First Workshop on Graph-enhanced LLMs for trustwOrthy Web data management (GLOW'26)WWW
uses Combines knowledge graphs (structured relationship networks) with language models to reason over web data while maintaining explicit logical constraints and connections between facts.
why it works Knowledge graphs encode ground truth relationships, so reasoning that respects those links stays grounded in fact. Language models can flexibly interpret natural language, but constrained by graph structure they cannot hallucinate unsupported claims.
A New Query Expansion Approach for Enhancing Information Retrieval via Agent-Mediated Dialogic InquiryWSDM
uses Breaks down a user query into multiple sub-questions, generates pseudo-answers from different viewpoints, then filters and weights them by relevance to create a richer expanded query.
why it works A search query is vague; exploring it from multiple angles generates diverse candidates for relevant documents. By keeping only the highest-signal pseudo-answers and building the expanded query from weighted combinations, the method amplifies recall without adding noise.
Knowledge-Graph Structure-Aware Conversational Entity RetrievalWSDM
uses Ranks candidate knowledge-graph entities using a neural architecture that models lexical and semantic relevance while propagating signals through the entity's neighborhood in the graph structure and conditioning on dialog context.

uses Find and map food-sharing groups by searching the web, refining queries with language rewriting, and updating the map as new groups emerge.

WEB&GRAPH 2026: Workshop on Web & Graphs, Responsible Intelligence, and Social MediaWSDM
uses This is a workshop on reasoning over networks and graphs to detect misinformation and build trustworthy systems.
why it works Graph reasoning works because false claims spread differently than true ones: false claims trigger outrage and jump communities quickly, true claims spread through trusted dense clusters more slowly. Tracking how information flows through the graph structure reveals its origin and nature.
Cyberpsychology: Emotion as the Hidden Driver of Social Behavior in Online NetworksWSDM
uses Track how emotions and moral sentiments spread through online networks, shaping polarization, trust, and collective behavior.
why it works It works because emotion is contagious in ways logic is not. When you measure what emotions accompany statements and which groups see which emotions, you can trace how affect organizes social fragmentation. A Spectral Heterogeneous Diffusion Framework for Knowledge-aware RecommendationWSDM

why it works It works because real knowledge graphs have errors and gaps, but they still reflect a distribution you can learn. By fitting that distribution and regenerating the graph from it, you remove noise while preserving the semantic structure humans would accept, focusing on recommendation-relevant parts.
Incremental Multi-Behavior RecommendationSIGIR
uses Train a graph model on streaming data with multiple behavior types (views, favorites, purchases), updating incrementally without forgetting what it learned about old data.
why it works Different behavior types reveal complementary preference signals. Incremental learning on streams avoids expensive retraining while multi-task learning ensures each behavior type's signal survives.
Same Frequency Begets Shared Interests: Popular-Niche Wavelet Graph Learning for Multimodal RecommendationSIGIR
uses Decompose user interests into popular and niche frequency bands, then spread each through separate graphs to balance recommendation diversity.
why it works It works because user interests naturally cluster at different scales: some people love blockbusters, others seek obscure gems. Frequency decomposition isolates these bands cleanly. Unsupervised 2D Image-Based 3D Model Retrieval via Decision Boundary Alignment and Graph Semantic PropagationSIGIR
uses Align decision boundaries across 2D and 3D domains using adversarial keeping it simple, then propagate semantic neighborhood structure across modalities via graph message passing.
why it works It works because the gap between 2D and 3D spaces is partly artificial: there exists a shared semantic structure that both modalities should respect. Aligning boundaries forces both sides to agree on what 'similar' means. Propagating neighborhoods afterward ensures the model treats similar shapes as near regardless of view modality.
Dynamic Memory Forest: Constructing and Tracing Conversational Trajectories for Long-Term ConversationSIGIR
uses Organize conversation memories into a forest of trees that grow by linking related memories and using voting to decide connections.
why it works It works because grouping related memories together makes finding relevant context cheaper, and voting on connections ensures only meaningfully related memories are linked rather than noise.
NeurPIU: Neurobiologically Inspired Personalized Intent Understanding in Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Model user mental states as a connected graph, then spread activation through it to retrieve the states relevant to the current query, with activation fading over time.
why it works It works because mental states are interconnected—thinking of one thing naturally activates related thoughts. By modeling this as network activation that weakens with time, you capture how recent events influence current understanding more strongly than distant history, just as the brain does.
DIGEST: Dynamic Graph Refinement with Dual Contrastive Semantic Transfer for Multimodal RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learns to recommend by comparing what users clicked before with images and text of items, iteratively pruning weak signals and keeping only connections to truly similar items.
why it works It works because most signal in the data comes from a few true relationships; weak connections add noise. By strengthening only the edges the model is confident about and aligning image/text meaning across views, it captures reliable patterns that transfer to new users.
GNN-Based Item Indexing for LLM-Enhanced RecommendationSIGIR
uses Creates short, meaningful item labels by learning which collaborative signals and attributes belong together, then organizing them hierarchically to balance label length against prediction quality.
why it works It works because meaningful labels encode genuine structure in how users interact with items. Short hierarchical labels let language models rapidly identify items without ambiguity, and organizing by collaborative patterns ensures the encoding preserves what matters for recommendations.
Hypergraph Diffusion-Based Sequential Ensemble for CTR PredictionSIGIR
uses Ensemble multiple click prediction models using a diffusion process that spread weights across user behavior sequences, applying structure-aware smoothing to preserve item dependencies.
why it works It works because diffusion across a behavior graph lets information from related items influence the prediction without destroying what we know about item connections. Structure-aware noise injection (from the graph) is smarter than isotropic noise because it respects actual relationships.
Sim.API: A Middleware to Simplify the Use of User Simulators for Shared Tasks in Conversational SearchSIGIR
uses Provide API middleware to simplify running user simulators in shared tasks; record interactions uniformly so conversational search systems can be evaluated consistently.
why it works It works because standardized evaluation infrastructure removes technical barriers, enabling researchers to focus on improving their systems rather than wrestling with infrastructure. Uniform run recording makes systems directly comparable since they all generate output in the same format.
Content-Based Dataset Knowledge Graphs for Dataset SearchSIGIR
uses Enrich dataset search by extracting relationships not just from metadata but directly from the data files themselves, then reranking results using those connections.
why it works It works because metadata is incomplete, but the data itself holds semantic signals—patterns and connections—and by treating those signals as a knowledge graph, you can score datasets not only by name-match but by how they relate conceptually to what you're looking for.
Retrieval-Augmented Contrastive Learning for Dynamic Graph Anomaly DetectionSIGIR
uses Learn what normal node behavior looks like by comparing similar nodes and finding similar exemplars in the graph, then flag nodes that deviate from this normal pattern.
why it works It works because anomalies are rare and similar normal examples far outweigh anomalies. By retrieving genuinely similar normal nodes and using them as the baseline, deviations become obvious and the method avoids false alarms from isolated normal nodes.
Delay-Aware Sequential Recommendation with Dynamic Graphs and Variate-Temporal DecompositionSIGIR
uses Predict next interactions by routing information across multiple time lags in a dynamic graph, accounting for delays in when logs arrive.
why it works It works because real logs often lag behind user actions by hours or days, creating a shifted history. By learning which lags matter and routing information across them, the model aligns its hidden state with the true timeline rather than the delayed visible timeline, fixing temporal misalignment.
TDHGNN: A Temporal Directed Hypergraph Neural Network for Bitcoin Fraud DetectionSIGIR
uses Model Bitcoin transactions as a hypergraph where transactions and addresses are players in a network, learning which ones are suspicious by how they connect across time.
why it works Fraud isn't about individual transactions—it's about patterns of flow. A hypergraph captures how one transaction connects many addresses together, and suspicious ones tend to have distinctive connection patterns (like unusual flows or timing). Learning these patterns finds fraud you'd miss in isolation.
A Multi-Granularity Game-Theoretic Approach to Weakly Supervised Temporal Article GroundingSIGIR
uses Ground video clips to text sentences using game theory where video clips and text units cooperate within their own layer to highlight important features, then cooperate across layers for alignment.
why it works Game-theoretic cooperation models how good features support each other. Within text, important words reinforce context sentences; within video, salient clips reinforce frames. Layered cooperation ensures word-level matches feed into sentence-level matches, avoiding the noise of flat similarity.
Named Entity-Driven Graph Smoothing to Enhance Pretrained Document Embeddings in Clustering TasksSIGIR
uses Extract named entities from documents, then smooth document representations using a network of entity similarity so nearby documents in the network are treated as similar.
why it works Documents sharing the same company or location are contextually related even if their words differ; spreading this entity-level signal as smoothness makes the metric capture human-meaningful similarity.
A Graph-Enhanced MLLM for Hierarchical Multimodal Emotion Understanding and Support in ConversationsSIGIR
uses Model emotion as information flowing across a graph of speakers and modalities, where edges capture who influences whom, then weight the paths by which ones matter most.
why it works Emotion spreads through conversation via who speaks to whom and which signals (voice, text, face) carry the most weight. By flowing information along those edges with learnable importance, you capture the real dependencies.
Cross-Category Basket Recommendation via Transactional Debiasing and Graph PropagationSIGIR
uses Score which products complement each other by tallying co-purchases while penalizing popularity, then spreading this signal across similar items.
why it works It works because true complements are rare and drowned out by bestseller noise. By downweighting globally-frequent items, you isolate real complementary signals. Spreading that signal via a similarity graph lets you recommend complementary items even if they're never co-purchased.
Precision at Scale: An End-to-End Graph-based Framework for Mitigating Network Interference in TikTok A/B TestsSIGIR
uses Learns how people influence each other in the network, then splits users into groups to measure true experiment effects more accurately.
why it works It works because when you treat interference as a learned pattern rather than a fixed guess, you get better groups. Then when you measure effects within groups instead of globally, you remove the noise from people affecting each other. CUPED further reduces random wobble by using data collected before the experiment started.
Cross-Stage Signal Propagation for Negative Filtering in Multi-Stage Ad DeliverySIGIR
uses Signals about low-value ads are passed backward from later ranking stages to earlier stages, preventing computation on ads destined for rejection.
why it works Multi-stage pipelines compute sequentially, wasting resources on ads later stages will filter out anyway. Backward signal propagation tells earlier stages which ads have historically been rejected downstream, so they can skip computation on those. This trades a small signal-passing overhead for large savings on useless computation.
MonacGraph: A Monadic Second-Order Logic Extended Graph Database System with Community-Aware StorageSIGIR
uses Query graph data using set constraints to find groups of related objects and retrieve structures like communities where items cluster together.
why it works It works because real-world entities form natural clusters; representing them in a graph and querying for cohesive subgroups finds these patterns efficiently, treating the graph structure itself as a index on which clusters exist.
Graph-Enhanced Sentence Retrieval for Multi-Document Summarization in Low-Resource LanguagesSIGIR

why it works Sentences interact via discourse (earlier sentences set context for later ones); spreading information through that graph captures which sentences are central to meaning. Ranking by this network-aware score selects faithful summaries.
302 papers

Turning meaning into nearness

A great deal of this field begins by placing every item — a word, a product, a person — as a point in a space, arranged so that things people treat as alike sit close together. Meaning becomes geometry.

Why it works — the principle

It works because once similar things are placed near each other, the vague question 'what is like this?' becomes the precise, cheap question 'what is nearby?' — and nearness is easy to measure and behaves sensibly. The deeper trick it exploits: relationships too tangled to define by hand turn into simple distances once the layout is learned well, and only a few directions in that space usually carry the real meaning.

Multi-view Semantic Contrastive Alignment for Multimodal RecommendationWWW
uses Aligns user-item relationships learned from behavior against enriched item relationships learned from images, text, and links by maximizing their mutual consistency.
why it works Different views of the same items should tell the same story about who likes what. When you force them to agree, you extract the true signal that appears across all views, filtering out the noise that only shows up in one.
Embedding Enhancement via Fine-Tuned Language Models for Learner-Item Cognitive ModelingWWW

why it works Language models encode rich semantics, but they optimize for text prediction, not educational diagnosis. Realigning their representations to match educational labels transfers their semantic knowledge to the right goal—like turning a compass needle from north toward your target.

Conditional Information Extraction with Diffusion Model on Fact-Condition Star GraphWWW
uses Extract fact triples and their conditional constraints by progressively refining noisy guesses into clean quintuples.
why it works Starting from noise and removing it step-by-step works because each step moves toward the data you actually want. When you know the hierarchical structure (facts in the middle, conditions around them), you can focus refinement on the parts that matter, not waste effort on all possible combinations.
RobustExplain: Evaluating Robustness of LLM-Based Explanation Agents for RecommendationWWW
uses Test whether language-model explanations for product recommendations stay consistent and sensible when user behavior is slightly disturbed.
why it works Small changes to input that don't change the right recommendation should barely change the explanation. If the explanation swings wildly, the model is relying on brittle details, not the core reason. Measuring multiple kinds of consistency (meaning, words, structure) reveals where the model is fragile.
Accurate Trajectory Recovery in Underserved Areas via Location Inference from Web Crowdsourced DataWWW
uses Build multi-scale spatial grids to reconstruct missing trajectory positions by sampling and refining details from coarse global patterns to fine local ones.
why it works It works because trajectories have structure at multiple scales: far-away context shapes broad movement direction, while nearby grid cells refine exact positions. Sampling around observed points and progressively refining captures both global and local patterns efficiently.

uses Sort features by their local topology pattern, then model both homophilic and heterophilic structures using dual-channel networks that handle features independently.
why it works Homophily and heterophily exist not just between nodes but within individual feature features. By sorting features before processing them, you align the computation to the actual structure, letting the model learn which features behave homophilically and which heterophilically.
Bridging Time and Domains: A Time-aware Framework for Cross-Domain Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Predict the next item by decoupling user preferences over time from the items themselves, then weight cross-domain information by comparing temporal densities.
why it works User preferences drift over time, and this drift is domain-specific. By separating the time pattern (which is universal) from the content pattern (which is domain-specific), you can transfer time-aware preference structure across domains without forcing domain-specific biases.
Macro-Micro Collaborative Learning for Logical Data Center Microservice Indicators ForecastingWWW
uses Model microservice dependencies as a hierarchy and forecast each indicator using causal relationships between indicators within services, weighted by interaction strength.
why it works Forecasting works better when you model the causal path: workload drives resource usage which drives latency. By explicitly modeling this causality and weighting the strongest causal links, you reduce noise and improve accuracy compared to treating all correlations equally.

TargetMR: Learning Modality Target for Multimodal RecommendationWWW
uses Identify which objects in images and text are central to the item, then weight their representations more heavily so that core content dominates over decorative elements.
why it works It works because items always contain both essential and cosmetic parts, but standard methods treat them equally. Identifying and emphasizing what's truly important lets the recommendation score reflect what the item actually offers, not noise from background decoration or irrelevant context.

why it works It works because a single fixed drawing can hide properties or make them hard to see in the image. Dir-GD: Directed Graph DistillationWWW

why it works It works because full training on a billion-edge graph exhausts hardware, but small communities capture local patterns. Training on pieces and aggregating preserves topology because community structure is already the essential skeleton. The compressed synthetic graph holds the key relationships without storing every edge.

Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Generalized Embedding Learning in Federated RecommendationWWW
uses Stabilize item numeric fingerprints during federated training by minimizing loss at points least likely to overfit when data distributions change.

why it works Comparing before and after helps the model learn which features control emotion versus which are incidental, so it can shift one while keeping the rest intact.
ARCHER: Shooting Straight in Multimodal E-Commerce Search at Alibaba with Progressive AlignmentWWW
uses Combines images and product descriptions into a shared measurement space, refining similarity step-by-step from category match to specific product differences.
why it works When image and text representations sit close in the same space, find similar becomes find nearby; progressively forcing them into alignment ensures only truly matched items cluster.
C-HyPOD: Causal Hyperbolic Representation Learning with Prototype Orthogonal Disentanglement for Graph Out-of-Distribution RecommendationWWW
uses Learns separate features for different user interests using curved space geometry that naturally models hierarchies without requiring labeled environments.
why it works Hyperbolic geometry compresses hierarchies efficiently; disentangling features removes confounding, letting each features capture one pure interest type.
The State of the Internet: Insights from Security IndicatorsWWW
uses Measures deployment of foundational security practices across the Internet using standardized, non-invasive indicators that capture the Internet security baseline.
why it works Standardized metrics aggregate heterogeneous systems into comparable scores; non-invasive measurement scales to measure entire Internet populations without damage.
EmeraldApp: An AI-Driven Tool for Detecting Greenwashing in Sustainability ClaimsWWW

why it works It works because grouping similar evidence together in a searchable store makes finding relevant facts fast and reliable. Combining two retrieval sources (database and knowledge graph) gives more angles to catch false claims—if one source misses context, the other often catches it.
MCoT-MVS: Multi-level Vision Selection by Multi-modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Composed Image RetrievalWWW
uses Weight different parts of an image by importance to the user's intent, then align those weighted parts with target images in a shared space where similar images sit close together.
why it works It works because the user intent is hidden—only certain image details matter to their modified request. Weighting by relevance lets you ignore visual noise. Node Role-Guided LLMs for Dynamic Graph ClusteringWWW
uses Represent nodes as two separate parts—one capturing their structural role (hub, bridge, etc.) and another capturing their cluster membership—then use learned role archetypes to explain why clusters formed.
why it works It works because roles and clusters are independent properties; a hub node matters structurally whether it sits in cluster A or B. Using five archetypal role anchors lets a language model discuss nodes in human terms ('this hub connects three groups'), making clusters interpretable.
ConceptFormer: Towards Graph-Native Grounding of Large Language Models via Latent Concept InjectionWWW

why it works It works because a knowledge graph's topology encodes relationships and meaning—by representing nodes as lists of numbers that capture this structure, you give the model access to organized world knowledge. Injecting these lists of numbers into the language model's native lists of numbers space means it can now reason with structured facts alongside learned text patterns, improving factual accuracy without rewriting the model.

why it works It works because noise in graph structure compounds through message passing—each layer amplifies perturbations. Filtering recovers the true underlying graph. The information bottleneck principle ensures explanations are both faithful to the model's decision and compact; you keep just enough information to explain, discarding noise and irrelevant details that bloat but don't clarify.
LongRanker: Efficient One-Pass Document Reranking with Long-Context Large Language ModelsWWW

why it works It works because ranking listwise (comparing all at once) beats sliding-window ranking (comparing subsets)—documents interact and contextualize each other. Hierarchical encoding efficiently tells the model document order and within-document words positions.
HL-CMR: Hypergraph Learning for Cross-Modal RetrievalWWW

why it works It works because real user-item graphs have varying density and structure; by letting the geometric space bend to fit the actual topology rather than forcing flat-space assumptions, distances in the surface capture true behavioral similarity.
OwlerLite: Scope- and Freshness-Aware Web Retrieval for LLM AssistantsWWW
uses Score web pages by relevance and freshness, then retrieve the top-scoring results that match the user's chosen scope.

CiteLLM: An Agentic Platform for Trustworthy Scientific Reference DiscoveryWWW
uses Scores candidate references by relevance and validates them by measuring how close their meaning is to the author's claims through paragraph-level matching.
why it works It works because ranking lets you put the best references first without needing perfect scores, and nearness in meaning-space lets you quickly tell if a reference actually supports a claim by checking how close their content sits together.

uses Extracts property terms from text using optimized prompts, then scores each term by how close it sits to standardized vocabulary concepts, aligning to canonical definitions.
why it works It works because terms that mean the same thing should sit close together in a shared meaning space. By mapping extracted text to a standard vocabulary through nearness, you force consistency—different authors' similar ideas now use the same terms, making the knowledge graph machine-readable and reusable.
Conditional Diffusion Guided Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Graph CompletionWWW
uses Generates entity numeric fingerprints via diffusion that start from a general space and are guided by multi-domain graphs, scores how close the final numeric fingerprints preserve both domain-general and domain-specific signals.
why it works It works because each knowledge graph is a partial view of the truth. Diffusion gradually refines numeric fingerprints from a neutral starting guess, and conditioning on all graphs at once means similar entities naturally sit close in the final space, while domain-specific differences are preserved because they're explicitly kept separate during refinement.
Many Hands Make Light Work: Group-based Information Diffusion Prediction over Long-Context CascadesWWW
uses Learns group numeric fingerprints where users adopting together sit close in a shared space, predicts the next group of adopters by finding nearby groups in long information cascades.
why it works It works because adoption spreads in groups, not individuals—one adopter influences many similar others. By placing users close in the numeric fingerprints space when they adopt together, finding the next group becomes finding the nearest cluster of non-adopters, and nearness is cheap to compute even in massive cascades.
Cross-Modal Rationale Transfer for Explainable Humanitarian Classification on Social MediaWWW
uses Learns which words and which image patches best explain a humanitarian label, transferring visual clues from text rationales so one mode teaches the other.
why it works Humans explain text decisions by pointing to key words, which costs time to annotate. Images need the same explanation effort. By learning which words matter, then finding image patches that sit near similar words in a shared space, the method reuses text annotation to teach image explanation without extra labeling. Similar pieces cluster together, so image regions near text explanations are likely relevant too.
Anatomy of Generative Scam Campaigns in Online Advertising EcosystemsWWW
uses Analyzes scam ad campaigns by decomposing them into persuasion templates, variants, and rotation schedules to understand how scammers scale and evade detection.
why it works Scammers don't send one ad; they send thousands of near-copies, swapping details and timing to avoid detection systems that spot identical content. By treating campaigns as multi-layer structures—templates plus variations—the analysis reveals that effective mitigation must detect patterns at the campaign level, not just individual ads. Campaign structure reveals intent and operation, which one-off detection misses; the pattern of coordination is the signal.
DiSCoQR: Diffusion-Driven Semantic Compression for Robust Image Steganography in Standard QR CodesWWW
uses Hides large images inside QR codes by compressing them to a semantic representation that can be stored as binary data and reconstructed with high fidelity.
why it works Images are huge but QR codes are tiny. A diffusion model learns the semantic features that matter for a class of images, not every pixel. Compressing to these features drops 400 pixels to 1 bit of information while keeping 'what the image is for' intact. Binary data embeds seamlessly into QR structure, and reconstruction retrieves the semantic version of the original, which serves the downstream task even if pixels differ—the essence survived the compression.
Quantum-enhanced Representation Learning and Matching Learning for RecommendationWWW
uses Quantum operations learn to score and match user preferences and items by encoding them in ways that preserve closeness of similar things.
why it works Quantum superposition can explore many feature encodings simultaneously and interference patterns can highlight which encodings keep similar items near; matching then reduces to finding nearest neighbors, making it fast and trustworthy.
Community-Preserving Temporal Graph Backboning via Joint Spectral Analysis of LaplaciansWWW
uses Find the most stable recurring patterns across time-snapshots of a network by treating them as waves and keeping only the lowest-frequency modes.
why it works Low-frequency modes persist across time, while noise and short-lived quirks vanish at high frequency; keeping them captures what actually matters and removes everything that's redundant, shrinking the network without losing the true story.
Missingness-aware Federated Contrastive Learning on Semantic GraphsWWW
uses Learn shared representations of incomplete graphs by estimating missing structure from available data, then compare nodes using similarity across these reconstructed learned patterns.
why it works Missing data breaks standard methods, but if you estimate the gaps as probable edges and reconstruct locally, nodes can still be compared fairly; similarity learned from reconstructed graphs captures meaningful patterns even when pieces are missing.
Robust Harmful Meme Detection under Missing Modalities via Shared Representation LearningWWW
uses Detect harmful memes by learning one shared representation space where text and image features live together, so you can compare them even when one modality is missing.
why it works Text and images are different modalities, so standard comparisons fail when one is gone; projecting both into a shared space means you can still measure closeness and compare against harmful patterns using whatever modality remains.
Retracing and Restoring: Chronological Context Preservation for Effective Dynamic RecommendationWWW
uses Retraces a user's interaction history in reverse chronological order and restores numeric fingerprints to their original context, capturing how preferences shift over time for better recommendations.
why it works It works because users change; restoring each past interaction to its original time-specific numeric fingerprints prevents current preferences from overwriting historical patterns, so you see the true trajectory of preference evolution rather than a blended average.
HiFi-WF: Toward Realistic Website Fingerprinting with Multi-tab and Subpage RecognitionWWW
uses Classifies websites and their specific subpages from network traffic by treating it as a hierarchical multi-label problem, weighting which features distinguish pages at each level.
why it works It works because websites have structure (homepage contains all subpages, subpages inherit parent features); modeling this hierarchy lets you share what's common while isolating what's unique at each level, reducing the features needed to separate fine-grained pages.
Evolving Proxy Kills Drift: Data-Efficient Streaming Time Series Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Detects anomalies in streaming time series by evolving a small proxy summary of historical data and selecting lightweight parameters relevant to the current distribution.
why it works It works because full historical data grows too large; a proxy that evolves with new patterns gives you representative historical knowledge without storing everything, and sparse parameter activation lets you adapt to new anomaly types without retraining the whole model.
Graph Aggregation Beyond Homophily Assumption: a more meaningful way to model networksWWW
uses Aggregates information on networks by weighting connections based on their curvature (geometric influence), combining node features, topology, and label information.
why it works It works because network curvature measures how 'bent' the space is between nodes; high curvature connections are unexpected (contradicting the network's natural geometry), so down-weighting them removes noisy edges while keeping structurally consistent ones.
SIsomap: Secure Collaborative Manifold Learning with Reducing Communication CostsWWW
uses Securely learns low-dimensional numeric fingerprints from datasets held by multiple parties without revealing their data by using shared secrets and fast shortest-path protocols.
why it works It works because surface learning finds the simplest low-dimensional space where distance is preserved; computing this securely is hard, but exploiting the specific properties of the shortest-path algorithm lets you skip expensive computations, and shared secrets let parties compute together without seeing each other's data.
Unleashing the Potential of Sparse Attention on Long-term Behaviors for CTR PredictionWWW
uses Focuses focus on the most important starting guess user actions by chunking behavior histories in ways matched to each person, using separate focus scorers for long-term interests, shifts, and recent actions.
why it works Computing focus to all starting guess actions is too slow and most actions are noise. By attending selectively to chunks that matter most per user and separating focus by timescale, the model sees signal without computing pointlessly over history.
WebGeoInfer: Structure-Free Multi-Stage Framework for Geolocation Inference from Exposed Device Web InterfacesWWW
uses Maps clues extracted from web pages into geographic coordinates by measuring how closely patterns match known locations.
why it works Geographic inference works because places have consistent, repeating patterns in language and layout. Measuring how similar unknown content is to known reference locations reveals the most likely position, just as finding what existing thing is most similar to a new thing tells you what category it belongs to.
Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative RecommendationsWWW
uses Predicts which items users want by learning hierarchical session structure and using focused focus only on the most relevant past interactions instead of considering everything equally.
why it works User preferences follow hierarchical patterns: sessions contain meaningful units, and not all past events matter equally for the next choice. By recognizing this structure and focusing computation on signal-rich moments, the model avoids noise that would cloud the true preference pattern, making predictions more accurate.
Towards Practical LLM Unlearning: Efficient, Modular, and Retain-FreeWWW
uses Removes unwanted concepts from language models by adjusting only the output layer to reorient the mapping between internal meanings and output words.
why it works The core layers of a language model learn general meaning and reasoning. The output layer learns which internal meanings should produce which words. By only adjusting that output layer, you block undesired outputs without disturbing the reasoning underneath, preserving what the model knows while controlling what it says.
What Should I Cite? A RAG Benchmark for Academic Citation PredictionWWW
uses Predicts which existing papers a new paper should cite by ranking them using a retrieval-augmented pipeline that finds similar papers then generates explanations.
why it works Citation is fundamentally about relevance: papers cited are those that share methods, problems, or ideas with the new work. By first retrieving papers similar in content and then re-ranking them through generation, the system exploits two truths: retrieval finds the neighborhood to search in, and generation refines which neighbors matter most.
Exploring Fine-Tuning for Tabular Foundation ModelsWWW
uses Tests when adjust tabular foundation models improves performance and calibration versus using zero-shot or simpler adjustment methods.
why it works Foundation models trained on diverse data learn general patterns that often transfer well to new problems. adjust adjusts those patterns for specificity, but risks overfitting to small quirks of the new task. The study reveals that when diversity and task similarity are high, zero-shot works; when the task is very specific, carefully-tuned adjustments help.
Robust LLM-Based Website Fingerprinting under Dynamic Real-World ConditionsWWW
uses Identifies which websites Tor users visit by learning a robust description of traffic patterns that stays accurate as websites change and network conditions vary.
why it works Traffic patterns drift: websites update, network conditions differ, users take new subpages. Real-world fingerprinting fails because patterns learned on old traffic don't match new traffic. By adjust on diverse, unlabeled real traffic and learning representations that capture essential patterns regardless of superficial change, the method finds the core signature that survives evolution.
