Train Large-Use Small: Optimizing within the Theoretical Limits of Embedding-based RetrievalWWW
uses Reduce the number of features in lists of numbers representations and combine multiple lists of numbers to search for relevant documents, overcoming the limitations of single dense lists of numbers.
why it works This works because high-dimensional space has a curse: points spread out and become far from everything, making 'nearby' nearly meaningless. Cutting features brings points back together; combining multiple lists of numbers gives you what a single lists of numbers cannot.
PWAVEP: Purifying Imperceptible Adversarial Perturbations in 3D Point Clouds via Spectral Graph WaveletsWWW
uses Removing points from a cloud by detecting which ones sit in high-frequency features (rough/noisy directions in the data), because attackers hide fake points there.
why it works It works because true geometry lives in smooth low-frequency patterns—if you remove rough noisy features the genuine points stay clean. Attackers must distort high-frequency channels to stay imperceptible, so filtering those out restores the true shape.
Cross-city Time Series Forecasting with Retrieval-Augmented Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Retrieve the most semantically relevant historical time-series patterns and reference documents from data-rich source cities, then use them as context clues to guide forecast predictions in data-scarce target cities.
why it works It works because cities with similar transportation patterns or weather dynamics tend to behave alike; if you find the right neighbors in the source data, their historical examples become valid lessons for the target. Choosing only the helpful neighbors avoids importing irrelevant or misleading patterns that would degrade the forecast.
Relation-Aware Multimodal Analogical Reasoning with Modality Fingerprints and Adaptive GatingWWW
uses Learn which input modalities (image, text, graph structure) are most trustworthy for each kind of entity, then use that trust weight to blend them adaptively when reasoning about analogies.
why it works It works because pictures clarify concrete objects but obscure abstract ideas; text and relationships work the opposite way. By scoring which modality aligns best with the current query context, you blend the right signals and ignore noise, making reasoning both more accurate and interpretable.
FalconScope: Effective and Efficient Detection of Hidden Web Interfaces in IoT DevicesWWW
uses Map out the true request routing paths inside device firmware, generate HTTP requests that trigger those paths, then validate if the device lets unauthorized users access them.
why it works It works because the firmware's internal logic routing is deterministic once you reconstruct it; you can then generate requests that exercise every path without guessing. Language model reasoning helps craft requests that actually match the communication protocol, making detection fast and thorough.
A Dual-Channel Contrastive Learning Framework for Anomaly Detection in Dynamic Graph StructuresWWW
uses Store how node features change over time, detect unusual nodes by measuring how different they are from learned similarity patterns at multiple time scales, using past snapshots as memory.
why it works It works because normal behavior is consistent across time; if a node's pattern suddenly diverges from what its neighbors historically looked like, that's a red flag. Keeping a memory of past states lets you spot one-off deviations cleanly and compare behavior at different speeds.
KMLP: A Scalable Hybrid Architecture for Web-Scale Tabular Data ModelingWWW
uses Learn flexible curved activation functions for each numerical feature individually to convert them to cleaner forms, then pass all cleaned features through layers that selectively weight and combine them into predictions.
why it works It works because real-world numbers often follow skewed or non-standard shapes; learning a custom curve per feature automates the tedious manual cleanup engineers usually do by hand. Once features are well-shaped, selective mixing (gating) of high-order combinations extracts only the interaction patterns that matter.
Taming the Long Tail: Efficient Item-wise Sharpness-Aware Minimization for LLM-based Recommender SystemsWWW
uses keeping it simple training by penalizing loss-landscape sharpness at the item level, focusing the penalty on products that the model struggles with, to improve accuracy on rare items without hurting popular ones.
why it works It works because sharp loss landscapes mean tiny weight changes flip predictions wildly—a sign of brittle, overfit solutions. Item-level sharpness focuses keeping it simple only where it helps: tail items benefit most from smoothing because they have fewer examples, while head items already have enough data to stay stable.
Collaborative Subgraph Learning based Spectrum Sensing under Partial ObservationsWWW
uses The system learns which radio frequencies are in use by treating all frequencies as a connected graph where each device only observes its nearby frequencies, then shares learned patterns across the network.
why it works Frequencies that behave similarly sit naturally close in graph space. When each device learns only from its local neighborhood but the graph connects everything, shared structure means a device seeing only fragments can infer the whole by following connections to neighbors' observations.
Frequency-Corrupt Based Graph Self-Supervised LearningWWW
uses The system learns graph representations by deliberately destroying low-frequency features and forcing the model to reconstruct them from high-frequency remnants, enriching how it captures important local structure.
why it works Deleting low-frequency patterns forces the model to extract and preserve local detail, the high-frequency signals that matter. When reconstruction demands both types of signals work together, the model learns to blend them effectively instead of ignoring one.
Towards Foundation Models for MMKG: Multi-Task Inductive Generalization via Task-Aware RoutingWWW
uses Route different types of information through specialized pathways based on which task is being solved, so each task gets only relevant signals.
why it works It works because different tasks (link prediction, entity alignment, entity linking) have conflicting needs for how information flows. Routing lets each task ignore noise and contradictions that would confuse a single universal path.
From Lexical and Semantic to Predictive Search: Evolution or Involution?WWW
uses Convert text and information into locations in a space where similar things are nearby, then use those spatial relationships to find and predict answers.
why it works It works because measuring nearness in a well-designed space is far cheaper and faster than parsing text word-by-word, and the space preserves semantic meaning as distance. Once you can measure similarity cheaply, search and prediction become tractable.
Riemannian Liquid Spatio-Temporal Graph NetworkWWW
uses Model how graphs change over time using differential equations on curved spaces that respect the graph's natural geometry.
why it works It works because many real graphs have hidden geometry (hierarchies, cycles, clusters) that Euclidean space distorts. Curved spaces preserve this geometry as distance, so differential equations solved on the curve capture dynamics faithfully without stretching or compressing the structure.
Efficient Learning of Sparse Representations from InteractionsWWW
uses Learn numeric fingerprints where most features are zero, keeping only a few active features per item to cut storage and serving cost dramatically.
why it works It works because recommendation patterns are sparse: each item matters for only a few user segments. By forcing numeric fingerprints to use only active features, you automatically encode an interpretable index where active features reveal which segment an item belongs to.
Moral Outrage Shapes Commitments Beyond Attention: Multimodal Moral Emotions on YouTube in Korea and the USWWW
uses Classify emotions in video thumbnails and titles by learning from human-labeled examples, then measure which emotions drive engagement.
why it works It works because emotional framing leaves detectable signals in both images and text: chosen colors, selected words, focal composition all express emotion. Learning these patterns from examples lets you classify at scale, then correlating emotions with engagement reveals which ones drive behavior.
Scalable and Provable Biclique-Preserving Clustering: The Power of Counting-based ApproachesWWW
uses Count how many dense bicliques pass through each edge to weight edges, then cluster nodes by high-weight edge adjacency.
why it works In a bipartite graph, edges that sit in many dense bicliques are central to the structure; weighting by count lets you use simple clustering to find cohesive groups without expensive enumeration. Counting is linear; enumeration is exponential.
PRISM: LLM-Guided Semantic Clustering for High-Precision TopicsWWW
uses adjust a text encoder on sparse language-model labels so texts about related topics sit close in numeric fingerprints space.
why it works When a few labeled samples mark topic boundaries, retraining the encoder to push similar texts together and far-apart texts apart reshapes the entire space so that clustering in that new geometry separates topics cleanly and locally.
IntraAI: Bridging Human-AI Understanding Through Intelligent Interface DesignWWW
uses Visualize the model's internal signals and reasoning patterns so users can see and score which behaviors to trust.
why it works Hidden alignment and reasoning are opaque; making them visible lets users rank model outputs by understanding the signals behind them, converting black-box interaction into informed judgment.
Interpretable Dynamic Network Modeling of Tensor Time Series via Kronecker Time-Varying Graphical LassoWWW
uses Decompose time-varying dependencies between many variables into separate mode-specific networks multiplied together via Kronecker product.
why it works Entangling all dependencies creates exponential complexity; a Kronecker factorization forces the dependencies to split into independent pieces per mode. This reduces parameters and computation while making each network interpretable.
Tracking the Stray Sheep: Understanding DNS Response Manipulation in the WildWWW
uses Trace resolution paths through DNS chains to link dynamic results and detect when responses deviate from expected patterns.
why it works Legitimate DNS chains follow predictable patterns; anomalies in CNAME chains and intermediate nodes signal manipulation. Linking via chain structure works even when the same domain resolves to different servers.
MiningWeb Evolution: A Dataset of DOM Changes Across WebsitesWWW
uses Record absolute XPath positions of DOM nodes over time to detect structural changes and predict evolution patterns.
why it works Web layout changes in predictable ways; capturing node positions as a sequence lets you model which elements move, appear, or vanish. This abstraction ignores content noise and focuses on structural signal.
BHGap: A Deep Iterative Prompting and Multi-stage Alignment Framework for Dynamic Facial Expression RecognitionWWW
uses Align audio and visual features layer-by-layer so they sit close in the same space, then use a state-space model to route guidance between modalities.
why it works When audio and video features start far apart, they're hard to compare. Bringing them closer lets patterns emerge clearly. Routing guidance at each layer compounds the alignment effect, so later layers see progressively better-aligned signals.
Adaptive Graph Reweighting for Collaborative FilteringWWW
uses Reweight weak edges in the recommendation graph to improve how information spreads, strengthening the backbone network connectivity.
why it works Graph filters that smooth information across recommendations work best when the graph structure is well-connected. Weak edges act as bottlenecks that block good recommendations. Strengthening them lets signals propagate further and recommendations reach users better.
Graph-to-Tree: Topological Decomposition for Self-Supervised LearningWWW
uses Decompose graphs into tree structures, compute importance scores for nodes at each level, then contrast nodes that co-occur in tree bags.
why it works Trees reveal the essential backbone structure that drives information flow. Nodes that sit together in multiple decomposition contexts are likely structurally similar. Contrasting co-occurring nodes against distant ones teaches the model which patterns matter for the graph's actual topology.
negMIX: Negative Mixup for OOD Generalization in Open-Set Node ClassificationWWW
uses Mix synthetic out-of-distribution nodes with in-distribution ones, then contrast nodes of the same known class across different graph neighborhoods.
why it works Contrasting similar nodes makes them cluster tightly; contrasting dissimilar nodes pushes them apart. Negative mixup creates harder examples that sharpen the boundary between known and unknown classes. Cross-layer contrast compounds the signal by enforcing similarity across topological distances.
Long Story Short: Auditing U.S. Political Polarization in Recommendations for Long- vs. Short-form Videos on YouTubeWWW
uses Score videos by how closely they match a seed video's political leaning, then rank by alignment strength.
why it works Because people who consume certain political content tend to seek out similar viewpoints; ranking by how 'close' a video is to what you already watch identifies the content the algorithm will actually serve. The algorithm optimizes for this signal because it predicts engagement.
Beyond Patches: Superpixel Token-based Transformers for Attribute-Specific Fashion RetrievalWWW
uses Segment an image into coherent color/texture regions (superpixels), weight regions by how much they match the target fashion attribute, then rank images by how well they respond.
why it works Fashion attributes (e.g., 'floral print', 'collar') occupy specific image regions, not the whole picture; superpixels respect those boundaries better than uniform patches. By measuring only the regions that matter for the attribute, you filter background noise and get precise similarity scores based on the right signal.
Unveiling the Resilience of LLM-Enhanced Search Engines against Black-Hat SEO ManipulationWWW
uses Rank results by how closely they match both the query terms and a learned 'quality' score from an AI model; test whether adversaries can create pages that fool this dual ranking.
why it works Traditional SEO attacks target keyword matching; AI-enhanced search adds a learned quality score. Because the AI model encodes distributional patterns of legitimate pages, it naturally suppresses outliers and highly unusual text patterns. This reduces surface area for manipulation, though new attack lists of numbers (rewritten queries, segmented text) can still partially bypass it.
RARD: Rationale-First Blockwise Autoregressive Diffusion in Rationale?Dominated Graph GenerationWWW
uses Discovers which edges in a graph are truly important (the 'rationale') by ranking edges in order from most to least significant, then builds graphs block by block along that ranking.
why it works It works because real-world graphs have a small core of edges that determine the outcome, and the rest is noise. By learning the true ordering of importance first, you add the meaningful parts early (when the model is uncertain) and can safely ignore noise later; this puts the model's learning effort where it matters.
PULSE: Socially-Aware User Representation Modeling Toward Parameter-Efficient Graph Collaborative FilteringWWW
uses Builds a user profile from social connections and item relationships without storing individual user scores; ranks items by learned social similarity.
why it works It works because users in the same social circle tend to like the same things, so you can infer what someone wants by looking at their neighbors' choices. You save memory by not storing each user as a separate row; instead you compute each user on the fly from their social context.
Towards Graph Foundation Model: Node Feature Transfer Invariant Modeling on General GraphsWWW
uses Finds the invariant features in graph node data that mean the same thing across different domains, then transforms all node features into a shared unified format.
why it works It works because different graphs use different node features, but the underlying structure they encode is the same (e.g., 'importance' is importance whether measured as degree or centrality). Finding those invariants lets a single model work everywhere, like how pixels work for all images.
Are LLM Web Search Engines Sustainable? A Web-Measurement Study of Real-Time FetchingWWW
uses Measures the network traffic and latency cost of fetching fresh pages for each user query, comparing AI language systems answer engines against traditional cached search.
why it works It works because any system that serves answers must pay a cost in network and computation; by tracing where that cost goes (fetching versus caching, deduplication, etc.), you reveal which architectures are wasteful. Averaging costs over queries and modeling them as 'human equivalent' makes the overhead visible.
Adaptive Model and Strategy Routing for Cost-Efficient LLM ServicesWWW
uses Learns how to score which language model and reasoning strategy to use for each question, picking the best pair within budget.
why it works It works because you don't need to understand why a model is good—just recognize patterns in its behavior (cost and accuracy) on different types of queries. Close behavioral similarities in the learned space mean similar model performance.
MCRec: Few-Shot Multimodal Cover Recommendation via User Interest ProfilesWWW
uses Fuses visual and text features to score which cover image best matches a user's interests, from few examples.
why it works It works because people's visual preferences cluster; if you place images near each other when users consistently like both, then matching a new image to user preferences becomes finding the nearest neighbors in that space.
Spatial-Temporal Inference of Indoor RSSI and CQI for 3D Coverage Mapping using Dynamic Graph Attention NetworksWWW
uses Builds a learned graph structure from signal measurements and propagates information across it to predict indoor wireless signal strength and quality.
why it works It works because wireless signals don't travel in straight lines—they bounce and bend. A learned graph captures these hidden paths. Once you know which measurements are related, spreading information along those connections recovers the signal everywhere.
PLM: Point-Language Maps for Zero-shot Object Goal NavigationWWW
uses Encodes point clouds and text into the same space, then uses proximity in that space to navigate toward requested objects without training.
why it works It works because vision-language models already understand both scenes and goals from their training. If you place points and goals in the same space using these pre-trained scores, proximity naturally aligns: nearby points help reach goals.
Text-attributed Graph Condensation via Text Selection and Attribute MatchingWWW
uses Compress a graph-with-text dataset by selecting representative text chunks that preserve information (via mutual information) and aligning similarity scores between the original and compressed versions.
why it works This works because information-theoretic selection picks text that carries signal about the downstream task, discarding noise without losing capability. By aligning similarity matrices (distances between nodes in the original and compressed versions stay proportional), you preserve the model's ability to learn from relationship structure even when the data shrinks. Stable similarity alignment defeats high-spread of error training, which is why most compression fails.
Multimodal Graph Conditioned Diffusion Model for Video CaptioningWWW
uses Build a weighted graph connecting video, text, and semantic concept nodes; generate caption text by diffusing under graph-structure guidance, then prune low-quality nodes to refine the structure.
why it works This works because diffusion models are strong at iterative refinement under constraints. By conditioning on the multimodal graph structure, the model learns which semantic concepts are reachable from the video and text, guiding the caption toward meaningful cross-modal correlations rather than surface patterns. Pruning weak nodes tightens the structural signal, forcing the diffusion process to rely on genuine relationships rather than spurious ones.
Cardinality is Not Enough: Super Host Detection via Segmented Cardinality EstimationWWW
uses Estimate how many distinct peers a host connects to, weighted by shared IP subnet prefix, using lightweight segment hashing to infer whether connections cluster locally or spread widely.
why it works This works because attackers and victims often talk to hosts in the same subnet (same network block) more than they do to random internet hosts. Standard cardinality counting treats all IPs equally, missing that signal. By weighting subnet-local connections higher, the method detects when a host's connections are tightly clustered (attack or intrusion pattern) versus dispersed (normal client). Lightweight hashing keeps memory low while capturing the structure that matters.
Adaptive Multi-Interaction Web Semantic Graph RepresentationWWW
uses Learns how different relationship types between entities reinforce or weaken each other, then combines those learned patterns to score how likely connections are to form.
why it works It works because real networks have multiple kinds of ties between people, and those ties interact—a shared interest may strengthen a work relationship or compete with it. Learning those interaction patterns lets you predict what new connections will form better than treating each link type separately.
Super-Resolution of Urban Socioeconomic Indicators via Graph-Based Recommender SystemsWWW
uses Learns from which users visit which businesses, then predicts detailed neighborhood income and demographics by how those visit patterns cluster in semantic space.
why it works It works because businesses and users in the same place share economic circumstances—a neighborhood with upscale restaurants attracts different income profiles than one with discount stores. That semantic signal encoded in visit patterns captures neighborhood character at fine granularity where census data is too coarse.
E2PL: Effective and Efficient Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multi-view Multi-Label Class Incremental LearningWWW
uses Learns prototypes for each class and each possible pattern of missing data views, then decomposes their parameters using number grids factorization to avoid exponential growth.
why it works It works because when you have many views and many missing patterns, the number of combinations explodes exponentially. Breaking down prototypes into atomic components that can be recombined lets you handle all patterns with only linear growth in memory—you build new combinations from shared atomic pieces.
DOS: Dual-Flow Orthogonal Semantic IDs for Recommendation in MeituanWWW
uses Creates semantic codes representing items and users using a shared space, then rotates and preserves that space so the codes stay faithful to language model understanding.
why it works It works because when you compress items into codes for generation, you lose detail. By making sure those codes line up with how a language model naturally represents meaning, generation becomes more accurate. Orthogonal rotation preserves distances between semantically similar items, so the codes stay meaningful.
Beyond Factual Queries: A Novel Predictive Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Scores recommendations by measuring how similar a user's past interactions are to candidate items, then weights the language model's prediction by that similarity score.
why it works It works because users reveal preferences through their past behavior. If a candidate item is semantically close to things they already chose, it's likely they'll want it. Feeding that similarity signal as a weight tells the language model to lean toward personalized predictions over generic ones.
Distribution-Aligned Synthetic Text Generation via Tail-Aware EnhancementWWW
uses Finds rare feature combinations that a language model skips over, then uses targeted prompts and a diversity score to generate examples covering the tail of the distribution.
why it works It works because when language models generate data, they naturally favor common, safe examples and skip rare edge cases. By explicitly mining which features are underrepresented in numeric fingerprints space and steering generation toward them with a penalty that rewards diversity, you rebuild the full natural distribution.
Saliency-Guided Embedding Alignment for Query-to-Document Legal Case RetrievalWWW
uses Align short queries and long legal documents by learning which document segments matter most for each query, placing semantically similar ones nearby in learned space.
why it works It works because when you place things that answer the same query close together in a learned space, finding relevant documents becomes finding nearby points, which is fast and captures semantic meaning. Learning segment importance lets the model focus on the parts that actually matter for each query rather than wasting effort on irrelevant boilerplate.
Multi-Granularity Multi-Modal Knowledge Graph Representation Learning via Subgraph-Aware Adaptive Fusion and Hierarchical Relation ModelingWWW
uses Represent knowledge graph entities by fusing text and visual information with entity-specific weights that change for each entity, placing similar entities nearby in a shared semantic space.
why it works It works because different modalities carry different signal for different entities; allowing weights to vary per entity captures which modality actually helps predict relations for that entity. Nearby placement in shared space makes relational reasoning a local neighborhood operation, which preserves structure.
SemaCDR: LLM-Powered Transferable Semantics for Cross-Domain Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Recommend items to users in a new domain by using language models to create domain-agnostic semantic descriptions, then placing users and items with similar behaviors and descriptions close in shared space.
why it works It works because semantic descriptions from language models capture meaning independent of domain specifics (a 'laptop' is similar across stores); nearness in this domain-agnostic space lets knowledge from one domain transfer to another. Similar behaviors + similar descriptions = high confidence the transfer is meaningful.
FedRGL: Federated Riemannian Graph Learning in Mixed-Curvature Spaces with Ricci-Gated ConvolutionWWW
uses Learn personalized graph representations across federated clients by mapping each client's graph data to its own geometric space—choosing the right curvature for that client's structure—then combining via weighted message-passing.
why it works It works because different graph structures have different natural geometry: tree-like graphs fit hyperbolic space, clusters fit Euclidean, hierarchies fit spheres. Letting each client choose its own geometry means distance metrics capture actual structure. Adaptive gating weighs how much to trust each neighbor's signal based on local topology.
Hyperbolic Multimodal Generative Representation Learning for Generalized Zero-Shot Multimodal Information ExtractionWWW
uses Learn representations in a curved non-flat space where hierarchies among categories naturally fit without distortion.
why it works Works because hierarchies embed more faithfully in hyperbolic geometry—head categories sit near the origin and tail categories spread out, so distance captures the natural ranking.
Frugal Agents: Efficient Bio Reasoning via Long-Sequence Compression and Prompt-Gated MemoryWWW
uses Compress long sequences into brief summaries and gate the agent's memory to keep only states relevant to the current question.
why it works Works because only a tiny fraction of a long sequence ever matters to answer one question—compression extracts that fraction, and gating selection discards irrelevant memory.
MGK-RAG: Multi-Granularity Knowledge Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Radiology ReportWWW
uses Align image regions with fine-grained report details to learn a space where similar clinical content sits nearby.
why it works Works because fine-grained alignment (matching specific report phrases to specific image regions) preserves clinical semantics; coarse alignment loses details that matter.
Anchor Drift No More: Hierarchical Consistency-Guided Prompt Distillation for Incomplete Multimodal LearningWWW
uses Learn a representation space with fixed class anchors by aligning incomplete multimodal views through hierarchical distillation.
why it works Works because anchoring prevents class prototypes from drifting when inputs are partial, and multi-level distillation ensures all views converge to the same stable geometry.
Riemannian Graph Tokenizer for Structural Knowledge TransferWWW
uses Tokenize graph structures by numeric fingerprints them in curved spaces using geometric vocabulary of trees, cycles, and sequences.
why it works Works because non-flat geometry naturally preserves graph structure without distortion—trees, cycles, and sequences embed distinctly as geometric primitives, so words transfer across domains.
A Simplex Approach to Synthetic Knowledge Graph GenerationWWW
uses Analyze the geometric structures (simplices) in an input knowledge graph to learn patterns, then use those patterns to generate synthetic graphs of any desired size.
why it works It works because the higher-dimensional structures in a graph reveal how entities truly cluster and relate; capturing these patterns ensures the synthetic graph mimics the real one's organization, not just its individual facts.
SDR-CIR: Semantic Debias Retrieval Framework for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image RetrievalWWW
uses Adjusts the similarity score between query and candidate images by subtracting a penalty that measures how much the modification text relied on the reference image, reducing noise from semantic bias.
why it works Semantic bias happens when the description misses or misweights what makes the target unique. By explicitly modeling the reference image's contribution and subtracting it from the score, you penalize candidates that match only the biased parts and reward those that match the true target.
EDTF: A Plug-and-Play Learning Framework for Estimated Delivery Time TaskWWW
uses Converts delivery-time prediction from direct regression to ordinal ranking, then aligns short-hop predictions with long-haul predictions to create a self-supervised signal that improves temporal reasoning.
why it works Delivery times are ordered (earlier is better), so ranking captures structure that raw regression misses. Enforcing consistency between the sum of hops and the total time gives the model internal redundancy: multiple ways to get right, so it learns more robust representations than from the target alone.
STARK: Structure-Aware and Adaptive Representation Learning for Continual Knowledge Graph EmbeddingWWW
uses Places entities and relationships in a space so that correct connections sit nearby, scaling how far apart incorrect ones should be by how many wrong answers exist.
why it works It works because keeping correct answers near and wrong ones far apart makes the ranking right. Scaling the boundary by candidate count is crucial—when there are many wrong options, push them further away.
DeepUL: Deep Unlearning via Model SparsityWWW
uses Removes the influence of specific deleted data from a trained model by pruning away connections and projecting learned weights away from that data.
why it works It works because many connections in a model are redundant. Pruning them first disconnects deleted data, then projecting pushes remaining weights away so they no longer respond to it.
HeteroSim: Towards High-Fidelity Heterogeneous LLM Training Simulation on GPUsWWW
uses Predict training time on mixed GPU hardware by modeling peak compute speed per GPU type and per-link communication costs, then simulating overlaps between compute and data movement.
why it works Each GPU type has a maximum throughput ceiling determined by its architecture. By measuring actual message sizes and link speeds, you can forecast exactly when communication will bottleneck compute. This prediction requires no full simulation—only the roofline ceiling and observed traffic patterns.
ATGFB-MFF: Adaptive Text-Guided Fiber Bundle Feature Fusion with LLMs for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis and Emotion Recognition in ConversationsWWW
uses Decompose emotion from text, video, and audio into a shared semantic space plus per-modality offsets; combine them by penalizing inconsistency across modes and deviation from expected structure.
why it works Fiber bundle structure lets each modality 'live' on its own layer while maintaining alignment through a common base. When you penalize both inconsistency (modes disagreeing) and disorder (offsets deviating from geometric structure), each modality pulls the others toward coherent emotion signals.
LLM-enhanced Federated Graph Learning with Geometry-aware Graph Projection and Shared Subspace AggregationWWW
uses Project graphs onto curved spaces where local structure is preserved via curvature measures; share a common subspace across clients while each learns their own task.
why it works Ollivier-Ricci curvature encodes how tightly nodes cluster locally. Projecting to surface with known curvature ensures that similar nodes stay near each other. When all clients aggregate updates in this geometry-aware space, each can specialize without breaking shared structure.
TimeMar: Multi-Scale Autoregressive Modeling for Unconditional Time Series GenerationWWW
uses Predict time series values step-by-step by first generating coarse patterns, then refining at finer time scales; separate trend from seasonal patterns to prevent one from drowning out the other.
why it works Coarse patterns need fewer examples to learn and are more stable. Fine patterns are local refinements of coarse ones. By predicting coarse-first, you ground fine predictions in stable structure. Separating trend and seasonality prevents the trend (slow drift) from absorbing seasonal variation as noise.
Scaling Collaborative Filtering with Multimodal Contrastive Fine-tuningWWW
uses Scores user-item pairs by compressing interactions into unified representations across diverse data sources, then ranks items by similarity to user profile.
why it works It works because diverse recommendation data sources contain overlapping patterns about what users like; by finding a shared representation space where similar interactions sit close together, ranking becomes finding nearby items, which scales with large datasets the same way language models do.
QChunker: Learning Question-Aware Text Chunking for Domain RAG via Multi-Agent DebateWWW
uses Learns to split documents into semantic chunks by optimizing whether resulting chunks align with question intent, rewarding chunks that preserve logical coherence and context.
why it works It works because questions reveal what information patterns matter; chunks that answer questions together naturally preserve meaning, whereas arbitrary splits fragment knowledge—questions act as ground truth for correct semantic boundaries.
S-Path-RAG: Semantic-Aware Shortest-Path Retrieval Augmented Generation for Multi-Hop Knowledge Graph Question AnsweringWWW
uses Finds answers to multi-hop questions over knowledge graphs by ranking candidate paths by semantic relevance, encoding them in a compact space, then fuses path clues into the language model.
why it works It works because graphs have structure—meaningful paths cluster around relevant entities—so encoding paths as learned scores that reflect semantic fit naturally ranks true answer chains first; fusing compact path signals into reasoning preserves interpretable traces while staying efficient.
Déjà Vu of Strange Stickers! Enhancing Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Sticker Retrieval via Cross-Modal Intent AlignmentWWW
uses Improves sticker retrieval by aligning the abstract expressive intent of queries and stickers in a shared space so that semantically matched items sit close together.
why it works It works because users care about what a sticker expresses, not its pixels—aligning intent across modalities means queries and stickers that convey the same feeling naturally fall near each other in the representation space, making retrieval robust to visual or textual variation.
TFWaveFormer: Temporal-Frequency Collaborative Multi-level Wavelet Transformer for Dynamic Link PredictionWWW
uses Predicts future links in dynamic graphs by decomposing temporal patterns into multiple time scales using wavelets, then fusing local wavelet features with global temporal dependencies.
why it works It works because real temporal dynamics operate at multiple speeds—some changes happen fast (hours), others slow (months)—and wavelets naturally separate these scales; tracking both simultaneously gives a complete picture of what's likely to happen next in the network.
StreamFP: Fingerprint-guided Data Selection for Efficient Stream LearningWWW
uses Learns compact summaries that score how similar each new data point is to important historical ones, then selects new data to learn from and old data to keep.
why it works If you represent your model's state as a compact summary (fingerprint), you can cheaply measure whether a new data point is similar to important ones you've already learned. Keeping similar data wastes effort; selecting only dissimilar or hard data accelerates learning and prevents forgetting old patterns.
SMART: Spatio-Temporal Attention-based Large Language Model for Real-Time Traffic PredictionWWW
uses Predicts traffic flow by learning which time patterns matter and which road locations interact, then uses both to estimate flow at each location.
why it works Traffic flow has two structures: temporal (patterns repeat at certain times) and spatial (nearby roads affect each other). Separating these structures—preserving learned temporal reasoning while adapting spatial interactions—lets you reuse old time knowledge while flexibly updating for new traffic topology.
Unifying Graph Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Detection through Spectral Contrastive Invariant learningWWW
uses Identifies which sub-graphs are reliable markers of normal or abnormal graphs, then measures distance in the space of these reliable markers to detect outliers in new graphs.
why it works Real-world graph data mixes two types of shift: the rules change (semantic shift) and the input distribution changes (covariate shift). Learning which sub-graph patterns are stable across both types of shift lets you find reliable markers. Measuring distance in that stable marker space is robust to both kinds of shift.
Bridging Cognitive Neuroscience and Graph Intelligence: Hippocampus-Inspired Multi-View Hypergraph Learning for Web Finance FraudWWW
uses Detects fraud by finding cross-transaction conflicts that don't fit neighborhood patterns and measuring how much each transaction deviates from what neighbors predict.
why it works In a transaction network, each legitimate transaction fits the expected pattern of its neighbors' behavior; fraud camouflages itself by mimicking that pattern. By measuring surprise (deviation from neighbor expectations) and detecting conflicts across different views of the same transaction, you catch fraud even when it looks locally normal.
Drifting with Intent: Generative Interest Trajectories for Multimodal Web RecommendationWWW
uses Models how user interests evolve as a drift toward content they care about over time, then generates personalized trajectories through item and user space to predict next engagement.
why it works User interests don't drift randomly—they trend toward things that match past choices. Modeling this drift as a directed equation (not random diffusion) lets you predict the trajectory. Tracking movement across both temporal time and relational space (how items relate to users and to each other) captures the full story of interest evolution.
Modeling Point-to-Point Dependency for High-Dimensional Long-Term Series ForecastingWWW
uses Predict future values in long time series by finding the strongest repeating patterns across both time steps and different variables.
why it works It works because real time series contain recurring structures—seasonal patterns, cyclical trends—that repeat at regular intervals. By detecting which past moments most resemble the present, you can predict what comes next based on what happened then.
ImVision: Adapting Pretrained Vision Models for Time-Series ImputationWWW
uses Fill missing values in time series by converting sequences into image patterns and using an image-filler trained on general visual data.
why it works It works because time series and images share structure: repetition, smoothness, local correlation. When you represent time data as a heatmap, generic image inpainting—trained once on millions of images—knows which patterns are likely to complete the picture.
STAR: Semantic Table Representation with Header-Aware Clustering and Adaptive Weighted FusionWWW
uses Retrieve tables by grouping similar rows, generating varied synthetic queries per group, and weighting how much table and query numeric fingerprints should contribute.
why it works It works because tables have internal structure that one global numeric fingerprints flattens away. By clustering rows into topics and assigning cluster-specific queries, you surface diverse aspects of the table's meaning. Weighting the final blend lets you adjust how much structural form versus query content matters.
Space-based Parameter Evolving with Lightweight Optimization for Graph Adaptation to Evolving ShiftsWWW
uses A small controller learns how the graph environment is changing and generates custom parameters to adapt without retraining.
why it works Change happens in hidden patterns; a compact state space tracking these patterns lets you adapt instantly by only tweaking parameters, not rebuilding.
A Contrastive Learning and Prompt-Driven Framework for Low-Resource User GeolocationWWW
uses User and location numeric fingerprints are learned so that similar users and their actual locations sit close together in a learned space.
why it works Closeness in a learned space only works if users who match similar posts end up nearby; the loss enforces this by penalizing dissimilar pairs.
A Framework for Continual Knowledge Graph EmbeddingWWW
uses As facts are added to a knowledge graph, numeric fingerprints for new entities are learned and old numeric fingerprints updated without forgetting starting guess knowledge.
why it works numeric fingerprints in low features capture structural roles; careful initialization and keeping it simple preserves learned roles while adding new entities.
ProvGuard: Logic-Aware Multi-View Contrastive Learning for Robust and Efficient Host Threat DetectionWWW
uses Learn representations from semantically valid graph views that preserve causal structure, using contrastive learning to detect anomalies even when attackers manipulate graphs.
why it works Anomaly detection works because normal and malicious behavior differ. Contrastive learning finds what's stable and what changes. If you augment views that preserve causal meaning, normal activity stays stable across views while attacks don't, letting the model distinguish them without needing to know what attack looks like.
MetriKG: Profiling Static and Evolving Knowledge GraphsWWW
uses Computes multiple quality measurements of knowledge graphs at different levels: how well connected they are, how deep their structures go, and how cohesive their parts fit together.
why it works It works because you can reduce any graph's structural quality to a set of measurable numbers: connection strength tells you navigability, inheritance depth reveals organizational structure, and cohesion shows whether related elements cluster together. These numbers summarize complex patterns humans use to judge graph quality.
DMAP: Human-Aligned Structural Document Map for Multimodal Document UnderstandingWWW
uses Organizes document elements into a hierarchical structure that mirrors human reading patterns, then uses this structure to retrieve and reason about related content when answering questions.
why it works It works because documents have intrinsic logical relationships—sections belong to chapters, figures are cited by text, tables answer specific questions. When you organize by these relationships instead of treating text as separate chunks, similarity becomes structural proximity, and retrieval naturally follows the paths humans trace through documents.
Joint Similar User Exploration and Informative Behavior Guidance for Multi-Modal New Item RecommendationWWW
uses Finds users with similar preference histories to the target user, extracts their most informative past behaviors from multi-modal content, and ranks new items by how well they match the patterns those similar users acted on.
why it works It works because users with similar tastes tend to like similar new items, and some past behaviors signal preference strength more than others. By focusing on informative behaviors of truly similar users—not spurious neighbors—you reduce noise in the signal and rank new items according to the strongest preference patterns you can detect.
E2SGNN: Reconciling Expression and Efficiency in Spiking Graph Neural NetworkWWW
uses Uses efficient binary spike signals to represent graph structure while adding selective real-valued adjustments at both fine and coarse scales, then simplifies the model by using only the number of processing steps each graph actually needs.
why it works It works because brains use sparse spike signals instead of dense arithmetic, which is inherently efficient. The dual-scale modulation preserves the selective amplification and suppression needed for expressiveness while staying in the efficient spiking regime. Adaptive latency removes computational waste on simple graphs that converge quickly.
Bridging Explicit and Implicit Intent: Unified Interest Generative Method for Joint Search-Recommendation ModelingWWW
uses Generates unified interest representations that combine explicit search queries and implicit behavioral signals, then uses these unified interests to guide which knowledge gets shared or kept separate between search and recommendation tasks.
why it works It works because search intent and recommendation intent are two views of the same underlying user need. By fusing them into a shared hidden representation, you align them at the source; then using this unified interest to allocate focus prevents one task from sabotaging the other by forcing competing feature allocations.
Mitigating Homophily Disparity in Graph Anomaly Detection: A Scalable and Adaptive ApproachWWW
uses Use two frequency bands (low and high) of graph-neighborhood information, fused adaptively per node to separate normal from unusual nodes in large networks.
why it works It works because normal nodes and anomalies have different signal frequencies in a network: normal ones cluster densely (low frequency), anomalies stand out (high frequency). Splitting the signal lets you weight each frequency differently for each node, and linear complexity works because you only store enough information to compute one node at a time.
Measuring Privacy Risks and Tradeoffs in Financial Synthetic Data GenerationWWW
uses Generate synthetic financial data using multiple methods (autoencoders, diffusion, copulas), then measure the tradeoff between preserving privacy, maintaining utility, and handling class imbalance.
why it works It works because synthetic data distances itself from real data by design, breaking the direct link an attacker could exploit. Different generators make different privacy-utility tradeoffs depending on how they work: statistical copulas preserve marginals but not patterns, diffusion adds controlled noise. Testing on imbalanced data reveals which methods actually handle minority cases without leaking them.
TaxoBell: Gaussian Box Embeddings for Self-Supervised Taxonomy ExpansionWWW
uses Represents taxonomy categories as Gaussian-shaped regions where the center is the main meaning and fuzziness around edges models uncertainty.
why it works It works because taxonomies have asymmetric containment—a category contains its subcategories like a box contains smaller boxes. Points (traditional numeric fingerprints) cannot model containment, but regions (boxes) do. Gaussians add uncertainty naturally—categories with ambiguous boundaries get fuzzy edges.
Graph Neural Network Model Transferability Estimation via Decomposition-Augmented Discriminant AnalysisWWW
uses Decompose source dataset into principal components, weight them by singular values, and project onto the direction that best separates classes to score transferability.
why it works Principal components capture the main structure of the source dataset cheaply; projecting onto the class-separating direction tells you whether that structure aligns with the target's class boundaries. High alignment means the model learned patterns that transfer.
SPGCL: Subgraph Pattern-Aware Graph Contrastive Learning for High-Order Structural RepresentationWWW
uses Learn representations where subgraph patterns that appear together are pushed close and patterns that never appear together are pushed far apart.
why it works Patterns co-occur for a reason—they are parts of the same higher-order structure. Making co-occurring patterns nearby forces the representation to capture that structure. Non-occurring patterns pushed apart prevent false similarities.
FairGE: Fairness-Aware Graph Encoding in Incomplete Social NetworksWWW
uses Represents the network structure of a social graph using principal eigenvector direction to evaluate whether recommendations treat people fairly when sensitive information is missing.
why it works It works because the principal eigenvector captures the dominant structure of a network—how things flow through it most strongly. Using spectral structure to measure fairness avoids reconstructing missing attributes (which would create bias), instead directly checking whether the model's decisions favor some groups through the network's inherent geometry.
Beyond Isolated Clients: Integrating Graph-Based Embeddings into Event Sequence ModelsWWW
uses Learn to combine event sequence order with graph structure to predict user behavior from their interaction history.
why it works Comparing similar and different pairs teaches the model what patterns matter; adding graph structure reveals which users and items relate globally, so the model captures both temporal flow and relationship context that isolated events alone cannot provide.
SCOUT: Structure-Aware Aspect and Anchor-Count Selection for Node Attribute Augmentation via Positional InformationWWW
uses Learn which distance measures and how many reference nodes to use for encoding node positions, then pick the most representative nodes and encode each node as distances to them.
why it works Works because nodes with similar connection patterns to far-away reference points must themselves be structurally similar, so distances to anchors become searchable coordinates. Automating the anchor count and metric selection avoids manual tuning while adapting to each graph's shape.
Scalable Anomaly Detection for Temporal Web Streams via Approximate Nearest Neighbor SearchWWW
uses Detect anomalies in high-dimensional time streams by finding neighbors of each observation in a fast hierarchical index, then score based on neighbor statistics weighted by relevance, with adaptive retraining as patterns shift.
why it works Works because anomalies are isolated points: normal data clusters together in high features while abnormal points sit far from any dense region. Neighbor-based scoring captures this without learning a model, and the hierarchical index makes querying fast. Adaptive retraining handles concept drift as normal behavior evolves.
Diffusion-based Kriging Model with Graph-enhanced AttentionWWW
uses Infer missing sensor values by using focus to dynamically learn which other sensors are similar to each unknown node, then progressively refine guesses by spreading information through the refined graph.
why it works Works because a sensor's unknown value depends most on nearby similar sensors, not distant ones or predefined connections. Dynamic focus finds true similarity from the data, and diffusion-style progressive refinement ensures corrections from multiple correlated sources combine smoothly without oscillation.
TGSBM: Transformer-Guided Stochastic Block Model for Link PredictionWWW
uses Combines a structured community-detection model with sparse focus scoring to predict missing links in networks by learning which pairs of nodes should be connected.
why it works It works because community structure genuinely explains network connectivity: nodes in the same group connect more often, so learning this structure lets you predict unobserved links. The focus captures which long-range patterns matter without checking every possible pair.
Multi-Aspect Mining and Anomaly Detection for Heterogeneous Tensor StreamsWWW
uses Decomposes event streams with mixed categorical and numeric attributes into hidden components tracking group structure and temporal trends to flag unusual group-level patterns.
why it works It works because real event data clusters naturally: similar events come from the same underlying group activity. Modeling each attribute type's true statistical shape lets you detect when a group's behavior shifts or becomes unusual, rather than losing signal by forcing all attributes into one shape.
Generalizable Graph-level Anomaly Detection via Prompted Anomaly Expansion and Normality ExtractionWWW
uses Simulates diverse unusual graph variants using learned prompts and filters graph substructures to keep only those that distinguish normal from anomalous graphs.
why it works It works because rare anomalies are too scarce to learn from alone; generating synthetic variants broadens your view of what abnormal looks like. Filtering substructures keeps the signal for abnormality while noise-substructures from normal graphs stop misleading you.
HierCon: Hierarchical Contrastive Attention for Audio Deepfake DetectionWWW
uses Weight layers and temporal frames hierarchically, then use contrastive learning to push real speech and synthetic speech apart in a shared space.
why it works It works because real and fake speech leave distinct patterns across layers and time; hierarchical weighting finds which layers matter for each artifact type, and comparing numeric fingerprints directly encodes the subtle differences that fool simple detectors.
PADD: Prefix-based Attention Divergence Detector for LLM JailbreaksWWW
uses Prepend a safety prefix to prompts and compare focus distributions to detect whether a prompt is adversarial or benign.
why it works It works because adversarial prompts distort focus in ways benign ones do not; when you compare how the model focuses on different parts with and without safety guidance, attacks create measurable divergence that benign queries avoid.
Breaking the Single-Reference-Vector Barrier in Approximate Nearest Neighbor SearchWWW
uses Define distance metrics for multi-reference queries where you find lists of numbers similar to all or any of multiple reference lists of numbers, then search efficiently on graph indexes.
why it works It works because extending nearest-neighbor search from one reference to multiple references by properly defining what 'all-match' and 'any-match' distance means preserves the efficiency of graph search while enabling richer queries.
VOICY: A Privacy-Centric Modular Architecture for Zero-Shot Voice Cloning and Fine-Tuned Speech SynthesisWWW
uses Use a similarity score (cosine) to measure how close a generated voice is to a reference voice, optimizing until they sound the same.
why it works It works because voices that sound alike to humans also sit close together in acoustic space—the same properties that make them audibly similar also make their numbers geometrically close. Measuring distance is faster and more reliable than human listening.
When Rules Fall Short: Agent-Driven Discovery of Emerging Content Issues in Short Video PlatformsWWW
uses Cluster new short videos by similarity, then infer what policy rules would govern them, automating discovery of emerging content issues.
why it works It works because new issues on social platforms share common visual and textual patterns. By grouping similar cases and extracting their common features, you reveal what rules are missing—clustering acts as a data-driven lens to see gaps in policy coverage.
GeoPBR: Multimodal-Guided PBR Material Generation from a Single ViewWWW
uses Blend guidance from images, text, and geometric shape to generate material properties (albedo, roughness) that look right under any lighting.
why it works It works because multiple sources of truth—a reference image, a verbal description, and structural geometry—each catch different details. Fusing them ensures the final material respects texture hints from the image, intent from language, and spatial consistency from shape.
Contextual Structure-Enhanced Selective Graph Convolutional NetworkWWW
uses Learns which neighbors matter for each node by examining their local structural role, not just label similarity.
why it works Works because in heterophilic graphs, distant neighbors matter more; detecting local structure patterns identifies true signal.
OpenDigger: A Practical Framework for Assessing Community Health and Sustainability in Open Source Collaboration PlatformsWWW
uses Measures open-source community health by computing network distance and activity metrics across developer collaboration platforms.
why it works Developers who frequently interact sit close together in collaboration space; measuring distances and densities in this space reveals community structure and health without needing to manually define what healthy means.
PrivSniffer: Graph-based Contextual Privacy Leakage Detection for User-Generated TextsWWW
uses Detects hidden personal information in text by searching a graph of words for paths that lead from explicit statements to implied sensitive facts.
why it works People's private information connects to what they say through inference chains; mapping these chains as a spatial graph lets you find which paths to search for to catch leaks that simple pattern matching misses.
Temporal-Series-Aware Adaptive Positional Encoding for Transformer-based Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Predicts user preferences by encoding the time gaps between past interactions, placing users close together if their engagement patterns match.
why it works How fast users act between clicks reveals their interest intensity; grouping users by similar time-gap patterns finds neighbors with matching intent, making next-item prediction accurate without needing to know absolute timestamps.
Dynamic Prototype-Augmented Stance Detection: Learning from the Seen to Reason about the UnseenWWW
uses Predict stance toward new topics by pulling similar examples closer together and pushing different ones apart, then updating prototypes as you learn.
why it works Pulling similar stances together and pushing dissimilar ones apart creates regions in space where each stance clusters. When a new topic arrives, similarity to stored prototypes reveals its stance instantly. Dynamically updating prototypes lets the model learn new patterns without forgetting old ones.
Bowling with ChatGPT: On the Evolving User Interactions with Conversational AI SystemsWWW
uses Track how user queries to ChatGPT shift in purpose, tone, and personalization over months to understand evolving human-AI interaction patterns.
why it works User behavior with AI systems is non-stationary—it drifts over time as users learn what the system can do and how to interact with it. By clustering queries and measuring shifts in their properties (topic, emotional disclosure, system suggestions), you can quantify how the relationship deepens from functional to social.
Edit-Level Tracking of Narrative Changes in 10-K FilingsWWW
uses Compares sentences year-to-year using learned sentence representations to classify which sentences were kept, deleted, or added, then measures sentiment difference between added and deleted portions.
why it works Learned representations embed similar sentences close together in a space, so semantic matching finds true rewrites versus genuine changes. Sentiment difference isolates real content shifts because boilerplate repeats identically, making deletion-to-addition ratios reveal what management actually changed its stance on.
Towards Efficient and Interpretable Medical Concept Representation via Ontology-driven Residual Vector QuantizationWWW
uses Compresses medical concepts into short discrete code sequences that align with the multi-level hierarchy of medical ontologies, learned from labeled healthcare data.
why it works Medical ontologies encode genuine hierarchical relationships (e.g., 'aspirin' is a 'pain reliever' is a 'drug'). Quantization that respects those levels forces codes to cluster consistently with real medical knowledge, so fewer codes capture the same semantic distinctions humans recognize.
Crowdsourced Collection and Visualization of Urban Mood via a Multisensory Interactive SystemWSDM
uses Collects sensory impressions and photos tagged with subjective moods at locations, then visualizes them on a map where proximity reflects both place characteristics and personality-driven perception similarities.
why it works This works because two people who perceive the same location similarly will tag it with the same sensory words; placing locations near each other in visual space when their sensory profiles are close makes that similarity readable at a glance.
Metadata Meets LLMs: Constructing Knowledge-Rich Citation Networks with CoT-Enhanced RepresentationsWSDM
uses Uses a language model to generate missing metadata for sparse citation record fields, encodes the augmented metadata with a learned text encoder, then uses the resulting features as node inputs to a graph network for author classification.
why it works Authors publishing together and in similar venues share research interests; by enriching sparse metadata and learning numeric fingerprints that place similar authors near each other in a learned space, the method extracts predictable patterns from the citation structure.
Waterlogformer: A Multimodal Model for Waterlogging PredictionWSDM
uses Predict how deep water will flood at a location by learning patterns from rainfall, terrain, and geographic features over time.
why it works This works because water accumulation follows physical laws that repeat: similar past rainfall and terrain shape always lead to similar flooding outcomes. If you arrange locations in a space where geographically similar ones sit close, nearby predictions become reliable.
Decoupling User Features for User Cold-Start App Recommendation: Static Attributes versus Behavioral SequencesWSDM
uses Recommend apps to new users by learning user attributes and behavior separately, then weighing each signal's importance based on how much it predicts the actual choice.
why it works It works because new users lack behavior history, so attributes must carry weight initially. But attributes and behavior encode different kinds of information—separating them prevents one from overwhelming the other, then balancing their signals.
DDIREC: Domain-Disentanglement on Item Representations for Cross-Domain RecommendationWSDM
uses Learn item descriptions as feature lists of numbers by separating words that matter for one domain from words shared across domains, preventing confusion between domains.
why it works It works because mixing domain-specific and domain-shared meanings leads to negative transfer; by explicitly separating these, you avoid applying rules learned in one domain wrongly to another.
Accelerating Generative Recommendation via Simple Categorical User Sequence CompressionWSDM
uses Predict what users will want next by remembering only the most important categories from their long history instead of every past click.
why it works It works because categories already aggregate similar items; throwing away redundant history details keeps only the signal, so the model trains faster and focuses on what matters.
N41: Leveraging One Target and Neighboring Features to Improve Anomaly Detection AccuracyWSDM
uses Find anomalies in time-series data by training on one target feature at a time and including its similar neighbors, letting the model focus deeply.
why it works It works because focusing training on one target feature avoids diluting error signals across many unrelated features; neighbors with similar patterns provide relevant context without adding noise.
A Preliminary Agentic Framework for Matrix DeflationWSDM
uses Decompose matrices by peeling off rank-1 slices using a language model to generate decompositions and a vision model to approve them, without preset stopping thresholds.
why it works It works because vision models can recognize when remaining structure is noise versus signal better than fixed thresholds; by using learned judgment instead of thresholds, you adapt to the data's inherent rank.
MerFT: A Framework for Social Conflict Meme Exploration via Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Fine-tuningWSDM
uses Score how well a meme interpretation ranks by how much it relies on relevant documents while avoiding misleading false-similar ones.
why it works It works because ranking answers by relevance to actual evidence naturally pushes correct interpretations to the top, while penalizing answers drawn from misleading distractors forces the model to distinguish between things that feel similar but point in wrong directions.
Taming Non-Stationary Knowledge Growth: Dynamic Global Memory Framework for Lifelong Knowledge Graph EmbeddingWSDM
uses Preserve a knowledge graph's structure as it grows by adaptively weighting old facts against new ones based on their relative importance.
why it works It works because knowledge graphs grow unevenly—some facts matter more than others—so weighting lets you lock in the core structure while integrating newcomers without forgetting what shaped the whole system.
Combining Structural and Textual Knowledge for Knowledge Graph Link Prediction via Large Language ModelsWSDM
uses Rank candidate entities for a knowledge graph link by scoring how well they align with both the graph's structure and the text descriptions, with weight tuned by the query context.
why it works It works because graphs and text carry different truths about relationships—structure shows how facts connect, text reveals why—so aligning both and letting the query decide their balance captures complementary signals that neither alone provides.
Building Human-Aligned AI through Representation Augmentation and StructuringWSDM
uses Build representations of human behavior and social networks that align across different languages, cultures, and professional contexts.
why it works It works because humans express intent through multiple channels—language, images, behavior—and across cultural boundaries they share underlying meanings even if surface forms differ, so unified representations capture the core intent rather than surface variation.
GNN Explainers 2.0: User-centric and Data-driven InsightsWSDM
uses Explain graph systems that learn from examples decisions by tracing how inputs flow through layers and identifying which parts of the input mattered most, in ways humans at different levels of expertise understand.
why it works It works because decision logic is inherited from layer to layer—each transforms the previous output—so tracing flow backward reveals where a mistake was born and allows users to verify the path matches what they'd expect.
Transfer Learning via User-Item Graph Convolution for Enhanced Cross-Domain RecommendationWSDM
uses Transfer user preferences from one domain to another by finding similar items across domains, then assuming users will like target-domain items similar to items they liked in the source domain.
why it works It works because preference patterns are tied to item characteristics, not domains—so if two items are similar enough, a preference shown for one transfers to the other regardless of which domain is familiar.
RPE4Rec: Enhancing Dynamic Node Retrieval with Efficient Relative Position Encoding for Recommendation SystemsWSDM
uses Improve item ranking for recommendations by encoding the position of recent interactions so similar items from the same moment rank higher than distant matches.
why it works It works because user tastes shift over time—items clicked close together often appeal for the same reason—so encoding recency and proximity lets you catch temporal coherence in preference without manual time features.
Prompt Tuning without Labeled Samples for Zero-Shot Node Classification in Text-Attributed GraphsWSDM
uses Classify nodes with no labels by learning what text and graph structure mean, then creating fake examples for each class and using them as prompts to guide classification.
why it works It works because generating synthetic examples from class names preserves class semantics even without real data—the generation model understands what each class represents—so synthetic examples carry the essence of real labels.
Scholar API: Search and Recommendations for Academic SearchWSDM
uses Rank papers by learned similarity scores computed from multiple different representations (numeric fingerprints from different methods), allowing users to mix and match.
why it works It works because papers can be similar in multiple ways that rank differently: citations reveal expert judgment, abstract content reveals direct relevance, graph structure reveals invisible connections. No single view is complete, so combining views from different lenses ranks papers by richer, more nuanced similarity.
Addressing Aggregation-Induced Information Loss in Graph Neural NetworksWSDM
uses Preserve both detailed features and connection patterns when combining neighboring node information in a network structure.
why it works When you combine many neighbors' information, unique details and patterns get erased. By actively preserving what makes each feature distinct and what makes each connection pattern important, you retain the signal that was getting lost in the averaging.
Efficient Vector-Based Label Propagation for Massive Low-Rank GraphsWSDM
uses Spread labels through a graph by working in the compressed numeric fingerprints space rather than with explicit edges, scaling to millions of nodes.
why it works compact graphs are secretly compressed — they can be represented by a smaller set of features without losing the connections. Computing label spreading in that smaller space costs far less but gets the same answer, because the connections are all there, just encoded differently.
Spectral Modeling of Periodic Phenomena in Scientific Data via Fourier–Galerkin RepresentationWSDM
uses Decomposes time series into a linear trend and periodic waves using learned sine and cosine components with adjusted phase offsets.
why it works It works because periodic phenomena repeat in predictable patterns—breaking them into sinusoidal waves lets you capture those repeating shapes efficiently. Once you know the main frequencies and their phase shifts, reconstructing the signal becomes a simple weighted sum.
Pre-training Language Model for Friend Recommendation: A Case Study of Large Social GraphWSDM
uses Learns node representations within local network neighborhoods using pretrained word-understanding models, capturing both network structure and feature meaning.
why it works It works because people in social networks behave similarly to people nearby in the graph. Pretrained models already understand human relationships and attributes; combining that understanding with local network topology lets you infer who would be good friends without processing the entire graph.
On-Device Large Language Models for Sequential RecommendationWSDM
uses Compresses large models using compact factorization and words-pattern smoothing, then refines each layer progressively to run recommendations on mobile devices without losing quality.
why it works It works because language models contain redundant parameters—many weights can be reconstructed from a small set of core features. Progressive layer-by-layer refinement ensures each compression step actually works before moving forward, avoiding cascading errors.
G-TRAC: Graph-textual Representations Alignment for Cold-start RecommendationsWSDM
uses Aligns textual descriptions and network structure into shared representations, letting new items or users be understood from description alone when network data is sparse.
why it works It works because text and network encode the same reality from different angles—what text says matches what neighbors are. Learning a joint space where both views converge lets you use text to bootstrap when the graph has gaps.
Towards Multifaceted Graph Condensation in Discrete RealmWSDM
uses Compress a large graph into a much smaller one by discretizing features and preserving local structure via compact approximation, then learn which smaller patterns matter most.
why it works It works because graphs have redundancy: many nodes behave similarly, and you only need a few patterns to explain the whole structure. Discretization removes noise, and compact approximation captures the dominant patterns—keeping what predicts behavior while throwing away the rest.
DDGCL: Dual Diffusion-based Graph Contrastive Learning for RecommendationWSDM
uses Generate two different views of the user-item graph via diffusion-based noise, then train the system to recognize when two views show the same information, emphasizing structure and long-tail items.
why it works It works because learning thrives on recognizing what stays true despite change. By adding noise in two ways and training the system to say 'these still match,' you force it to understand the core pattern. Long-tail items benefit because the conditional diffusion uses global structure to guide their cleanup.
RankID: A Unified Semantic ID Learned through Multi-Stage Semantic Alignment of Multimodal FeaturesWSDM
uses Align and merge semantic meanings from images, text, and interaction data into one unified identifier that ranks recommendation candidates in order of relevance.
why it works It works because different data types carry the same underlying meaning—a video, its description, and how creators interact all describe similar things. Alignment makes these meanings live in the same measurement space, so a single identifier can capture what matters across all sources at once.
Efficient Sparse Retrieval with Lightweight Superblock PruningSIGIR
uses Skip large blocks of candidate items by computing quick summary scores, keeping computation efficient without losing the best matches.
why it works You never need to look at every candidate, just identify which blocks contain the winners. A fast approximate score that correctly ranks the blocks already saves you most of the work.
Reconstructing Content with Collaborative Attention for Universal Multimodal Representation LearningSIGIR
uses Train a model to compress all semantic meaning from text and images into a single point, so things people treat alike end up close together in space.
why it works If you force the model to reconstruct the original input from that single point, it must pack all the important patterns there. Compression creates compactness, and compactness makes similarity mean nearness.
MLLMRec: A Preference Reasoning Paradigm with Graph Refinement for Multimodal RecommendationSIGIR
uses Describe images in natural language, reason about user preferences as descriptions, then clean up the graph of related items by removing low-confidence edges and fixing missing connections.
why it works Natural descriptions bridge the gap between visual and textual modality. Removing noise from the item graph ensures the model learns from high-confidence relations, not spurious patterns.
Selective Constraint Learning for Unsupervised Cross-Domain Image RetrievalSIGIR
uses Build a bank of high-confidence positive and negative pairs from a pretrained model, then pull images toward their positives and push away from negatives while anchoring to prototypes.
why it works A good external model gives you stable semantic truth that transcends domains. Anchoring to prototypes keeps each domain coherent while alignment forces cross-domain matching.
Drift-Aware Incremental Token Adaptation with Collaborative Semantics for Generative RecommendationSIGIR
uses When new items arrive, identify which existing items drift in meaning, then selectively update their codes to stay aligned with the generative model without breaking everything.
why it works Retraining from scratch is wasteful. Identifying true drift lets you update only what changed, preserving the model's learned alignment for stable items.
Why Advanced Encoders Lag on Sparse Retrieval? The Answer and an Approach to Bridging Vocabulary GapsSIGIR
uses Map a modern model's learned patterns into a simplified, normalized vocabulary designed for keyword matching, keeping the model's geometric structure while aligning to sparsity.
why it works Modern models scatter related concepts across redundant words. Normalizing the vocabulary reduces wasted capacity, and preserving the geometry means the model's learned distance relations stay valid.
Unifying Granularity and Reliability: A Robust and Efficient Framework for Text-based Person RetrievalSIGIR
uses Learn fine and coarse visual-text alignments, downweight unreliable image-text pairs, and verify cross-modal agreement to match person descriptions to images.
why it works It works because identity has multiple scales: broad appearance and fine detail both matter, and some training examples are corrupted or inconsistent. By learning at both scales and trusting only reliable examples, the model captures genuine correspondence patterns that generalize across unseen scenarios.
Chunk-Wise Quantization for Graph Collaborative FilteringSIGIR
uses Compress recommendation graphs by partitioning node numeric fingerprints into chunks and applying low-bitwidth quantization to each chunk, adapting chunk boundaries during training.
why it works It works because node numeric fingerprints are redundant: many features carry correlated signals. Chunking groups similar features together and quantizes each chunk independently, so low precision affects only redundant information while preserving the few patterns that drive ranking decisions.
Balanced Frequency Decoupling: Energy-Aware Multi-Scale Preference Modeling for Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
