uses Model short and long-term preferences in separate branches by decomposing frequencies, suppress low-energy noise, and combine branches via learned gating to improve ranking.
why it works It works because user behavior operates at multiple timescales: immediate context and long patterns matter differently. Decomposing by frequency isolates these scales naturally. Low-energy components are typically noise. Routing signals through separate pathways then gating them prevents fast and slow patterns from interfering with each other.
Search for Coverage: Learning Coverage-Aware Retrieval with Augmented Sub-Question AnswerabilitySIGIR
uses Learn to rank search results so they cover diverse fact-nuggets needed for comprehensive synthesis.
why it works It works because if search results are ordered by how well they add new facts rather than just relevance, synthesis has all the pieces it needs and nothing is missing or redundant.
A Voronoi Cell Formulation for Principled Token Pruning in Late-Interaction Retrieval ModelsSIGIR
uses Prune words by measuring how much each one's influence region overlaps with others in numeric fingerprints space.
why it works It works because if you keep words whose regions matter most, you preserve the information needed to find neighbors without storing every words's details.
Formalized Information Needs Improve Large-Language-Model Relevance JudgmentsSIGIR
uses Score documents as relevant when full descriptions and context narratives agree, not just raw queries.
why it works It works because complete problem statements filter out false positives — a document matching a raw query might be irrelevant once you see the full context, so agreement across rich formulations ensures true relevance.
Set-Based Cross-Domain RecommendationSIGIR
uses Build user representations by treating their history as an unordered set of item-rating pairs and mixing them permutation-invariantly.
why it works It works because user history is naturally a set with no fixed order — the same person likes items A then B as much as B then A for building preferences — so order-invariant mixing respects this truth and is robust.
Countering Interest Over-Smoothing: Distilling Latent Factors via Diffusion for Multi-Interest RetrievalSIGIR
uses Distill distinct user interests by reconstructing interest lists of numbers rather than aggregating them, preserving each interest's strength.
why it works It works because averaging interests blurs important patterns into an indistinct middle; reconstructing each lists of numbers separately forces the model to find and preserve what makes each interest distinct and strong.
Graph Diffusion Gated Embeddings for Recommender SystemsSIGIR
uses Mix compact cluster numeric fingerprints using probabilistic gates derived from diffusion patterns, not hash collisions.
why it works It works because diffusion spreads influence smoothly through the graph, revealing which clusters co-occur; using this structure for gating is more accurate than random hashing and respects relationships.
Struct-Align: Zero-Shot Text-to-3D Scene Retrieval via Locality-Aware Structural AlignmentSIGIR
uses Convert both 3D scenes and text queries into aligned textual descriptions, then find matches by measuring how close those text representations sit together.
why it works It works because text numeric fingerprints models already know how to place semantically related statements near each other. By expressing both sides in the same language and using the same numeric fingerprints model, you can leverage that learned nearness without needing paired training data.
Revisiting Collaborative Filtering by Unleashing the Power of SimilaritySIGIR
uses Compute user-item similarity at group levels and across multi-hop paths by using a sketch-based hash method that estimates complex combinatorial similarities with linear cost.
why it works It works because you don't need exact similarity values, only their relative ordering. The hash sketches capture enough information to preserve ranking, so a cheap approximation that respects the order already captures everything needed to find good neighbors without the exponential cost.
A Comparative Study of Users' Information-Seeking Practices Across Search Engines and Generative AI ChatbotsSIGIR
uses Compare how users assess and select search engines versus chatbots by measuring the distance between their stated tool preferences and actual usage patterns.
why it works It works because user choice is fundamentally a similarity judgment—they pick the tool that best matches their current task. Measuring the gap between preference and actual behavior reveals when the tool they expect to use differs from the one they actually choose, exposing hidden task-specific tradeoffs.
How Variability Influences Podcast Search: Queries, Transcriptions, and JudgesSIGIR
uses Evaluate podcast search by testing many query versions, transcript versions, and ranking systems, then scoring results using multiple independent judges.
why it works It works because variation hides real signal. By averaging judgments across many independent raters and testing many configurations, random disagreement cancels out and true ranking quality emerges.
Minimal-Perturbation Counterfactuals through Guided Denoising Diffusion for Recommender Systems ExplanationSIGIR
uses Use a diffusion process to generate small changes to a user's history that would flip a recommendation, showing what must change for a different outcome.
why it works It works because diffusion gradually uncovers the shape of realistic histories. By guiding the diffusion toward counterfactuals, you find minimal, semantically valid changes instead of arbitrary perturbations, making explanations actionable.
Agentic Search in the Wild: Intents and Trajectory Dynamics from 14M+ Real Search RequestsSIGIR
uses Track how agents search multi-step by analyzing millions of real logs, measuring whether new query terms come from recently retrieved evidence.
why it works It works because agents learn from what they retrieve. By measuring how often new terms appear in starting guess results, you expose whether the agent is building iteratively on evidence or diverging; this signal improves future agent design.
Recasting Web-Scale Query Suggestion as dense retrieval: Efficient, Up-to-Date, and Context-Aware SuggestionsSIGIR
uses Suggest the next search query by finding the most similar historical query among millions using learned nearness, weighted by session context.
why it works It works because query patterns repeat; what humans searched before is a strong signal for what they'll search next. Learning asymmetric similarity (what query predicts what suggestion) is faster and more up-to-date than generating new queries from scratch.
Aspect-Aware Content-Based Recommendations for Mathematical Research PapersSIGIR
uses Recommends math papers by learning which aspects of proof techniques, logical chains, and author lineage make papers similar, even when they share few words or citations.
why it works It works because mathematical relatedness is conceptual—papers can be connected through ideas and reasoning paths rather than vocabulary. By fusing textual meaning with author history and citation structure, it captures the true relational fabric mathematicians recognize.
Distribution-aware Re-representations for Multi-Scenario RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Recommends across different scenarios by learning global reference points and mapping each scenario's representations around them, measuring how far each scenario's distributions diverge.
why it works It works because users behave differently across scenarios (home, local, live) but those behaviors share common underlying preferences. Using shared reference points as anchors, then mapping scenario-specific variations around them, separates global signals from local distribution shifts, enabling knowledge transfer.
Beyond Exposure Diversity: Debiasing News Consumption With Topic-Locality Calibration and Personalized Preview NudgesSIGIR
uses Nudges news readers toward balanced consumption by calibrating recommendations based on topic and geography, showing personalized previews that highlight article relevance to starting guess reads.
why it works It works because people follow familiar patterns; highlighting how new articles connect to what they've already read both feels relevant and gently expands their boundaries. By calibrating topic-geography balance at the system level, you reshape consumption gradually without resistance.
Cognitive Style Shapes Search Behaviours: An fNIRS Study of Exploratory SearchSIGIR
uses Maps individual thinking styles to neural brain activation patterns to predict how people interact with search results.
why it works It works because consistent thinking styles produce consistent brain activity and search behaviors, so measuring one lets you reliably predict the other without needing a perfect causal chain.
Bridging LLM Embeddings and VAE Parameters for Disentangled RecommendationSIGIR
uses Uses a language model's compressed knowledge of user preferences to guide what features a recommendation system should learn.
why it works It works because language models capture rich patterns about what people want, and steering the recommendation model's learning toward those patterns focuses it on meaningful user interests rather than noise.
RegionSLM: Region-aware Question Answering on Document ScreenshotsSIGIR
uses Learns which parts of a document matter most for answering a question, then pools only those regions into compact words.
why it works It works because most of a document is irrelevant clutter; identifying and keeping only the relevant bits preserves the signal needed to answer while throwing away everything that distracts.
Constructing Hard-Positive Query-Document Pairs for Dense Retrieval via Phrase RepresentativenessSIGIR
uses Discovers phrases in documents that retrieval models rank poorly, then uses those phrases to construct challenging queries.
why it works It works because every model has blind spots; if a phrase that appears in a document is ranked low by the model's internal scoring, queries built around that phrase reveal the retrieval model's failure mode.
Modular Representation Compression: Adapting LLM Representations for Efficient and Effective RecommendationSIGIR
uses The method learns which layers and features of a language model matter most for recommendations, then compresses away the rest without losing quality.
why it works It works because middle layers capture diverse task-relevant information while final layers specialize too narrowly. By explicitly choosing which parts to keep and how to adapt them, you preserve the general knowledge needed for good recommendations while shrinking storage costs.
Adaptive Sparsity Optimization with Learnable Soft Top-K and Per-Term Thresholding for Efficient RetrievalSIGIR
uses The method learns to keep only the most important words in search queries and document descriptions, using soft ranking and per-word thresholds to trim the rest.
why it works It works because language models produce far more words than you need for retrieval. By learning which words actually predict relevance and dropping low-value ones, you shrink lists of numbers dramatically without losing the signal needed to find good matches.
Adaptive Rich-kernelized Contrastive Learning for Capacity Enhancement in Collaborative FilteringSIGIR
uses The method learns a flexible similarity function—built from polynomial terms—that maps users and items into a space where it can represent complex preference patterns while staying fast.
why it works It works because standard similarity (dot product) cannot express all possible top-K patterns no matter how many features you use. By learning a richer similarity similarity function that acts like a transformation into an implicit higher space while keeping single-lists of numbers speed, you gain expressiveness without computation cost.
mKG-RAG: Leveraging Multimodal Knowledge Graphs in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-intensive VQASIGIR
uses Match images and text by computing their nearness in a shared space, then retrieve the most similar structured knowledge graph entries to feed into question answering.
why it works When you align images and text into the same geometric space where similar things sit close, retrieval becomes a simple nearest-neighbor search. Adding structure via knowledge graphs helps because it lets you follow meaningful relationships rather than just grabbing isolated facts.
Pretrain-then-Adapt: Uncertainty-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Text-based Person SearchSIGIR
uses Estimate how confident a person-image match is by checking if image-to-person and person-to-image retrievals both rank it highly, then retrain the model only on high-confidence matches.
why it works When two independent rankings agree, that agreement signals genuine alignment rather than noise. The system works because disagreement between directions reveals uncertainty, and low-uncertainty matches are more reliable as targets for retraining.
Disentangling from Collaborative and Semantic Views: Graph Collaborative Filtering for Q&#38;A RecommendationSIGIR
uses Build separate graphs for collaborative signals and semantic signals in Q&A pairs, score matches in each graph, then merge the scores to rank pairs.
why it works It works because collaborative patterns (who likes what) and semantic patterns (what topics relate) are governed by different rules. Keeping them separate lets each scoring method exploit its own structure, then combining them captures the full picture.
SSR: Structured Subgraph Retrieval for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering with LLMsSIGIR
uses Extract subgraph patterns and temporal windows from questions, retrieve the subgraph from the knowledge base that matches those patterns, then compress and feed to language model.
why it works It works because structured subgraphs preserve the relational patterns that question answering needs. Instead of losing structure by converting to plain text, you keep the skeleton of how facts relate and when they were true, making reasoning more direct.
Where Relevance Emerges: A Layer-Wise Study of Internal Attention for Zero-Shot Re-RankingSIGIR
uses Look inside a AI language systems layer-by-layer to find which internal focus signals show relevance, then use only the strongest layers to rank documents faster.
why it works It works because relevance signals don't spread evenly through all layers—some layers concentrate the useful information while others add noise. Finding and using only the peaked layers cuts waste without losing accuracy.
Reproduction Beyond Benchmarks: ConstBERT and ColBERT-v2 Across Backends and Query DistributionsSIGIR
uses Represent documents with multiple weighted lists of numbers and score matching by taking the maximum similarity between any pair, but this architectural choice limits handling of long queries.
why it works Maximum-of-similarities ranking works for short contexts because words matches are decisive. But on long narrative queries, this uniform weighting cannot distinguish real clues from filler—it plateaus because the maximum operation treats all words equally.
Insights into the Efficiency of Open-Source Score-at-a-Time Search Engines: A Reproducibility StudySIGIR
uses Compare two search engine strategies: Score-at-a-Time (generate scores in ranked order) versus Document-at-a-Time (score all documents), examining latency and compression trade-offs.
why it works Score-at-a-Time works because scoring documents in high-to-low order stops early once you've found enough—it exploits the fact that you only need the top K, not all scores. It trades off which compression method fits best on each hardware setup.
A Replicability Study of Joint Product Quantisation for Effective Space-Efficient Dense RetrievalSIGIR
uses Split numeric fingerprints features into groups, assign each group to nearby center points, then retrain the centers and the query encoder jointly to minimize retrieval error.
why it works It works because most features in numeric fingerprints carry redundant or weak signals. Compressing to cluster centers loses little while cutting storage dramatically. Joint retraining adapts the centers to the actual data, recovering most of the lost precision.
TREC iKAT 2025: A Test Collection for the Offline and Interactive Evaluation of Conversational SearchSIGIR
uses Model user preferences from conversation history and profile data; predict which responses best match each user's information needs.
why it works It works because past behavior reveals what users value: if a user repeatedly asks certain types of questions or accepts certain answers, that pattern generalizes to future requests from the same user. Personalization exploits the stability of individual preference.
BioCLEAR Benchmark for Biomedical Text SimplificationSIGIR
uses Learn a mapping from technical scientific abstracts to plain-language summaries by example, capturing discourse structure across sentence and document levels.
why it works It works because aligned pairs of complex and simple texts reveal the systematic patterns of what makes writing hard: jargon, sentence length, implicit concepts. By learning these patterns from examples, the model can apply the transformation to new texts.
TM-Bench: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Low-Resource Traditional MongolianSIGIR
uses Benchmark language models across 18,357 understanding and generation tasks in Traditional Mongolian; measure reasoning, knowledge, and linguistic proficiency through test accuracy.
why it works It works because test performance on diverse tasks reveals both what a model knows and where it fails. Grading on multiple features captures different aspects of language ability. Comparing across models with the same benchmark isolates which systems advance the field.
CTCL: A Cross-Language Benchmark for Matching Patients to Clinical TrialsSIGIR
uses Match patients to clinical trials in multiple languages by scoring how closely patient profiles align with trial inclusion criteria.
why it works It works because patient eligibility and trial requirements are multidimensional, and by numeric fingerprints both into a shared space where similar profiles sit close together, you turn matching into simple nearness, which remains meaningful across languages.
JFinTEB: Japanese Financial Text Embedding BenchmarkSIGIR
uses Ranks documents by how similar their meaning is to a search query, using distance in a high-dimensional space.
why it works It works because when you position documents so that ones with the same meaning sit close together, searching becomes finding what is nearest, and nearness is fast and cheap to measure.
AlpsBench: An LLM Personalization Benchmark for Real-Dialogue Memorization and Preference AlignmentSIGIR
uses Extracts what a person likes from their chat history, stores it, then retrieves it when needed to personalize future responses.
why it works It works because consistent person traits appear repeatedly in their messages; capturing what shows up often in conversation creates a stable profile that predicts what they will prefer.
WeatherArchive: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning over Historical Weather ArchivesSIGIR
uses Searches old news articles for mentions of weather events and assesses how society reacted, combining retrieval and question answering on messy historical text.
why it works It works because relevant historical stories use similar language and describe related impacts; finding articles using that language finds eyewitness accounts, which directly answer questions about societal response.
AgentSim: A Platform for Verifiable Agent-Trace SimulationSIGIR
uses Records step-by-step reasoning traces as an agent searches documents, building ground truth examples of good problem-solving paths.
why it works It works because reasoning is reproducible: when a model's intermediate steps match reality, those steps become trustworthy training data showing exactly what kind of reasoning leads to correct answers.
Does LLM Relevance Labelling Work for Arabic?SIGIR
uses Scores whether Arabic documents match a search question by comparing semantic meaning, then checks if those scores correctly order search systems.
why it works It works because language does not change the core idea: if your relevance scores put the best results first, they correctly rank which system performed best, regardless of the language used.
The Matryoshka HypencoderSIGIR
uses Represents each query as a small systems that learn from examples that scores documents, using fewer parameters when speed matters than when accuracy matters.
why it works It works because the most important scoring patterns are the same at all sizes; discarding the least-important details still preserves the strongest signals, trading almost nothing in accuracy for big speed gains.
Load-sensitive Selective Pruning in Dense RetrievalSIGIR
uses Shrink search numeric fingerprints to fewer features as query traffic increases, trading some accuracy for speed to avoid query backlog.
why it works It works because query traffic is unpredictable and full precision isn't always necessary. By reducing features under load rather than dropping queries, the system guarantees service while losing minimal accuracy since the largest-signal features stay intact.
Reformulating Post-Training as Matrix Factorization for Joint Embedding RefinementSIGIR
uses Jointly re-align user and item numeric fingerprints in a compact factorized space by preserving angular structure while reinforcing high-confidence preferences.
why it works It works because numeric fingerprints were originally trained as a pair under the assumption they span a low-dimensional subspace. If you refine one side only, you break that alignment. Jointly refactoring restores the pairing while keeping what was learned about which users and items are close.
FAST-MEL: A Fast, Accurate, and Storage Efficient Solution for Multimodal Entity LinkingSIGIR
uses Match entities by computing similarity between mention and entity using compact fixed-size representations combining text and visual information.
why it works It works because fixed-size representations trade some richness for speed and storage. By carefully compressing both modalities into compact lists of numbers, the system keeps the core similarity signal that humans use to recognize the same entity in images and text, while cutting storage and lookup time dramatically.
How Fine-Grained Should a RAG Benchmark Be? A Hierarchical Framework for Synthetic Question GenerationSIGIR
uses Create questions at different levels of detail and pick the detail level that makes answers most different from each other, so the test catches more variation between systems.
why it works Questions that are too coarse hide real differences; too fine and they're noisy. The sweet spot is where the spread of answer quality (standard deviation) peaks—there the test becomes most sensitive to which system is actually better.
MSW-NTM: A Spherical Wasserstein Autoencoder for Multimodal Neural Topic Modeling with LLM-Guided Topic RefinementSIGIR
uses Learn topic representations that sit on a unit sphere, using a distance measure that respects spherical geometry and a distribution-matching technique for stable learning.
why it works Normalized text descriptions naturally live on a sphere (each point has length one). Using sphere geometry instead of flat space means your distance measure reflects true similarity. Matching distributions with Wasserstein distance keeps training stable by penalizing mode collapse without forcing slope to vanish.
An Asymmetric-difference based Document Exact Similarity Search AlgorithmSIGIR
uses Compare documents by measuring how many words they share, using separate upper and lower bounds to skip candidates that can never be similar enough.
why it works If two documents must share a threshold number of words to be similar, then documents with too few possible overlaps can be pruned without full comparison; tighter bounds mean fewer candidates to check.
HuffmanEmbed: Using Huffman Coding for Embedding Table Compression in Deep Learning Recommendation ModelsSIGIR
uses Encode frequent items with short codes and rare items with long codes, then compress the lookup table by using these variable-length codes instead of fixed-width entries.
why it works Frequently accessed items benefit from short codes; rarely accessed items can afford long codes. Overall storage shrinks because the average code length is shorter than storing every item with the same width.
PEARL: Profile-based Explainable Agent for Edge LLM Recommendation via Latent DecompositionSIGIR
uses Maps user and model fingerprints into a shared low-features space where finding the best model becomes finding the nearest point to the user.
why it works Once you rotate high-dimensional data into a space where less important directions are removed, finding the nearest neighbor in that space is fast and direct. Projecting both users and models through the same lens means 'similar in important ways' becomes 'close together,' letting exact geometric nearness solve the matching problem.
Spectral Tempering for Embedding Compression in Dense Passage RetrievalSIGIR
uses Learns how much to downweight or amplify each features when compressing high-dimensional text representations, based on how much signal versus noise each features carries at different sizes.
why it works Useful features have strong signals; noisy ones amplify garbage. By measuring the ratio of real signal to noise in each direction, you can reweight before compression—features with worse ratios get suppressed, preserving what matters while discarding clutter.
HALO: Hyperbolic Adaptation via Lift Overlay for Hierarchy-Aware Cross-Modal RetrievalSIGIR
uses Adapts Euclidean text-image numeric fingerprints to hyperbolic space (where hierarchy is native) for similarity scoring, preserving Euclidean training while adding hierarchy awareness.
why it works Hyperbolic geometry naturally encodes hierarchies: moving from coarse to fine detail corresponds to moving outward radially, distances expand exponentially. By computing similarity in hyperbolic geometry while keeping all training Euclidean, you get hierarchy for free at matching time without retraining.
Cross-Sensory Comparison of EEG Signals for Brain-Based Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Trains models to map brain signals (EEG) close to text passages with matching meaning, comparing modalities under controlled sample sizes and vocabularies.
why it works If the model pulls brain signals and text together in a shared space only when they convey the same meaning, later 'nearness to a query' becomes 'finding passages the brain recognizes.' Controlling data and vocabulary isolates real neural differences from artifacts.
Sparse Contrastive Learning for Content-Based Cold Item RecommendationSIGIR
uses Trains a content encoder to map new items into a space where item-to-item similarity predicts user preference, using sharpened loss to ignore uninformative candidate items.
why it works If you build a space where items users prefer sit close together, then 'find recommendations' becomes 'find neighbors.' Sharpening the loss (zeroing slope for obviously wrong items) focuses learning on hard distinctions, ignoring noise that doesn't change rankings.
Clustering-Based Methods for Vector-Based Pseudo-Relevance FeedbackSIGIR
uses Cluster retrieved documents to find core object concepts, then use those cluster centers as expansion terms that make dense retrieval better.
why it works Cluster centers represent the shared essence of similar documents. Using them as new search terms works because they capture generalizable patterns that similar documents shared, expanding coverage beyond the original query.
PeaCap: Patch-Level Retrieval for Lightweight Retrieval-Augmented Image CaptioningSIGIR
uses Break images into patches, retrieve similar patches from elsewhere, extract objects found near them, then weight which retrieved objects matter most when generating captions.
why it works Small regions of an image often match small regions in other images with different objects. By searching at that finer grain and weighting objects by how often they appear with your patches, you find rare things that whole-image search would miss.
Not All Imputations are Trustworthy: An Uncertainty-aware Multi-modal Entity Alignment FrameworkSIGIR
uses Estimate how reliable each imputed modality is via uncertainty, then down-weight imputed features when fusing multimodal evidence for entity matching based on that uncertainty.
why it works Features generated by imputation carry estimation error. By quantifying that error (uncertainty) and using it to suppress noise during fusion, you prevent bad imputations from swamping the signal from real data.
EvoMem: Timeline-Grounded Validity Adjudication for Non-Monotonic Multi-Agent MemorySIGIR
uses Convert agent memory traces into a timeline, select key timepoints, and suppress outdated claims—treating validity adjudication as finding the most recent, consistent version of each fact.
why it works Memory is non-monotonic: claims get revised, retracted, resurfaced. The truth is the final, most recent version supported by evidence. By mapping changes onto a timeline and downweighting old claims, you extract what's actually true now.
ColBERTSaR: Sparsified ColBERT Index via Product QuantizationSIGIR
uses A document search index compresses the tiny meaning-indicators from each word in a document using a mathematical squashing technique so the index becomes a true search structure instead of a heavy compressed archive.
why it works Squashing meaning-indicators into compact codes works because the real information that tells whether a document matches a query lives in which indicators light up, not their exact values, so aggressive compression loses almost nothing.
Prototype-Calibrated Graph Prompting for Few-Shot Graph AdaptationSIGIR
uses For adapting a fixed graph model with few examples, score edges by how well they connect to learned prototypes from the examples, then keep only the highest-scoring edges per node.
why it works It works because the prototypes capture what the fixed model has already learned to recognize as important; by only creating edges to high-prototype-matching neighbors, you inject signal that the fixed model can use; per-node budgets prevent dense local rewiring that drowns out signal.
Latent Retrieval Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Instead of putting retrieved text into the prompt or encoding it as model weights, compress each document into a tiny meaning-summary and blend those summaries into the model's hidden thoughts as it generates.
why it works It works because meaning lives in the semantic space that the model already thinks in; by working in that space rather than forcing knowledge through words bottlenecks or parameter updates, knowledge integrates more naturally and uses less space.
Layer-wise Token Compression for Efficient Document RerankingSIGIR
uses Reduce the number of words to score at middle layers of the ranking model, dropping redundant text while preserving ranking quality.
why it works It works because most of the ranking signal is redundant—many words add no new information to the decision. Aggressively pooling words at deeper layers (where semantics are richer) preserves what matters while cutting noise, keeping speed gains without quality loss.
jina-embeddings-v5-text: Compact and Robust Text Embedding Models using Task-Targeted DistillationSIGIR
uses Compress text into small numeric codes that capture meaning, trained by making similar texts map close together and different ones far apart.
why it works It works because language meaning is relational—words and ideas are similar or different by degree. Placing all similar texts near each other and dissimilar ones far apart in the space means 'find similar' becomes just 'find nearby', and nearness is fast and mathematically well-behaved.
From Doxa to Logos in Scientific Peer ReviewSIGIR
uses Audit peer reviews by retrieving supporting evidence from papers to check if reviewer claims are grounded, scoring similarity of review text to manuscript content.
why it works It works because reviewers should cite the paper they're evaluating. By finding which parts of the paper are actually mentioned or implied in the review, you can identify when reviewers are speculating unsupported. Text-to-text nearness reveals what the reviewer was responding to.
Probe-then-Plan: Environment-Aware Planning for Industrial E-commerce SearchSIGIR
uses A model first samples what items the system can actually retrieve right now, then reasons about how to rewrite the query, ensuring the plan matches reality instead of guessing blind.
why it works Query rewriting fails when it ignores what the system can retrieve. By peeking at the retrieval landscape first—a cheap probe—the planner reasons with ground truth about what's possible, avoiding impossible requests and latency-killing corrections.
CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation SystemsSIGIR
uses Instead of treating all past clicks as one messy list, the model untangles them into separate coherent themes and learns from each theme independently.
why it works A user's history is chaotic—clicks on shoes, then recipes, then hiking gear come from different underlying wants. One sequence model drowns the signal. By untangling history into pure strands (each theme separate), each strand becomes clear and focused, letting the model learn genuine intent patterns instead of averaging across noise.
Agentic Query Reformulation for Contextualized Hyper-Personalized Product SearchSIGIR
uses When users search broadly, the system reasons through their purchase history to rewrite the query more precisely, using pre-computed candidate lists for speed.
why it works A broad query (e.g., 'blue jacket') is ambiguous. Past purchases reveal the user's actual style, size, and price range. Reasoning through this history and rewriting the query to be specific ('waterproof hiking jacket, size M, under 150') converts ambiguity to clarity. Pre-computing top rewrites for each query makes this instant.
Next Interest Flow: A Generative Pre-training Paradigm for Recommender Systems by Modeling All-domain MovelinesSIGIR
uses The model views user intent as a path through a high-dimensional space, learning smooth continuous paths that evolve naturally over time instead of jumping between discrete categories.
why it works User interests do not change in discrete jumps; they flow smoothly—from casual to committed, shifting gradually between domains. Modeling this as continuous motion through a space (not discrete symbols) preserves the real topology of how interests actually change. Smoothness constraints (geodesic keeping it simple) enforce that evolution is gradual, capturing the true structure of human need.
All the News That Fits in Bits: Learned Rotation-Aware Binary Projections for Efficient News Retrieval at NDTVSIGIR
uses The system converts dense float lists of numbers into short binary codes that preserve neighbor relationships, enabling 4-6x faster search with only modest accuracy loss.
why it works Dense lists of numbers are slow to search at scale. Binary codes are fast—a computer can compare them in a few machine cycles. Learning a projection that keeps neighbors neighbors ensures that a fast binary search returns almost the same top results as slow float search. Moderate bit-widths (3000 bits instead of millions) prove sufficient because you only need enough precision to preserve ordering, not exact distances.
Surface-Form Neural Sparse Retrieval: Robust Fuzzy Matching for Industrial Music SearchSIGIR
uses The system learns short words patterns (at most 3 characters) that are robust to misspellings and phonetic drift, pre-computes them offline, and searches them online with no delay.
why it works Misspellings (searching 'Beyonce' for 'Beyoncé') and phonetic variations ('Beatles' vs 'The Beatles') break traditional word matching. By learning sparse patterns on very short words, the model captures fuzzy surface-form similarity without memorizing exact spellings. Pre-computing all patterns during indexing makes online queries instant, fitting strict latency budgets for music search at scale.
Don't Contrast the Impossible: Region-Constrained Batching for Contrastive User Modeling on a Local Community PlatformSIGIR
uses User representations are learned by placing users close to items they engaged with and far from items they couldn't have seen due to geographic limits.
why it works It works because true negatives (items users genuinely cannot see) are different from false negatives (items they could see but didn't). Treating impossible items as negatives teaches the model false distinctions; using only feasible items teaches which real users differ.
Gesture Clustering for Real-Time User Disentanglement in Shared-Account RecommendationSIGIR
uses Gestures (screen touches, swipes, taps) are grouped into clusters so that identity-revealing patterns in how people hold and manipulate a device become distinct signals for recommending.
why it works It works because gesture patterns are instant (no history needed) yet encode habit—identical twins don't swipe the same way. Clustering separates identity signals so cleanly that the main recommender receives explicit cues about who is touching the screen, enabling real-time user disentanglement.
ReST: A Plug-and-Play Spatially-Constrained Representation Enhancement Framework for Local-Life RecommendationSIGIR
uses Long-tail (unpopular) local items are given stronger representations by aligning them with spatial attributes, so they compete fairly against popular items in recommendation.
why it works It works because spatial attributes anchor unpopular items to meaningful features they share; this makes their representations less dependent on sparse interaction history. When weak signals get tied to what they truly are (a restaurant in a neighborhood, a service available in a zone), recommenders find them more easily.
User Activity Modeling under Inflated DistributionSIGIR
uses Splits user activity prediction into two parts: first detecting whether a user is at an extreme (completely inactive or fully active), then modeling the distribution for everyone else.
why it works It works because the data has two peaks at the extremes. Treating the extremes separately prevents those outliers from warping the model for the middle users. Each part can now assume a simpler distribution shape.
From Queries to Playlists: An LLM-Driven Architecture for Semantic Music Search at ScaleSIGIR
uses Encodes music tracks and queries into a shared semantic space using a language model, then re-ranks candidates with a cross-encoder to find matching playlists.
why it works It works because semantic distance in the shared space now captures subjective similarity. Tracks with similar meaning sit nearby even if they share no keywords. Re-ranking refines the rough ranking cheaply, and distilling its signals into the encoder reduces cost at serving time.
Automated Feature Lifecycle Management in Large-Scale Continual Ranking SystemsSIGIR
uses Learns which input features matter during rapid retraining by using discrete binary masks, then relaxes them to continuous importance scores for serving.
why it works It works because online data changes fast, so features become obsolete. Learning masks during training (with straight-through estimators) lets slope descent decide what to keep. Relaxing to probabilities at serving time gives both a deterministic score and interpretability without extra computation.
Enhancing Enterprise Assistant Responses with Rich Multimodal Artifacts from Product DocumentationSIGIR
uses Find and return images and videos from documentation that are most similar to what the user is asking about.
why it works It works because when you represent both the question and the multimedia content in a shared space where similar ideas sit close together, finding the nearest neighbors gives you the most relevant artifacts. This way, procedural videos and diagrams naturally bubble up when they match the user's intent.
Pin-SCALE: Semantic Cascading and Alignment Learning for Engagement-Aware IDs in Cold-Start RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Learn item representations that group similar things close together, especially for new items, by contrasting what users engage with against what they ignore.
why it works It works because when you push items users interacted with closer together and pull apart items they ignored, the geometry of the space encodes real collaborative signals. New items inherit predictive power from their semantic neighbors without needing existing engagement data.
COMET: Compatibility-Oriented Multi-modal Embedding Transformer for Visual RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Determine which visual features matter for each pairing of products by learning where text and images align, treating compatibility as conditional retrieval.
why it works It works because fashion compatibility is context-dependent; a sofa-table pairing looks for different features than sofa-curtain. By conditioning which visual features to examine based on the relational text context, you capture nuanced style rules that rigid global features miss.
Scalable Multi-vector Retrieval for Policy Enforcement on E-commerce MarketplacesSIGIR
uses Rank content policies by relevance to each product listing using dense retrieval, reducing computational cost by filtering to likely-matching policies first.
why it works It works because enforcement is a retrieval problem: find policies that a product might violate. Ranking policies by how close their semantic meaning is to the product description gives a fast filter that catches most violations, letting expensive verification focus on genuine suspects.
Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence ModelingSIGIR
uses Represent videos by their semantic category hierarchies and compress ultra-long user watch histories using a specialized focus that folds time efficiently.
why it works It works because atomic video IDs are sparse and wasteful; semantic hierarchies compress the numeric fingerprints space and generalize to new content via shared prefixes. Temporal folding reduces the quadratic explosion of focus, letting you model much longer histories without exploding memory or latency costs.
PGSF: Profile-Guided Semantic Fusion for Decoupled Industrial Pre-RankingSIGIR
uses Train a recommendation model to encode fine-grained user-item interactions during learning, then deploy in a fast two-tower form by injecting user profile guidance and discretized interest spaces.
why it works It works because two-tower models are fast but lose rich interactions. Training with target-item guidance teaches the model to capture nuance, then compressing interests into discrete semantic clusters preserves expressiveness while keeping inference decoupled and efficient.
SECRET: SEarch query Classification with label RETrievalSIGIR
uses Place queries and category names near each other in space when they mean similar things, then find nearby categories for new queries.
why it works It works because if you position things so that semantically similar items sit close in space, then 'find the right category' becomes simply 'find what's nearest', and nearness is fast to compute and meaningful. This lets the model generalize to new categories it has never seen before.
Policy-Grounded Dynamic Facet Suggestions for Job SearchSIGIR
uses Retrieve candidate facets using semantic similarity, then score each candidate using learned patterns to rank which facet best matches the user's current query and context.
why it works It works because facets and queries naturally form a semantic space where similar ideas sit close. Scoring candidates within that space exploits learned patterns of which attributes help disambiguate common query types. Ranking by learned score puts the most relevant facet on top.
Scaling and Stabilizing Large-Scale Embedding-Based RetrievalSIGIR
uses Train an encoder to place similar queries and products close together using a large, diverse set of negative examples, then transfer learned knowledge to a more powerful encoder.
why it works It works because diverse negatives force the encoder to make finer distinctions, so the learned space reflects true similarity more accurately. Transferring to a new encoder preserves this hard-won knowledge: the new model inherits the domain-specific refinements from the old model, starting it ahead rather than relearning from scratch.
A General Framework for Multimodal LLM-Based Multimedia Understanding in Large-Scale Recommendation SystemsSIGIR
uses A multimodal language model generates descriptive captions from images and videos, which are then tokenized as categorical features in the recommendation model.
why it works Raw images are high-dimensional and hard to reason about. A pretrained language model trained on billions of image-caption pairs already knows how to extract semantic meaning. Converting images to captions transforms the problem into text, which recommendation systems handle well, while preserving semantic signal.
From Unstructured to Structured: LLM-Guided Attribute Graphs for Entity Search and RankingSIGIR
uses Products are ranked by relevance computed over structured attributes extracted from product text, reducing words cost by using structured representations instead of raw text.
why it works Raw text is high-dimensional and variable; structured attributes are compact and normalized. Extracting attributes first removes noise and redundancy, then ranking on attributes is faster and cleaner. The semantic meaning is preserved in the structured schema while reducing per-product cost by 57%.
MCP Servers for Pyserini and RankLLM: Enabling Agentic Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Find and rank search results by relevance, then apply learned scoring models to reorder them, grounded in the language model's understanding of the question.
why it works It works because ranking first narrows the candidates before expensive scoring, and language models can learn to rank by comparing how closely each result aligns with the question's meaning through similarity in a learned space.
H-MAPS: Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Proactive Search Assistant for Scientific LiteratureSIGIR
uses Infer the reader's research interests from their reading behavior and background, then search and retrieve papers similar to what they are reading but tailored to their specialization.
why it works It works because a reader's background and current paper implicitly define their interests as points in a knowledge space; retrieving other papers nearby in that space produces relevant results personalized to that researcher's needs.
WISE: A Multimodal Search Engine for Visual Scenes, Audio, Objects, Faces, Speech, and MetadataSIGIR
uses Index scenes, objects, faces, and speech as points in space so searching means finding nearby points in that space.
why it works When you represent different modalities (images, audio, text) as positions in the same space, similarity naturally becomes distance: closer things are more alike, and distance queries become fast lookups.
Towards Building a Standard Benchmark for Low-Resource Nepali Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Score and rank Nepali documents against queries using learned numeric fingerprints that capture morphological structure.
why it works Words with similar roots should place near each other in numeric fingerprints space; learnable scoring of that nearness ranks relevant documents highest despite morphological variation in the language.
Morphology-Aware Retrieval for Low-Resource Environments: Advancing Information Retrieval for Shona LanguageSIGIR
uses Score and rank Shona documents by learning numeric fingerprints that preserve morphological relationships to improve retrieval.
why it works Morphologically related words should score as similar; learning that structure places documents with related word forms near the query in numeric fingerprints space, retrieval by proximity then ranks them highest.
ViCSR: A Large-scale Benchmark and Lightweight Two-Stage Framework for Vietnamese Case-to-Statute RetrievalSIGIR
uses Place legal cases and statutes in a learned space where similar ones sit near each other; rank by distance; refine ranking using citation network structure.
why it works It works because if you arrange documents so that similar ones are placed close together, finding similar items becomes simply finding nearby neighbors, which is cheap to compute. Citation structure adds a second signal: documents frequently linked together are genuinely related, so incorporating network edges into ranking improves precision.
Efficient Continual Adaptation of Generative Retrieval Systems over Dynamic CorporaSIGIR
uses Update AI search models continuously as corpus grows, selecting which old knowledge to keep and which to discard to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
why it works It works because incremental model updates on new documents tend to overwrite old knowledge unless you deliberately preserve important features. By selecting which parts of past knowledge matter most for current performance, you retain skills on old documents while learning new ones.
How Should Multimodal Information Be Chunked for Complex Question Answering?SIGIR
uses Chunk multimodal evidence (text, tables, images) into fine-grained retrievable units and rank by relevance to the question across all modalities.
why it works It works because retrieval precision improves when units are smaller and more focused: a single paragraph is easier to judge relevant than a whole document. With multimodal content, breaking into modality-aware chunks (a table as one unit, a figure as another) lets ranking systems score each piece independently based on its relevance.
Trustworthy Personalized Retrieval in the LLM Era: Fairness, Bias Awareness, Privacy, and MultimodalitySIGIR
uses Scoring search results and recommendations by learning which features matter for each person, while detecting and correcting bias that would unfairly rank results.
why it works Learning lets you fit the score function to real user behavior, and weighting lets you dampen the influence of features that encode unfair distinctions. Measuring bias and fairness directly makes it possible to catch when outcomes harm minorities.
Bridging Personalization and AI: From RAG to AgentSIGIR
uses Personalizing search and recommendation by learning which documents and items matter for each user, at three stages: choosing what to fetch, ranking what you found, and phrasing the answer.
why it works Learning the user's preferences from their history lets you tailor the score function; personalizing at multiple stages compounds the effect because each stage can refine the result. This is more effective than one-size-fits-all because different users need different evidence.
Temporal Information Retrieval and Extraction: From Foundations to RAGSIGIR
uses Finding documents relevant at specific times by extracting when events occurred, ranking documents by temporal validity, and reasoning about time in multi-step question answering.
why it works Time is a crucial features because information changes: a fact true in 2020 may be false in 2026. When you explicitly model when something is valid and rank by temporal relevance, you avoid serving outdated or future information. Time-aware ranking makes the system adaptive to reality's evolution.
ReNeuIR at SIGIR 2026: The Fifth Workshop on Reaching Efficiency in Neural Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Measuring and reducing the cost (latency, memory, compute) of neural retrieval models while keeping search quality high, using standardized benchmarks so different systems can be fairly compared.
why it works Efficiency matters because slow systems hurt real users and waste resources. Finding the settings that minimize cost while keeping quality high is a constrained optimization problem. Fair comparison requires identical hardware and metrics, so you don't accidentally favor models that happen to run on expensive machines.
LLM-UP: SIGIR 2026 Workshop on LLM-powered User Profiling for Search and RecommendationSIGIR
uses Extracting user preferences and intents as summaries from language, then using them to personalize search results and recommendations.
why it works It works because users who express similar preferences tend to want similar results; if you capture what each user cares about, matching new queries to their profile becomes a nearness problem.
145 papers

Ranking by a learned score

Search, recommendation, and advertising all come down to the same act: give every candidate a score for how well it fits the moment, then sort and show the top few.

Why it works — the principle

It works because you almost never need the exact scores — only their order. A rough score that merely gets the ordering right already floats the best results to the top, so the real problem is far easier than pinning down a true number for every item, and small scoring errors that don't change the order don't matter at all.

Beyond Item-Level Prediction: Fine-Grained CVR Modeling with Price SKU in E-Commerce RecommendationWWW
uses Predict whether someone will buy at the fine-grained price level instead of just item level, grouping variants by price to keep signal without breaking the system.
why it works Buyers decide at the price level: the same item at ten prices is ten different choices. Item-level models miss that. Direct price-level modeling breaks sparse data into pieces too small to learn from. Grouping by price keeps the signal that matters (this person likes this price range) while merging sparse variants.
Talos: Optimizing Top-K Accuracy in Recommender SystemsWWW
uses Learn a threshold that separates top-ranked items from the rest, then score and rank items against that threshold.
why it works Ranking positions are expensive to compute directly, but you only need to know which items beat a cutoff score. By learning the threshold smartly from random samples, you avoid ranking the entire catalog while still getting the correct top-K items.
Learning to Alleviate Familiarity Bias in Video RecommendationWWW
uses Learn personalized debiasing scores that downrank familiar content by estimating how much each user overfavors content they already know.
why it works Users are predictably biased toward the familiar even when it's not optimal. By learning this bias for each user and subtracting it from recommendation scores, you flatten the ranking so that novel content can compete fairly and still emerge if it's truly relevant.
PruneRAG: Confidence-Guided Query Decomposition Trees for Efficient Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Build a tree of subquestions, score each node's confidence, then prune branches with low confidence and retrieve only entity-level anchors needed for reasoning.
why it works Confidence-guided pruning keeps only branches that retrieve truly useful evidence, reducing noise that would otherwise dilute the model's ability to combine facts into correct answers.
Evolving Notions of Success on the Web: From Retrieval to ExperienceWWW
uses Web success evolved from ranking documents by relevance to ranking experiences by user satisfaction over time.
why it works Experience metrics aggregate signals from repeated interactions; persistent value is more predictive of system utility than isolated relevance judgments.
RPO-RAG: Aligning Small LLMs with Relation-aware Preference Optimization for Knowledge Graph Question AnsweringWWW
uses Retrieves reasoning paths from knowledge graphs and trains the model to rank them by semantic relevance, then reasons using only the ranked useful paths.
why it works Explicit ranking via preference signals teaches the model to ignore noise; small models benefit from curated, organized inputs over raw unfiltered retrieval.
Personalized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Foundation Models for Multimodal RecommendationWWW
uses Split users into interest groups, assign each group its own tuning module so it learns to emphasize the item features each group cares about, then apply this personalized tuning when scoring items.
why it works Generic tuning ranks all items by one scoring function; personalized tuning lets different user groups weight different item aspects (color-focused vs. durability-focused). Because each group's tuning module only tunes for its own group, it learns finer distinctions in the aspects that group values, while keeping the overall parameter footprint light (one small module per group, shared foundation model).
MetaKube: An Experience-Aware LLM Framework for Kubernetes Failure DiagnosisWWW
uses Learns diagnostic patterns from past cases, scores how confident the model should be about each solution, and routes between fast pattern lookup and slower reasoning based on confidence.
why it works It works because Kubernetes failures repeat in patterns—once you score how similar a new failure is to past ones you know, fast lookup beats slow reasoning. Routing by confidence lets you spend time reasoning only when patterns don't help, balancing speed and accuracy.
Red-Teaming Privacy-Protective Perturbations: Blind Face Restoration as an Attack StrategyWWW
uses Scores how successfully face restoration defeats privacy protections by tuning attack settings, measures image identity consistency as the key metric to attack.
why it works It works because the best privacy defense is one that can't be circumvented by known attacks, so finding the attack settings that work best reveals which protections are truly robust. Measuring identity consistency directly tests whether the core defense—making faces unrecognizable—actually holds.
GreenWebInspector: A Tool for Real-Time Web Energy Efficiency AssessmentWWW
uses Score webpage energy consumption by learning a pattern from webpage structure features that predicts how much device battery a page will drain, without measuring actual power during browsing.
why it works Energy use correlates with page complexity and content type; by learning which structure features predict high energy on test devices, you can score any page instantly from its design, avoiding the need for expensive real-time measurement.
A Taxonomy-Driven Cryptographic Dependency Inventory for Post-Quantum Migration in Decentralized Systems: Triage Rules and a Worked ExampleWWW
uses Catalogs which cryptographic components in decentralized systems need post-quantum upgrades most urgently by ranking them by exposure, governance friction, and verification cost.
why it works Not all cryptographic parts pose equal risk or require equal work to upgrade. Ranking by concrete risk factors and deployment friction identifies where to spend effort first so limited resources tackle the highest-impact vulnerabilities.
From Token to Item: Enhancing Large Language Models for Recommendation via Item-aware Attention MechanismWWW
uses Score each item's usefulness based on its internal content and how it relates to other items users have liked, then rank items by these scores.
why it works This works because recommendations are fundamentally about prediction: if you learn a scoring function on past behavior, the scores capture patterns of what makes items relevant. Separating item-level relationships from words-level noise lets the scorer focus on what users actually care about: items themselves, not the words inside them.
Prototype-Aligned Federated Soft-Prompts for Continual Web PersonalizationWWW
uses Maintain personalized short-term and server-shared long-term prompts that route queries to the most relevant user prototypes, balancing quick adaptation with stable long-term memory.
why it works This works because users have both session whims and stable taste: by maintaining two timescales, you adapt fast without forgetting. Tying long-term memory to a shared prototype library lets all users benefit from collective patterns while staying private.
Dynamic Experts Synergy for Multi-Task RecommendationWWW
uses Dynamically partition specialized experts into leaders and auxiliaries, then recycle auxiliary knowledge through utility, diversity, and task relatedness to strengthen recommendations across multiple goals.
why it works This works because expert systems work best when knowledge is reused: a task that struggles has experts with low scores but useful patterns. By classifying and recycling that hidden knowledge, you get task-specific gains without rebuilding from scratch.
Towards Responsible Recommendations: A Daily Updated Ranking Model for Content Issue DetectionWWW
uses Scoring videos daily for problematic content using behavior patterns plus author metadata plus fast algorithm outputs, updated each day to catch new issues immediately.
why it works It works because content issues evolve weekly or daily (new videos, new exploits), so a system that updates monthly misses them. By combining user behavior feedback (which shows real harm immediately) with video-side signals, you detect genuine issues while they're still small.
What Is Your AI Agent Buying? Evaluation, Biases, Model Dependence, & Emerging Implications of Agentic E-CommerceWWW
uses The study measures what products AI shopping agents choose given different layouts, prices, and reviews, revealing how agents rank and weigh options differently than humans or each other.
why it works Agents learn rankings from their training data, but different agents prioritize different signals. By varying one feature at a time and watching choice change, you identify what ranking rule each agent actually learned, exposing hidden biases and assumptions baked into them.
FlowRAG: Continual Learning for Dynamic Retriever in Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Adjust the retrieval ranker to match both semantic relevance and the downstream language model's generation quality.
why it works The retriever and language model are chained; aligning the retriever to the model's likelihoods directly optimizes end-to-end quality rather than just local retrieval accuracy. Small updates to numeric fingerprints weights compound into better ranking.
Detecting Miscitation on the Scholarly Web through LLM-Augmented Text-Rich Graph LearningWWW
uses Use a language model to reason about citation chains, then distill those reasoning patterns into a graph systems that learn from examples for fast detection.
why it works Language models are slow but understand semantic nuance; graph networks are fast but miss context. Distilling the model's reasoning into the network captures the best of both: semantic accuracy without per-citation cost.
LegalKit: A Modular Toolkit for Efficient Legal AI EvaluationWWW
uses Benchmark legal language models across diverse scenarios using a unified evaluation framework that standardizes task definitions and scoring.
why it works Legal tasks are heterogeneous. A shared scoring methodology makes comparisons fair and reproducible. Standardized benchmarks reveal which models perform best at the tasks that matter, guiding real-world deployment.
CC-OR-Net: A Unified Framework for LTV Prediction through Structural DecouplingWWW
uses Decompose the customer-value problem into an ordered ranking (low to high spender) and a precision-focused regression (adjust value within each tier), solving both simultaneously.
why it works High-value customers are extremely rare and numerically lost in standard regression; by first ranking customers into tiers and then fitting each tier separately, you give the rare 'whale' segment enough signal to train on without the low-value majority drowning them out. Structural tier separation works because tiers are inherently ordered.
Following the TRAIL: Predicting and Explaining Tomorrow's Hits with a Fine-Tuned LLMWWW
uses Uses pairs of items (one popular tomorrow, one not) to train a model to score how viral each item will become, then explains those scores in plain language.
why it works It works because learning from pairs of dissimilar examples forces the model to discover what actually separates hits from misses, rather than memorizing coincidences. Comparing winners and losers directly reveals the causal signal in sparse data.
Data-Driven Function Calling Improvements in Large Language Model for Online Financial QAWWW
uses Trains a language model to match user questions to the right financial API by building a dataset from past queries and inventing variations to cover missing parameter types.
why it works It works because the model learns from examples what each parameter means; when you show it variations of the same idea stated different ways, it learns the semantic boundaries. The trained model can then generalize to phrasing it has never seen.
Towards Multi-Label Text Interpretation with Chain-of-Thought Prompting and Contextualized KnowledgeWWW
uses Learns which text segments and words belong to each label by following explicit reasoning chains, improving label assignment.
why it works It works because step-by-step reasoning reveals why each piece of text actually connects to a label. Making the reasoning explicit forces the model to find real justifications rather than spurious correlations.
Explainable Graph Sparsification with Shapley ValuesWWW
uses Uses importance scores (Shapley values) to identify which edges are least important and removes them without hurting accuracy.
why it works It works because Shapley values fairly distribute credit: an edge that barely influences predictions gets low credit. Removing low-credit edges keeps the model's decisions intact because those edges weren't doing much work anyway.
DRMD: Explainable Depression Detection Based on Metaphorical Conceptual MappingWWW
uses Predict depression severity by scoring social media text according to metaphorical expressions and their psychological patterns.
why it works Works because metaphors are linguistic fingerprints of mental state; the way people describe abstract experiences through metaphor is a stable marker of depression level.
URLBank: Data-Driven URL Discovery via Temporal Link GraphsWWW
uses Rank candidate websites by how long their links persist and how often they publish new content, then greedily select the best ones that add the most new coverage.
why it works It works because persistence and productivity are signals of value—websites that keep their URLs stable and publish frequently will yield the most new discoveries per crawl, so targeting them first maximizes coverage fastest.
TopKGAT: A Top-K Objective-Driven Architecture for RecommendationWWW
uses Design a recommendation network whose forward pass directly optimizes the top-K ranking metric by using a smooth approximation of which items rank in the top K.
why it works It works because recommenders usually optimize loss functions that don't match the actual goal (top-K accuracy); aligning the network architecture with top-K slope means the model naturally learns to put the best items first, not just rank them well on average.
Docs2Synth: A Synthetic Data Tuned Retriever Framework for Documents UnderstandingWWW
uses Trains a retriever to rank and extract the most relevant pages from domain documents, then uses them to ground a AI language systems's answers to questions.
why it works It works because a language model on its own hallucinates facts; ranking pages lets it only say what documents actually contain. Retrieval grounds the model in truth.
Triple Modality Fusion: Aligning Visual, Textual, and Graph Data for LLM-based Multi-Behavior Recommender SystemsWWW
uses Score each item by combining a ranking built from historical user behaviors as a graph, visual features, and text features; weight each source by focus to balance their influence.
why it works Historical behavior graphs reveal what users actually do (the signal). Text and images reveal intent. focus learns which matters most per user-item pair—some users care most about product images, others about recommendations from similar users. Separate scores fused by learned weights beat fusing raw features.
Temporal Information Retrieval And Question Answering in the Age of LLMsWWW
uses Rank retrieved information by both topical relevance score AND validity over time; adapt retrieval when knowledge changes to reflect current rather than historical truth.
why it works On a changing web, recency matters as much as topical match. A document can be relevant but outdated. Temporal ranking accounts for when the document was true. Adaptation ensures systems track concept drift in the world, not memorize stale patterns.
HyperRAG: Reasoning N-ary Facts over Hypergraphs for Retrieval Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Find the best multi-step reasoning path through n-ary facts by scoring and ranking candidate paths using both structural reasoning and guidance from the language model's internal knowledge.
why it works N-ary facts (e.g., 'who did what to whom when') preserve semantic coherence better than binary triples, so fewer hops are needed. Fewer hops mean fewer chances for errors to accumulate. AI language systems guidance learns which facts are actually true, so beam search prioritizes coherent factual paths over plausible noise.
AliBoostV2: CTR-Growth Balanced Boosting Framework in Billion-Scale Recommendation PlatformWWW
uses Boosts visibility of unpopular items by predicting which users will click them AND how much future natural growth they'll generate, then targets users where both scores are high.
why it works A click on a cold item helps twice: immediate revenue and seeding future organic discovery. By forecasting both impacts for each user-item pair, you can rank users not just by likelihood to click, but by long-term value they unlock. Balancing growth with immediate clicks sustains ecosystem health.
A Large Language Model-based Agent for Automated Machine Learning Workflow ConstructionWWW
uses Build machine learning workflows from natural language by breaking requests into hierarchical steps and scoring which tools best fit each step.
why it works It works because complex tasks decompose naturally into subtasks, and each subtask has a small set of appropriate tools. By ranking tools based on task intent rather than guessing from raw text, the system avoids dead ends and picks genuinely useful operations.
Breaking Cross-modal Alignment in Embodied Intelligence: A Multimodal Adversarial Attack Framework for Vision-Language-Action ModelsWWW
uses Adversaries craft invisible image changes that disrupt alignment between vision, language, and action, causing wrong commands.
why it works If small perturbations break the mapping between modalities, the alignment was brittle; the attack exploits this fragility to expose design flaws.
AlignCP: Noise-Aware Preference Alignment for LLMs via Confidence and Polarity ReweightingWWW
uses Assign training weights to preference pairs based on a confidence score from the reward model and whether it agrees with human labels.
why it works It works because noisy examples that contradict the reward model's own judgments waste training effort. Downweighting them lets the model learn only from coherent signals, like keeping only the reliable voices in a crowd voting on preferences.
Calculating Narrative Tension for Ad Placement in Online Narrative FictionWWW
uses Train a language model classifier to label narrative paragraphs by tension level, then place ads in low-tension paragraphs.
why it works Readers are least immersed during low-tension passages, so ads interrupt less and annoy less. Placing ads by learned tension rank minimizes disruption to reading experience relative to random placement.
Multi-Behavior Sequential Modeling with Transition-Aware Graph Attention Network for E-Commerce RecommendationWWW
uses Scores which pairs of user behaviors should be connected in a graph structure, then learns from those behaviors to predict what a user will do next.
why it works It works because user actions follow patterns—clicking and buying are related, so placing them nearby in a structure lets you predict transitions. By learning which transitions matter most, you exploit the hidden rules governing how user intentions evolve.
LLMs Killed Q&A Stars? Analyzing the Impact of LLM-Generated Answers on an Online Q&A PlatformWWW
uses Score answers as generated by an AI language systems or written by humans, using text features and stacked classifiers to rank them correctly.
why it works A learned score that captures patterns like length, punctuation, and lexical variety can separate generated from human text because each style leaves statistical fingerprints; combining multiple weak scorers amplifies the signal.
Automated Model Selection for Multivariate Time Series ForecastingWWW
uses Encode raw time series using a pre-trained model, extract repeating temporal patterns as features, then classify each series to recommend which forecasting method works best for it.
why it works Works because different forecasting algorithms excel on different data characteristics: one handles trend, another handles cycles, another handles noise. Learning to classify series by their true patterns lets you pick the specialist best suited to each, rather than training every method then comparing.
Dual-Branch Multi-Granularity Network with Structured Contrastive Ranking for Cross-Modal RetrievalWWW
uses Rank images and text by learning which pairs belong together and which don't, then putting look-alike pairs close in a shared space.
why it works When you place things so that ones people treat alike sit close together, finding similar ones becomes finding nearby ones, which is fast and reliable. Contrasting good matches against bad ones teaches the system which patterns matter most.
Triple-R: Iterative Query Rewriting and Refinement for Retrieval-Augmented Fake News DetectionWWW
uses Iteratively rewrite news queries to retrieve better evidence for fact-checking, optimizing queries based on feedback from a detector.
why it works It works because the query that retrieves the most useful evidence is usually not the original words. By learning to translate news into effective search terms—using feedback on which evidence actually helped—you align retrieval with verification needs.
Room Matters: Dynamic Room-level Collaboration Information Modeling for Live Streaming RecommendationWWW
uses Scores live streams by tracking how users, rooms, and streamers interact moment-to-moment.
why it works Works because live recommendations must adapt to instant feedback; modeling interaction as a dynamic graph captures rapid shifts.
Visual Content Moderation in Messaging SystemsWWW
uses Assigns each image a category score using learned patterns to identify spam across eight classes.
why it works It works because spam images share consistent visual features. Learning finds those patterns, so images with similar visual markers to known spam rank high and get caught.
From Generation to Detection: Leveraging Empirically Derived Linguistic Hints for LLM-Based Fake News DetectionWWW
uses Scores news headlines on toxicity, sentiment, and framing patterns to classify AI language systems-generated versus human-written articles.
why it works It works because AI language systems have consistent linguistic quirks that differ systematically from human writing. These measurable features form a reliable fingerprint that classifiers can learn and recognize.
EcoThink: A Green Adaptive Inference Framework for Sustainable and Accessible AgentsWWW
uses Routes queries by estimated complexity: simple ones skip reasoning, hard ones get full reasoning—adaptive routing cuts computation.
why it works It works because question complexity is skewed. The majority are simple facts needing only lookup, so bypassing reasoning for them cuts emissions massively without hurting accuracy on legitimate hard cases.
Click-to-Ask: An AI Live Streaming Assistant with Offline Copywriting and Online Interactive QAWWW
uses From product images and text, generate sales copy and answer viewer questions about products in real time during a livestream.
why it works Structured product data extracted offline becomes a lookup table during the stream—when a viewer question arrives, you rank stored answers and product facts by relevance and blend them into a coherent response. This works because static preparation eliminates latency, and ranking-then-blending is faster than generating from scratch.
EmoTg: Modeling Social Response to Telegram Posts Using LLM and NLP FeaturesWWW
uses Predict how Telegram post content will influence audience sentiment, toxicity, and humor by extracting linguistic and semantic features and scoring them as classifiers.
why it works Post features correlate with comment patterns—word choice, tone, and emotional signals carry information about likely audience reaction. Training classifiers on these features works because readers respond to the same signals the system extracts; ranking feature importance reveals which signals matter most for each reaction type.
PI2I: A Personalized Item-Based Collaborative Filtering Retrieval FrameworkWWW
uses Ranks items for a user by scoring each based on its interaction patterns with similar items, then personalizes the scoring function to weight what matters most to that specific user.
why it works Item-to-item similarity is stable across users (people who buy X also buy Y). Personalizing which similarities count for each user (weighting some edges high, others low) lets you adapt a universal structure to individual taste without retraining from scratch.
Conversational Entity Retrieval from a Knowledge Graph using Aggregation of Fine-grained Relevance Signals with Graph Convolutions and Self-AttentionWSDM
uses Extracts multiple fine-grained relevance signals between a dialog query and each entity in a knowledge graph, then learns to combine and rank those signals through graph layers to score candidate answers.
why it works Each relevance signal captures one aspect of fit; by learning to weight and spread those signals across the entity's neighborhood in the graph, the method discovers which combinations of signals best predict the right answer.
Towards Building an Enterprise World ModelWSDM
uses Score and rank enterprise documents by how well they align with brand voice and legal rules, then use top-scoring ones to shape language model outputs.
why it works It works because scoring documents by alignment allows you to retrieve only the best context before generating, making the language model inherently compliant and brand-true without full retraining.
Calibration in Dynamic Recommender SystemsWSDM
uses Adjusts recommendation weights over time to reflect how user interests shift, ensuring the distribution of recommended topics matches the user's actual interest distribution.
why it works It works because recommender systems naturally amplify main interests and suppress minor ones through optimization. By explicitly tracking each interest's true weight and forcing recommendations to match that ratio, you prevent echo chambers and give users the breadth they actually want.
REFLEX: Reinforcement Feedback Learning with Large Language Models for E-commerce Query ExpansionWSDM
uses Expands user search queries using a language model trained with real-time feedback from the search engine, optimizing for both relevant matches and catalog coverage.
