why it works It works because user intentions are ambiguous but the search engine reveals truth—which expanded queries retrieve relevant results and which don't. Learning directly from search feedback means the model optimizes for real success, not proxy metrics.
Cold-Starting Podcast Ads and Promotions with Multi-Task Learning on SpotifyWSDM
uses Learn a scoring function that ranks podcast ads and promotions by predicted user interest, using feedback on streams, clicks, and follows to weight which signals matter most.
why it works It works because user actions reveal what truly matters: if someone clicks or streams after seeing an ad, that interaction teaches the system which features predict genuine interest. Weighted scoring captures this—emphasizing the signals that actually drive behavior.
Rule Mining and Learning for Structured Knowledge RetrievalWSDM
uses Discover hidden retrieval rules by iteratively selecting high-value patterns, then learn scoring functions that rank candidates according to those rules, guided by task feedback.
why it works It works because humans reason in patterns—'to find papers by an author, first find co-authors, then find their papers.' By coupling pattern discovery with scoring refinement, the system learns both what paths to follow and how to rank results along those paths, improving with each correction.
LLM Agent-based Shilling Attack on Recommender SystemsWSDM
uses Use language models to generate fake user profiles and reviews that mimic human behavior, then strategically inject these profiles to manipulate recommender systems toward chosen targets.
why it works It works because recommender systems learn from user behavior, and language models are now fluent enough to forge that behavior convincingly. By generating reviews that exploit known patterns in recommendation scoring, the attack injects fake signals the system cannot distinguish from real ones.
From Search to Ask to Act: The Evolution of Information Access in the Age of Large Models and AgentsSIGIR
uses Retrieve evidence greedily when needed, then feed it to a reasoning model to generate answers and plan which questions to ask next, iterating to refine search strategy.
why it works It works because reasoning models are expensive, so you only invoke them when retrieval surfaces relevant evidence, then let them ask what to search for next. This closed loop between searching and reasoning prevents expensive reasoning on irrelevant facts while keeping search focused on what the reasoning step actually needs.
Logit Inflation in ListMLE: Theoretical Analysis and Mitigation StrategiesSIGIR
uses Prevent ranking models from learning unreasonably large confidence scores by adding temperature controls during training and suppressing slope that push scores unnecessarily high.
why it works It works because ranking only needs scores in the right order, not arbitrary magnitude. By bounding how large scores can grow relative to that ordering, you prevent overconfidence while maintaining ranking quality, yielding predictions you can trust numerically.
GCA-KBQA: A Step-Wise Logical Form Generation Approach for KBQA with Knowledge-Assisted CalibrationSIGIR
uses Build database queries one hop at a time, correcting each intermediate result using knowledge base facts before moving to the next step, assembling the final query from validated fragments.
why it works It works because complex queries have many steps, and early mistakes cascade. By validating each hop against actual knowledge base content and only continuing with feasible paths, you catch and fix errors incrementally rather than producing unsalvageable final queries.
Incentivizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Inner Adaptive Context SelectionSIGIR
uses Let the language model itself decide which retrieved documents it actually needs during generation, rather than keeping all of them.
why it works The model knows best which facts matter for the specific answer it is building. Self-selection cuts cost and noise without needing an external filter to guess.
Learning to Rank with Multi-Criteria LLM-Judge AnnotationsSIGIR
uses Use language model judges to score documents on exactness, coverage, topicality, and fit, then use those scores as features to teach a ranking model what the best results look like.
why it works A judge gives you multi-dimensional truth. Weak systems benefit most because they lack signal; as a system gets better, its native score already dominates, and judge signals become tie-breakers.
Diagnosing and Mitigating Mid-Sequence Degradation in Recommender SystemsSIGIR
uses Fix ranking bias that over-weights sequence edges by masking during training and adjusting scores afterward to remove positional artifacts.
why it works It works because the bias is systematic and predictable: edges capture real signals but also artificial position-only signals. Removing those false signals lets the learner rank by genuine preference patterns, not boundary artifacts. Testing this directly via controlled perturbations proves the bias is architectural, not accidental.
RULER: Robust Unified LLM-based Efficient Retrieval for Legal InformationSIGIR
uses Combine retrieval and reranking in one model sharing parameters, then suppress phantom high scores on irrelevant documents using hard negative examples and how much surprise keeping it simple.
why it works It works because the phantom-hit problem stems from the model over-confident on irrelevant items. Explicitly including pure negatives and penalizing unjustified confidence forces the model to reserve high scores for genuinely relevant documents, improving both early retrieval and final ranking.
Contrastive Flow Matching for Collaborative FilteringSIGIR
uses Generate personalized rankings by applying contrastive learning to intermediate model representations rather than to final scores, allowing shared preferences without false repulsion.
why it works It works because contrastive learning separates, but output rankings should separate users only when their preferences differ. By contrasting at an intermediate layer, the model learns distinct representations while allowing different users with overlapping tastes to produce identical final rankings. This avoids forcing users apart when they should naturally agree.
MUDY: Multi-Granular Dynamic Candidate Contextualization for Unsupervised Keyphrase ExtractionSIGIR
uses Score each keyphrase candidate by its local importance in its segment and its generation likelihood globally.
why it works It works because keyphrases matter most when they represent local topics, not just when they appear often everywhere; scoring both features captures which phrases actually summarize their section.
Generation-Augmented Video Corpus Moment RetrievalSIGIR
uses Retrieve video moments by reconstructing the query from the video, not just matching features, and pinpoint boundaries.
why it works It works because if a video segment can regenerate the query linguistically, it means the model deeply understood the connection, not just surface similarity; understanding is richer than matching.
SPRINT: Scalable and Predictive Intent Refinement for LLM-Enhanced Session-based RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predict session intent selectively with language models for uncertain cases, then learn a lightweight predictor for all sessions.
why it works It works because language models are powerful but expensive; using them only where uncertainty is high lets you keep the insights they provide while scaling to all data via a simpler model.
Hierarchical Cluster-based Open-World Graph Active LearningSIGIR
uses Find informative regions by clustering nodes, then identify which clusters likely hold novel classes or unclear examples.
why it works It works because a dense cluster of uncertain nodes is likely to contain either hard examples of known classes or examples of new classes; finding such regions is more efficient than scoring every node individually.
Optimizing Marketing Subsidies via Counterfactual Learning with Asymmetric Reward FunctionSIGIR
uses Predict the optimal subsidy amount for each customer using their purchase behavior and an asymmetric loss function that penalizes errors differently above and below the true threshold.
why it works It works because the asymmetric loss pays more focus to getting the decision boundary right than to the exact score value, and ranking customers by their subsidy-improvement potential puts the highest-impact ones first. The two-stage refinement ensures the critical threshold is accurate where it matters most for profit.
Chain of Evidence: Pixel-Level Visual Attribution for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Score document relevance by reasoning directly over pixel-level image evidence from retrieved pages, then output the exact location of supporting visual details.
why it works It works because visual layout and diagrams carry irreplaceable information that text extraction loses. By scoring and citing pixel locations directly, you preserve spatial reasoning and let users verify the evidence themselves, making the ranking both better and trustworthy.
Adaptive Mix Preference Optimization for Generative RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learns to rank recommended items by mixing how likely the model thinks they are with how well they match the user's stated preferences, adjusting confidence per example.
why it works It works because user signals vary in how strongly they indicate true preference—some signals are clear intent, others are noisy. Weighting each signal by its confidence focuses learning on the trustworthy patterns and avoids overfitting to ambiguous feedback.
Large-Scale Online Learning for Generative List Recommendation in E-commerce: An Environment Policy Optimization ApproachSIGIR
uses Directly optimizes the total quality of a ranked recommendation list by computing how to nudge each item position.
why it works It works because the quality score itself is a smooth function you can differentiate with respect to item positions, so you can follow the slope to improve the whole list at once instead of approximating indirectly.
PLAID-PRF: Pseudo-Relevance Feedback with Centroid-like Tokens in PLAIDSIGIR
uses Refines search rankings by adding new query terms chosen from top results, keeping only the most informative expansions.
why it works It works because the top-ranked results already contain relevant ideas; extracting and amplifying rare high-value query terms found there sharpens the search without adding noise from common irrelevant terms.
OPS: An Order-Preserving Sorting Network for Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Learns to sort items optimally by directly training on ranking order rather than individual scores, handling ties in relevance.
why it works It works because you only care about the final ranking order, not the exact scores; learning the permutation directly captures that structure and handles incomplete labels by allowing multiple valid orderings.
Demand-Calibrated Facet Diversification with Deployable Soft Quotas for E-Commerce SearchSIGIR
uses The system estimates from user behavior what mix of product categories users actually want on results pages, then adjusts ranking scores slightly to match that desired mix.
why it works It works because search results that show only top-ranked items often miss what users actually want when their intent is unclear. By learning the demand for diversity from real engagement and steering results to match it with minimal changes, you improve revenue without breaking relevance order.
SilverTorch: A Unified Model-based System to Democratize Large-Scale Recommendation on GPUsSIGIR
uses The system learns to quickly find top-ranked products using a unified deep learning model that combines word filtering and nearest-neighbor search on GPU.
why it works It works because separating indexing from scoring creates bottlenecks and wasted transfers. By building everything into one deep model on GPU, word filtering becomes free (just learned layer thresholds) and nearest-neighbor search fuses directly with scoring, cutting both memory and latency.
BEAR: Towards Beam-Search-Aware Optimization for Recommendation with Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses The method adjust a language model to rank recommended items, ensuring that high-probability items stay ranked high through each word of the sequence—not just overall.
why it works It works because beam search greedily prunes low-probability prefixes even if they lead to good completions. By enforcing that each words of a correct answer must rank well locally, you prevent false pruning while maintaining efficiency.
GNN-based Anchor Embedding for Efficient Subgraph RetrievalSIGIR
uses The system pre-computes small graph patterns as indices, then uses a learned graph model to test which stored patterns match the query, guiding a fast search through the data graph.
why it works It works because exact graph matching is expensive when done fresh for each query. By pre-indexing small patterns and using learned tests to prune candidates sharply, you trade one-time computation for dramatic query speedup without losing correctness.
FAIR-RAG: An End-to-End Framework for Mitigating Political Bias through Fair Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Rank retrieved documents by their political stance balance, then weight which ones go to the language model based on fairness criteria rather than just relevance.
why it works When you score documents by multiple fairness features and weight the balanced ones higher, you push the final answer toward representing more perspectives. The system works because it catches bias at the retrieval stage before it gets amplified during generation.
Cohesive Group Discovery in Interaction Graphs under Explicit Density ConstraintsSIGIR
uses Rank vertices by how much information spreads outward from them, then extract subgraphs that maintain a minimum density threshold of connections.
why it works It works because vertices that spread information widely sit near tightly-connected clusters. By ranking by diffusion strength and extracting subgraphs that sustain density, you find natural cohesive groups even in sparse graphs.
Spectral-Adaptive Adversarial Hashing for Robust Image RetrievalSIGIR
uses Compress images into short binary codes for fast lookup while staying robust when someone deliberately corrupts the input to fool the system.
why it works The method works because it protects the frequency components of the learned function that actually matter for ranking similar images together, while letting the adversarial training strip away only the unstable, noisy parts. This keeps the signal strong without breaking under attack.
Can QPP Choose the Right Query variant? Evaluating Query Variant Selection for RAG PipelinesSIGIR
uses Predict which query rewrite will produce the best final answer before running the full retrieval and generation pipeline.
why it works It works because most rewrites that improve ranking do not improve answers, so a cheap predictor that identifies which variant actually leads to good answers saves computation. Early lightweight predictors often match expensive post-retrieval ones because the quality they measure aligns with the goal.
Hypencoder Revisited: Reproducibility and Analysis of Non-Linear Scoring for First-Stage RetrievalSIGIR
uses Let a hypernetwork generate custom scoring weights for each query instead of using fixed inner-product scoring, enabling a learned neural function that judges relevance.
why it works It works because one fixed scoring rule (inner product) is too rigid to capture all the ways a query can match a document. A query-specific scoring function learned from examples can express richer relevance patterns while still encoding queries and documents separately.
A Standardized Re-evaluation of Conversational Recommender Systems on the ReDial DatasetSIGIR
uses Predict which movie to recommend in a conversation by learning from dialogue history, but measure success carefully to avoid inflated scores from recommending the same items.
why it works Ranking by relevance works because starting guess preferences are the strongest signal. But traditional recall metrics reward repeating popular items, so incorporating novelty measures reveals when systems succeed at genuine conversation versus exploiting shortcuts in the data.
Price-Aware Recommender Systems: A Cross-Paradigm Reproducibility StudySIGIR
uses Recommend products by learning from user histories while explicitly incorporating price as a core feature, comparing three neural graph architectures on multiple datasets.
why it works It works because price is a strong predictor of purchase behavior. Learning price jointly with preference patterns lets the model express trade-offs like 'recommend expensive when high-quality signals are weak, cheap when quantity matters.' The hypergraph architecture captures these trade-offs best.
Lost in Decoding? Reproducing and Stress-Testing the Look-Ahead Prior in Generative RetrievalSIGIR
uses Generate document identifiers by autoregressively predicting one symbol at a time, using a look-ahead scorer to plan which branches to explore, but test robustness under small query variations.
why it works Look-ahead planning works because it simulates future decoding steps to avoid local traps—it finds the high-scoring path before committing. But the planning signal relies on exact prefix matching, so even small typos or reorderings can shift which prefixes look promising, making the plan fragile.
CalmSet: A Domain-Specific Test Collection for Affective Music Retrieval for Children with ASDSIGIR
uses Train classifiers to score music tracks by their therapeutic intent for children with autism.
why it works It works because labeled examples of music and its therapeutic effects teach the system to recognize patterns that predict which songs will help specific children, transforming subjective therapeutic judgment into a learnable scoring function.
TReB: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Table Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Evaluate AI language systems on their ability to understand and reason about structured table data through 26 different reasoning tasks.
why it works It works because tables have hidden structure and semantics, and testing across many task types reveals which reasoning abilities models lack, exposing whether failures come from understanding tables or from reasoning itself.
SQuTR: A Robustness Benchmark for Spoken Query to Text Retrieval under Acoustic NoiseSIGIR
uses Score retrieval system robustness by mixing real speech with 17 types of environmental noise at varying loudness levels, then measuring rank quality degradation.
why it works It works because noise is random variation that degrades signal, and by controlling exactly which noise and how much, you isolate what breaks retrieval from what stays robust, revealing the true weaknesses systems will face.
KuaiLive: A Real-time Interactive Dataset for Live Streaming RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predict which live streamers users will interact with next by learning from real-time engagement signals like clicks, comments, likes, and gift-giving.
why it works It works because live streaming is constantly changing, and by predicting the next action from recent interactions rather than static history, the model captures that user preferences evolve in real-time as content flows.
SurGE: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Scientific Survey GenerationSIGIR
uses Evaluate automated survey generation with a protocol that combines objective metrics and learned scoring from expert judgment across multiple features.
why it works It works because survey quality is multifaceted—fluency, structure, citations, coverage—and no single metric captures it all, so combining objective measures with learned expert judgment gives a robust score that aligns with what human reviewers actually value.
MIRA: An LLM-Assisted Benchmark for Multi-Category Integrated RetrievalSIGIR
uses Scores items from different categories by how well they answer a user's question, then ranks them together in one unified list.
why it works It works because you never need the exact scores, only their correct order, so a rough relevance score that gets the ranking right already puts the most useful results on top.
Modalities of Expert Search: How Users Transition Between Names and TopicsSIGIR
uses Analyzes search sessions to find when people switch from looking for a specific expert to exploring a topic, predicting mode changes from clicks.
why it works It works because interactions reveal intent: clicks indicate successful searches, and successful searches precede mode changes more often, so recent success is a signal that curiosity will shift.
Learning Evidence of Depression Symptoms via Prompt InductionSIGIR
uses Learn interpretable guidelines for what counts as evidence for each depression symptom, then use those guidelines to classify text.
why it works It works because annotators and models apply inconsistent criteria when classifying rare symptoms. By extracting what the labeled examples actually mean into explicit rules, the model can apply those rules consistently to new text, even for symptoms with few training examples.
One Pass, Any Order: Position-Invariant Listwise Reranking for LLM-Based RecommendationSIGIR
uses Rank recommendation candidates with stable scores that don't change when the input order changes, using special focus masking and position encoding.
why it works It works because the best item shouldn't depend on whether you listed it first or last. By blocking focus across candidates and using rotation-based positions, the model scores each item based on its merit alone, not its position in the prompt sequence.
APR: Adaptive Personalised Reranking For Conversational SearchSIGIR
uses Rank search results adaptively: use fast similarity-based scoring for simple queries and generated instructions for complex constraint-heavy queries.
why it works It works because query complexity varies. Instruction-following is powerful but slow and prone to noise on simple queries. By routing queries based on complexity and only invoking instruction-following when constraints are present, the system gets guidance exactly where it helps without wasting time on straightforward queries.
On the Robustness of LLM Re-RankingsSIGIR
uses Test whether language models rank documents differently depending on whether you ask for best first or worst first, showing sensitivity to prompt wording.
why it works Ranking should depend only on relevance, not instruction phrasing. If the same model produces different orderings from different prompts, it means the model is using surface-level cues (like word position) instead of true understanding, which breaks reliability.
Optimal Re-Ranking DepthSIGIR
uses For each query, predict the optimal number of top results to re-rank by using a quality score of the first-stage retrieval, avoiding wasted re-ranking beyond the sweet spot.
why it works Re-ranking improves results until good candidates are exhausted; after that, quality stagnates or drops. Measuring the spread of quality in initial results tells you when this saturation happens. Query-specific prediction avoids re-ranking everything equally, saving compute without losing accuracy.
Revisiting BM25 Feedback Models using HyDESIGIR
uses Rank search results by combining word-frequency scores from both the original query and AI-generated expansions, weighting each contribution.
why it works Word frequency captures which documents best match what people searched for; AI-generated answers help identify synonyms and related concepts, so combining their signals captures more search intent.
Every Preference Has Its Strength: Injecting Ordinal Semantics into LLM-Based RecommendersSIGIR
uses Learn to rank items by their predicted rating (1-5 stars), using the strength of past preferences to align recommendations with users' actual taste.
why it works Strong preferences (5 stars) and weak ones (2 stars) reveal different patterns; including this strength makes the learner distinguish truly loved items from merely acceptable ones.
LTRR: Learning To Rank Retrievers for LLMsSIGIR
uses Learn to score each available search method for a given question, then route each question to the search method predicted to retrieve the best answer.
why it works No single search method works best for all questions; learning per-question routing exploits that different questions favor different retrieval strategies.
Auditing Query Drift: Do Users Actually Benefit from Pseudo-Relevance Feedback?SIGIR
uses Learns when feedback will hurt or help by comparing user reactions to rankings with and without query expansion, scoring harm-avoidance higher than benefit-gain.
why it works Users explicitly show what they like or dislike by their clicks and dwell time. Collecting enough paired comparisons (expansion vs. no expansion) reveals the true probability expansion helps that user on that query. Avoiding losses matters more than chasing gains because the cost of one bad result outweighs many mediocre gains.
Targeted Parameter Selection for Rank-Biased MeasurementSIGIR
uses Selects decay weights for ranking comparisons using power-law distributions, choosing parameters so top results receive emphasis matching experimental goals.
why it works Comparisons only need to order results correctly, not score them truly. A carefully chosen decay weight can boost top items while ignoring tail differences. Finding the right weight shape means top-ranking results dominate the signal while irrelevant details stay quiet.
G-CoS: An Interpretable Gain-Cost Framework for User Satisfaction Estimation in Generative Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Model satisfaction as a balance between response quality and interaction cost, where users trade off better answers against effort spent.
why it works Users want good answers but also want to spend minimal time and effort. These trade off—a perfect answer that takes five searches is worse than a good answer that takes one. By measuring both quality gain and cost together, you capture what users actually optimize for in their behavior.
BeLink: Biomedical Entity Linking Meets Generative Re-RankingSIGIR
uses Instruct-tune an open model to rank candidate entities for biomedical linking, treating multiple candidates as a set to choose from.
why it works Large pretrained models work well at ranking when you teach them what ranking means through instruction tuning. Set-wise tuning lets the model see multiple candidates together, so it can compare them directly. This is faster and more accurate than scoring them independently.
DisCoRec: Disentangled Conformity-aware Recommendation with LLM-Guided Multi-View LearningSIGIR
uses Score each user-item pair using a learned model that weights different factors—genuine interest vs social influence—differently for each one.
why it works By learning to separate what users actually want from what they're doing because others do it, you can score predictions more accurately. Weighting the true factors more heavily pushes good recommendations to the top.
HE-DeepFM: An FHE Inference System for CTR Prediction with Efficient FM InteractionsSIGIR
uses Score click-through likelihood using encrypted computation that computes feature interactions efficiently without ever exposing the raw data.
why it works The math works inside the encrypted domain by packing related calculations together so you can do pairwise interactions without the expensive quadratic blowup. The ranking stays accurate because the core scoring formula is unchanged.
One-Pass Decoding for Generative Recommendation with WFST-Constrained A* SearchSIGIR
uses Score all possible next item identifiers in a single forward pass, then use A* search through the space of valid sequences to find the best recommendation without backtracking.
why it works Computing scores once instead of iteratively avoids error propagation from early greedy choices. A* search guarantees you find the optimal sequence because it explores only valid paths, weighted by one-pass scores that are consistent across all positions.
LLM-based Semantic and ID Representations for Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses Score items in sequences by learning textual and collaborative features together, then rank the items with highest scores.
why it works It works because combining multiple sources of understanding (what the item is semantically and who interacts with it) captures user preference more accurately than any single signal alone. Learning from the data teaches the scoring function to weight signals appropriately.
GraphSynthQA: Knowledge-Graph-Guided Query Synthesis and Step-Level Preference Optimization for Web AgentsSIGIR
uses Rank web-search steps by comparing successful paths to failed attempts, training the model to prefer actions that lead downstream to correct answers.
why it works It works because comparing success-and-failure pairs teaches the model which decisions matter most. By contrasting paths that work against those that don't on the same query, you isolate the causal steps that move toward truth, without needing to explore all possibilities expensively.
Rank-R1: Enhancing Reasoning in LLM-based Document Rerankers via Reinforcement LearningSIGIR
uses Improve ranking by first reasoning about why a document is relevant, using reward signals from correct rankings to strengthen that reasoning.
why it works It works because humans rank by thinking first, so teaching the model to reason before ranking lets it discover what details actually distinguish better answers. The ranking feedback tells the model which reasoning patterns led to good decisions.
Beyond Semantic Similarity: Explicit Intent Modeling for Query-Product MatchingSIGIR
uses Score query-product matches by scoring individual attributes separately then combining them, focusing on attributes the query explicitly mentions.
why it works It works because buyers specify attributes (color, size, brand) that are non-negotiable, not soft preferences. By scoring each attribute independently you catch when a product violates one hard constraint, then combining ensures all attributes are satisfied. Weighting mentioned attributes heavily ensures they dominate.
LLM Agents Factory: Retrieval of Domain-Specific LLM AgentsSIGIR
uses Retrieve pre-built agent profiles matching a user query from a large repository, scoring semantic similarity to find the most appropriate agent.
why it works It works because good agents for a domain already exist or follow patterns. Instead of designing each agent on-the-fly (expensive and unstable), retrieving from a known set reuses proven templates. Semantic matching finds agents similar to the current task, and they transfer because agents in the same domain share structure.
BERT-Based Cross-Encoder for Large-Scale Engagement Prediction and Re-ranking in Walmart Search EngineSIGIR
uses Score engagement by learning from query-item text pairs labeled with actual user engagement, capturing what buyers truly prefer.
why it works It works because user intent is hidden in language patterns, not historical clickrate statistics. Learning directly from text and true engagement labels teaches the model to recognize the language features that signal what will actually get added to cart. This works even on tail queries where statistical patterns don't exist.
MMRM: A Multiplex Multimodal Representation Model for Product Ranking in E-commerce SearchSIGIR
uses The system learns a single rich description of each product using multiple signals at once, then uses that description to rank items and understand users.
why it works Products have multiple facets—their image, text, and how users interact with them—and a single shared model can learn from all these signals together. One complete description is more efficient and more accurate than treating each signal separately, because shared understanding reveals patterns no single signal shows alone.
Population-Guided Intent-Aware Query Rewriting for Web SearchSIGIR
uses A system learns to rewrite search queries to match mainstream search intents, scoring rewrites by how well they align with what populations search for.
why it works It works because population-level patterns reveal what most people actually want to find; by learning this intent from search logs, rewrites naturally align with real user goals. The learned rewriter improves on fixed rules because it discovers patterns that static templates miss.
Calibrate Your Items! Train CTR Models in Two Steps for Robust RecommendationsSIGIR
uses A neural model learns to predict click rates while being trained to also predict whether its scores fairly represent different groups of items.
why it works It works because calibration (predicting fairness alongside predictions) prevents the model from relying on shortcuts that work for frequent items but fail for rare ones. When scoring is constrained to be honest across all groups, downstream systems that multiply scores by other factors (like auction bids) work correctly.
MedNQS: Medical State-Aware Dual-Stage Next-Turn Question Suggestion for Online Medical ConsultationsSIGIR
uses A system tracks the medical conversation state, retrieves question candidates filtered by what makes sense given that state, then ranks them using data on which questions users actually chose.
why it works It works because medical consultations follow patterns; knowing the dialogue state (what was discussed, what condition) narrows possibilities to relevant ones. Ranking by real user preferences (not guesses) ensures suggested questions actually help the conversation.
PCANet: Price Change Aware Framework for Mitigating Inconsistencies in Large-Scale Ranking SystemsSIGIR
uses Flight rankings are scored using both relevance and user sensitivity to price changes, dynamically adjusting which flights rank high based on whether a person will tolerate fare surprises.
why it works It works because two people finding the same flight relevant does not mean showing both will convert equally; one might abandon if the price jumps, the other won't. Scoring by relevance times sensitivity per individual prevents wasted ranking effort on flights that will shock away price-sensitive users.
SkyDistill: Navigating Fuzzy Flight Search Ranking via Precise Intent DistillationSIGIR
uses Knowledge learned from precise flight searches is transferred to a smaller model for fuzzy searches using three layers of hints: feature alignment, confidence-weighted transfer, and ranking order preservation.
why it works It works because fuzzy search data is sparse but precise search is rich; precise search fundamentals (what makes a flight attractive) are reusable. The three alignment layers ensure the smaller model doesn't just copy rules but learns to adapt: features map correctly, weak confidence signals are filtered out, and relative preferences stay consistent.
A Cost-Efficient AI Copilot for High-Volume E-commerce Customer SupportSIGIR
uses A copilot rewrites each customer message into a complete, standalone question, retrieves relevant policies and procedures, then generates a draft response based on all three.
why it works It works because customer messages alone are ambiguous—rewriting makes them self-contained so context is never lost. Ranking relevant policies ensures responses align with actual company practice. The draft+edit model lets humans verify that automation hasn't hallucinated while cutting the time they spend on routine reasoning.
PersonaPlugin: A Multi-Source Persona Framework for LLM Personalization in TelecommunicationsSIGIR
uses Telecom user signals (calls, app usage, location) are converted into structured personas that are then injected into language model responses to personalize answers.
why it works It works because raw signals (call duration, app opens, location) are noisy; structuring them into personas (preferences, constraints, context) gives the language model semantically meaningful input. Personas act as filters: instead of the model guessing what matters, it gets explicit signals about the person it's addressing.
Building a Production Shopping Agent at ScaleSIGIR
uses Routes customer requests to specialized retrieval, reasoning, and tool-calling systems, optimizing for accuracy, speed, cost, and reliability at massive scale.
why it works It works because each subtask (product search, Q&A, actions) has different optimal strategies. Routing to specialized components lets each solve its problem cheaply and accurately. Production constraints force this modularity rather than a single end-to-end model.
When Search Is Not Enough: Ranking Content for Query-Less Browse SurfacesSIGIR
uses Learns to rank content within browse categories using actual user browsing session data instead of treating the category name as a search query.
why it works It works because browsing is different from searching: users explore without clear intent. Category names are imperfect proxies for what users actually want to see. Learning from click sessions directly captures true preferences within each curated collection.
NBA-Net: Next-Behavior-Aware Network for Intent RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predict what a user will do next, and use that prediction to improve the ranking of intent suggestions for their immediate need.
why it works It works because current intent is not independent from future actions; they are coupled. By predicting the next behavior and propagating that signal backward, you capture the trajectory of user goals, making intent recommendations more aligned with what users actually intend to accomplish next.
BEATS: Bootstrapping E-commerce Attribute Taxonomies for Search through Iterative Human-AI CollaborationSIGIR
uses Generate and refine product attribute schemas from scratch by iteratively generating attributes, checking quality, and collecting human feedback to improve prompts.
why it works It works because attributes are domain knowledge. Bootstrapping via iterative human-in-the-loop refinement progressively tightens the definition of what attributes are valid, so each round learns from error patterns. Human annotation anchors the semantic space, guiding the system toward marketplace reality.
Preliminary Study of an Evaluation Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Fashion E-CommerceSIGIR
uses Test how well different vision-language models extract fashion attributes and product information, measuring which models and prompts work best per task.
why it works It works because operational deployment requires task-specific assessment. General-purpose benchmarks miss fashion nuances. Testing multiple models and prompts reveals that best performance is task-dependent and error patterns are model-specific, so continuous monitoring is necessary for reliability.
Fast and Feasible: Permutation-based Constrained Reranking for Revenue MaximizationSIGIR
uses Reorder search results to maximize revenue from paid placements while keeping relevance and fraud risk within acceptable bounds using discrete optimization.
why it works It works because reranking is a constrained optimization problem: change the order to improve one metric (revenue) without breaking others (relevance, fraud). A fast approximation algorithm that swaps neighboring items greedily reaches most of the ideal revenue gain within the latency budget required by live serving.
Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation SystemSIGIR
uses Predict purchase conversion by learning how item discount rates trend over time and correcting for bias in which users see which discounts.
why it works It works because discounts drive purchasing decisions but their effect is entangled with selection bias (some users always get discounts, others never do) and time trends (holidays spike discounts). Separating the true discount signal from these confounds lets the model learn how discounts truly influence purchase likelihood.
What Gets Cited: Competitive GEO in AI Answer EnginesSIGIR
uses Score each source on factors like relevance and recency, then measure which factor predicts being cited first when two sources compete for the first reference.
why it works It works because you never need exact scores, only their order. A learned scoring function that correctly ranks which source matters more is enough to put the most citable source first. This means partial, learned signals are sufficient.
DPEO: Dynamic Preference Evolution Optimization for Self-Evolving CTR PredictionSIGIR
uses Two competing models take turns as reference and target, with the target learning to surpass the reference, creating a moving benchmark that drives continuous improvement.
why it works Pure external competition for single best score gets stuck in local optima. An internal dual-model setup where they compete with each other creates constant evolving pressure: the target always has a fresh opponent to beat, preventing stagnation and guiding both toward better solutions.
LiBRA: Enhancing Live-streaming Recommendation with Bigraph-based Capacity-aware Ranking ApproachSIGIR
uses Streamers are ranked by estimated relevance to viewers, but the score is adjusted downward if the streamer is near capacity, balancing matching quality with fair traffic distribution.
why it works Pure relevance ranking concentrates all viewers on popular streamers, degrading their experience. When you embed capacity as a hard constraint in the ranking objective, you force the system to find the best match for each viewer that the servers can actually handle, improving overall experience across all streamers and viewers.
ESCOMIC: User Adaptive Explainable Search for Comic BooksSIGIR
uses Re-weight importance of facets (genre, character, pacing) based on user interaction signals to reorder search results.
why it works Users clarify intent through subtle actions; weighting facets by feedback adapts the ranking to match each person's evolving goals, making results more relevant than a one-size-fits-all score.
Visual RAG at Scale: Tile-Level Spatial Pooling for Efficient Multi-Vector Document RetrievalSIGIR
uses Pool many small lists of numbers scores across a page into summary scores at coarser tile scale, then rerank using full detail.
why it works You only need the rough order for candidate generation, not exact scores; averaging coarser patches gives that order fast. Only the top candidates need exact rescoring, so the two-stage approach cuts work quadratically.
EasyRAG: A Beginner-Friendly and Interactive Framework for Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Rank and combine retrieved passages by learned scores to feed most relevant sources into response generation.
why it works Learned ranking assigns higher scores to passages that actually help models generate correct answers. Reranking before generation lets the model focus on gold-signal facts rather than processing all possibilities.
From Translation to Retrieval: Evaluating LLM-Based Information Retrieval for Hausa and FongbeSIGIR
uses Rerank and expand queries using large models to improve search for low-resource languages (Hausa, Fongbe).
why it works Large models encode multilingual knowledge even for rare languages; reranking candidates with learned scores from that knowledge surface relevant results despite sparse training data for the language itself.
Bridging the Language Gap in Text-to-SQL: Adapting LLMs for Chichewa in a Low-Resource SettingSIGIR
uses Score and rank retrieval results to feed relevant schema snippets into models that map natural language to SQL.
why it works Models make fewer mistakes when shown similar past queries and schemas; ranking retrieval results by relevance puts gold examples first, improving in-context learning and reducing hallucinated SQL.
Toward a Telugu Question Answering Dataset for Agricultural IR to Serve Marginal Farmers in Drought-Prone Rayalaseema: A Gap Analysis and RoadmapSIGIR
uses Benchmark systems that score and rank agricultural answers for drought-prone Telugu-speaking farmers.
why it works A standardized ranking benchmark with human judgments lets researchers measure whether scoring functions improve real-world information access for farmers without benchmarks, enabling fair comparison of methods.
Local Information Access in Marathi: Evaluating LLM-Native Web Retrieval in a Low-Resource EnvironmentSIGIR
uses Score web results retrieved by AI language systems to measure accuracy of Marathi information retrieval, analyzing search depth effects.
why it works Scored rankings reveal whether shallow or deep search ranks correct answers highest; measuring score distributions exposes failure modes and cost-accuracy tradeoffs, guiding deployment strategy.
Retrieval for User-Centered Translation: Lessons from RAG-based Tools for Low-Resource DomainsSIGIR
uses Score and rank in-domain examples from translation memory and glossaries to weight AI language systems post-editing and improve machine translation.
why it works Domain-specific terminology matters most; ranking retrieved examples by relevance to current phrase and weighting their influence over the baseline translation focuses the model on high-confidence domain knowledge.
Offline-First Information Retrieval for Curriculum-Aligned STEM Resources in Low-Resource Namibian SchoolsSIGIR
uses Rank documents by a statistical score of how well they match query terms, adapted for low-bandwidth search.
why it works Ranking works because you don't need the exact score values, only their order. A fast statistical score that correctly ranks which documents are more relevant gets the best results on top, and this ranking is robust even when computed cheaply on limited devices.
Evaluating Proactivity in Conversational Search through Anticipatory RetrievalSIGIR
uses Infer what information the user will need next in a conversation by predicting their future queries, then rank documents for those predicted needs before they ask.
why it works It works because multi-turn conversations have coherent goal sequences: users refine or explore related subtopics in predictable patterns. If you model what comes next in that sequence, you can surface relevant information before the user explicitly asks, reducing wasted turns.
Adaptive Personalisation for Effective Conversational Search SystemsSIGIR
uses Learn when to personalize each query using a classifier; weight past interactions differently for different users; blend rankings based on user intent.
why it works It works because not every query benefits from personalization—sometimes a generic search is better—and user history is noisy. A classifier learns which queries actually benefit from historical context, while weighted blending lets personalization help only when it actually improves precision, avoiding the trap of applying personalization uniformly.
LLMs as Search Engine Components and Users: Infrastructural Adaptations to a Dual TransformationSIGIR
uses Adapt search pipeline components to handle AI-generated queries, which have different statistical patterns than human queries.
why it works It works because AI generates queries with different structure (more reformulations, faster sequences, different syntax) than humans. Ranking and filtering functions trained on human query patterns fail on AI queries; retraining on AI query distributions aligns system behavior to actual traffic.
LLM Personalization: Foundations, Breakthroughs, and FrontiersSIGIR
uses Personalizing language model outputs by learning user memories and preferences, then adjusting the model's generation at inference time to match each person's style and goals.
why it works Language models are generic; personalizing them works by storing what you learn about each user and steering the model toward that user's context at each step. Learning to adapt the model to user context beats using the same generic model for everyone because context shapes what the right answer is.
The 10th Workshop on Search-Oriented Conversational Artificial Intelligence (SCAI'26)SIGIR
uses Answering questions asked conversationally by holding context from previous turns, retrieving relevant facts, and generating multi-turn responses that adapt to what the user just said.
why it works Conversation is sequence: each turn depends on all starting guess turns. Learning to rank and generate conditioned on conversation history works because it models the temporal dependency—you answer differently after context changes. Personalization compounds this because you also adapt to the individual user.
63 papers

Predicting what comes next

Behaviour and language arrive as ordered streams — the pages you visited, the words in a sentence — and the useful move is to predict the next item from what came before.

Why it works — the principle

It works because the recent past genuinely constrains the near future: what you clicked last shapes what you'll click next, the last few words shape the next word. So a system that captures those local dependencies can predict well without holding the entire history in mind at once.

Rise: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Enhanced Immersive System for EducationWWW
uses Answer student questions and assess engagement by retrieving relevant educational content and personalized context from a learner's history.
why it works Pulling in retrieved context prevents the model from forgetting starting guess interactions, so it can recognize when a question connects to earlier topics and tailor answers to that student's level.
ES-MemEval: Benchmarking Conversational Agents on Personalized Long-Term Emotional SupportWWW
uses Evaluate whether chatbots remember fragmented user disclosures across sessions, extract implicit needs, spot conflicts, and personalize support over time.
why it works Emotional support requires the model to reconstruct a coherent user profile from scattered hints, so measuring these capabilities separately reveals which memory failures break personalization.
VK-LSVD: A Large-Scale Industrial Dataset for Short-Video RecommendationWWW
uses Build recommendation models from a massive dataset of user interactions with short videos, training on sequential feedback to predict which video a user will watch next.
why it works It works because users' interests change rapidly with short videos—each watch influences the next choice. Modeling sequences lets the system learn those rapid shifts from real user behavior. Scale matters: with 40 billion interactions, patterns in interest evolution become statistically clear, and cold-start (new users or videos) can be addressed by finding similar users or content in the large corpus.
ONeRec: Towards Openness-Aware and Adaptive Proactive News RecommendationWWW
uses Recommend intermediate articles that balance current interest alignment with gradual drift toward a target topic, weighted by the user's openness.
why it works Users resist radical shifts but accept gradual ones; weighting by openness prevents rejection. Intermediate articles act as stepping stones, each one slightly closer to the target than the last.
Statistical Analysis of 12V Power Load Uncertainty Using Conditional Probability for SDV Energy ManagementWWW
uses Uses conditional probability of power load given the past 60 seconds of history to predict upcoming battery demand and reduce uncertainty.
why it works It works because driver behavior is partially predictable within short windows; conditioning on recent history removes noise from one-shot predictions and captures momentum in usage patterns, revealing true upcoming load better than static averages.
Swen: A Cross-Platform Desktop Assistant for Instant and Personalized Large-Language-Model InteractionWWW
uses Identify what the user wants—translation, explanation, or summary—then generate the matching response tailored to their background and preferences.
why it works It works because intent recognition reduces the problem: instead of one model trying to do everything, you classify what you're solving for first, so the right specialized logic runs. And tracking what the user likes lets you personalize by remembering their style.
LLM-Enhanced Web-Centric Spatio-Temporal Intelligence: Methods, Applications, and Frontier ResearchWWW
uses Predicts the next move or location in a trajectory by learning patterns from sequences of places and times, applying the learned patterns at location, trajectory, and region scales.
why it works It works because human movement is sequential—where you go next depends on where you've been. Learning from trajectories means you capture real patterns of motion that simple statistics miss, and applying the same learned patterns at all scales lets you use local knowledge to predict regional flows.
Accurate and Efficient Personalized Query Rewriting in Baidu SearchWWW
uses Rewrites a user's search query to better match their personal intent by training a fast model to reason like a language model but without the reasoning overhead.
why it works Large reasoning models take too long for real-time search, but chain-of-thought helps them pick the right query. The method first teaches a smaller model to mimic reasoning outputs, then trains it to skip the reasoning steps and jump straight to the answer. Since the small model learned to replicate reasoning results, it keeps the accuracy gains without the latency, exploiting the fact that you need reasoning's output, not its speed.
Is More Context Always Better? Examining LLM Reasoning Capability for Time Interval PredictionWWW
uses Compares how well language models predict the time until a user's next purchase versus statistical models that learned the time patterns directly.
why it works It works because language models are trained on text prediction but not number prediction; statistical models built for time intervals exploit the mathematical structure of the data (how long until next event) whereas language models must convert numbers to text and back, losing precision.
Generative Archetype-Grounded Item Representations for Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Predict the next item a user will interact with by learning representations of items based on their ideal target audience and adjusting those representations to match actual user behavior.
why it works This works because item identity has two sources of truth: who the item is designed for (semantic) and who actually uses it (behavioral). Combining both grounds the model in reality rather than description alone.
MIGC-CMamba: Cross-Domain Mamba with Multi-Scale Imaging and Granular-Ball Computing for Traffic Flow PredictionWWW
uses Converting traffic sensor readings into image-like patterns, then finding which places and time-scales matter most for predicting traffic flow a few hours ahead.
why it works It works because traffic flow has both fast (minute-to-minute) and slow (daily cycle) rhythms that mix together—treating data as images lets vision techniques extract both local and global patterns at once. Granular-ball clustering finds which regions truly influence each other.
TRACE: Trajectory Recovery with State Propagation Diffusion for Urban MobilityWWW
uses Reconstructing missing GPS points in sparse trajectories by iteratively denoising fragments while remembering intermediate results from starting guess steps.
why it works It works because trajectory segments follow smooth motion rules—as you gradually reduce noise from the denoised version, a memory mechanism holds and refines partial recoveries so complex hard-to-fill gaps don't collapse back to noise.
Token-level Collaborative Alignment for LLM-based Generative RecommendationWWW
uses Score recommendations by combining signals from users' past choices with signals from predicting the next words in text.
why it works It works because user preference patterns and text prediction patterns contain complementary information: one shows what items people actually liked, the other captures semantic understanding of content. Fusing both gives richer recommendations than either alone.
SEAR: LLM-Powered Sequential Recommendation via Fusion of Collaborative, Semantic, and Rating InformationWWW
uses Predict the next item by fusing three separate signals about collaborative patterns, semantic meaning, and past ratings, weighted by preference.
why it works It works because users' next choice is influenced by all three factors simultaneously: who they are like (collaborative), what the items mean (semantic), and how much they've enjoyed similar things (ratings). Fusing all three captures more nuance than any single signal.
Dynamics of Human-AI Collective Knowledge on the Web: A Scalable Model and Insights for Sustainable GrowthWWW
uses Model how archive size, quality, human skill, model skill, and question volume co-evolve through inflows and feedback loops.
why it works Collective knowledge emerges from competing inflows (humans vs. machines) and learning pathways that reinforce or weaken each other. Simple differential equations capture steady states and instabilities, predicting when quality rises or collapses.
From Prediction to Understanding: Leveraging Reasoning in Large Language Model-based RecommendationsWWW
uses Trains the model to first generate written reasoning about why a user likes items, then predict the next item based on that reasoning.
why it works It works because making the reasoning explicit lets the model rehearse its logic before deciding. Humans reason out loud before acting; training a model to do the same unlocks better sequential predictions.

uses Generate search queries from news posts using a continually-learning model, score them by engagement and author authority, and use preference learning to prevent forgetting during online updates.
why it works This works because posts with rising engagement signal emerging trends before search volume forms, giving real-time signal unavailable to keyword-frequency methods. By pairing preference learning with continuous updates, the system learns to rank trending queries higher without catastrophic forgetting—comparison-based learning lets the model update on new preferences while retaining old knowledge, staying aligned with changing real-world trends.

uses Model long user purchase sequences efficiently using polynomial basis functions for smooth long-term trends and gated convolutions for sudden behavioral bursts, avoiding quadratic cost.
why it works It works because Legendre polynomials are a compact basis—they express smooth functions with few terms, capturing long-term patterns cheaply; gating mechanisms then toggle focus to sudden spikes, achieving both scales in linear time.

uses Predict click-through rates by first generating clusters of immediate user intent, then using those clusters as context to score candidates, balancing long-term preference with current needs.

S2CDR: Smoothing-Sharpening Process Model for Cross-Domain RecommendationWWW
uses Gradually corrupts user-item interaction records into noise-free blur, then recovers them to predict what new users will want across domains.
why it works It works because gradual corruption without random noise preserves structure longer than adding noise would. Reversing the corruption from blur back to sharp preferences means you can borrow structure from related domains.
Suicide Risk Prediction via Comment-Influenced Mental State TrajectoriesWWW
uses Tracks how a user's suicide risk evolves over time, learning whether comment support reduces risk and harmful comments increase it.

CitiLink-Summ: A Dataset of Discussion Subjects Summaries in European Portuguese Municipal Meeting MinutesWWW

Probe-and-Fetch: Dynamic KV Cache Pruning for Accelerated Long-Context Inference in Web-Scale AI SearchWWW
uses Predicts which parts of long documents the model will actually need to read, then loads only those parts instead of storing everything in memory.

uses Models cryptocurrency price changes as hidden states with transition probabilities, fitting parameters to blockchain data to predict profitable arbitrage moments.

Reinforcement Learning-Constrained Segmented User Modeling with Large Language Models for RecommendationWWW

EEO-TFV: Escape-Explore Optimizer for Web-Scale Time-Series Forecasting and Vision AnalysisWWW

Alignment across similar users pools their weak signals into one stronger one, turning scarcity into strength.

why it works Works because sequential graphs are driven by timing, not just identity; frequency filtering separates signal from noise.
Re-Diffusion: Modeling Latent Residuals with Diffusion for Time-Series ForecastingWWW
uses Improves forecasts by modeling what the errors look like, then using that to adjust predictions.
why it works Works because systematic biases remain after initial prediction; modeling error distribution lets you correct them.
DynaFLUX: Implicit Dynamics-Preserving Reinforcement Learning for Topology-Free Influence MaximizationWWW
uses Finds influential spreaders in networks without knowing the actual connections, by learning hidden time-series patterns and optimizing seed selection through trial-and-error learning.
why it works Observable behavior encodes network structure even when links are hidden; learning this structure from time-series and using reinforcement learning to optimize seed selection works because the optimal set must be the one with the best historical influence signal.
Make It Long, Keep It Fast: End-to-End 10k-Sequence Modeling at Billion Scale on DouyinWWW
uses Recommends videos by processing very long user histories efficiently, training on short sequences but applying the model to long ones with minimal computation.
why it works The model learns to generalize from short to long sequences; replacing expensive self-scoring with one-way lookups and batching by user reduces the math cost without losing quality because the core patterns are the same at any length.
A Two-Stage Anomaly-Aware Framework for Robust Traffic Forecasting with Memory-Guided GNNsWSDM
uses Predict traffic flow by learning normal patterns first, filtering out unusual events, then modeling how congestion spreads across roads and time with memory of past anomalies.
why it works It works because normal and anomalous traffic follow different rules. Filtering anomalies first means your model learns the true underlying flow pattern; memory of anomalies teaches what triggers breakdowns without poisoning normal predictions.
Sequential Recommendation with Generative Intent Prediction Utilizing User Search-BehaviorWSDM
uses Predict what a user will want next by learning their intent from both past browsing history and search queries they've entered.
why it works It works because search queries reveal intent directly—they say what the user is hunting for—while browsing shows what they actually consider, so combining both captures both aspiration and behavior for richer prediction.
Dual Conditional Diffusion for Sequential RecommendationWSDM
uses Generate recommendations by mixing implicit knowledge of user behavior patterns with explicit signals about what users actually clicked, both embedded in a denoising process.
why it works It works because user behavior has two layers: surface patterns (what they clicked) and deeper preferences (why they click). numeric fingerprints both guides generation to stay faithful to real behavior while preserving individual preference nuance that gets lost if you compress everything into one summary.
GSDiffRec: Enhancing Personalized Sequential Recommendation via Diffusion Augmentation and Guidance OptimizationWSDM
uses Predict next interactions by refining denoising through shaped focus and enforcing that predictions stay on the surface of user preference geometry.
why it works It works because user preferences live in a lower-dimensional space. Constraining the denoising to stay on that surface prevents the model from drifting into unrealistic regions during generation. The shaped focus focuses learning on the most predictive behavior patterns.
An Action-Aware Generative Sequence Modeling for Short Video RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predict short-video preference by modeling sequences of user actions in time, capturing how action timing reveals diverse interests.
why it works It works because when someone likes one moment and follows on another, those actions at different times reveal different intents; temporal sequence captures intent better than treating the video as one unit.
GenRecEdit: Adapting Model Editing for Generative Recommendation with Cold-Start ItemsSIGIR
uses Injects knowledge of new items into a recommendation model by identifying where in its reasoning each item code appears, then updating those specific locations without full retraining.
why it works It works because each item that a recommender predicts shares specific reasoning steps with others in the sequence. By updating only the internal connection points relevant to new items, you inject knowledge efficiently, avoiding the noise and cost of retraining on sparse new feedback.
TAR: Generative Auto-Bidding and Budget Pacing via Multi-Scale Trajectory ModelingSIGIR
uses Plans ad spending over time by generating coarse-then-fine budget trajectories with compressed internal states, learning from sparse feedback by aggregating at multiple timescales.
why it works It works because feedback arrives aggregated over time, not instantly for each decision. By planning at multiple scales—coarse scales give dense reward signals to learn from, fine scales let the model adjust tactically—it transforms sparse feedback into dense learning signals across resolutions.
RecPFN: Prior-Fitted Networks for In-Context-Based RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Recommends new items by learning from synthetic data that mimics real causal patterns, then applying that learned pattern to real sequences in a single forward pass without updating weights.
why it works It works because the true causal structure of how users interact with items is similar across domains—choices follow consistent patterns even if the items differ. By learning that structure from diverse synthetic examples first, the model amortizes the learning and can instantly adapt to new domains with few real examples.
Beyond Static Diffusion: Explicitly Modeling Temporal Patterns in Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predicts next items by modeling how preferences evolve through time, mixing in temporal patterns at each step.
why it works It works because user preferences drift over time; explicitly representing how the past state influences the next state captures real temporal dynamics better than treating time as a static condition.
From Existence to Exhaustiveness: Unveiling the Compounding Failures of LLMs in Multi-answer Event Temporal ReasoningSIGIR
uses Tests whether models can find all answers to a temporal question, not just the first one, from long unstructured text.
why it works It works because exhaustiveness requires different logic than existence; once you find one answer, you must keep searching for others, which current models fail at because they stop after the first match.
Recursive Short-to-Long Generalization for Multi-hop ReasoningSIGIR
uses The model learns to reason through multi-step questions using only short examples, by predicting the next reasoning step and learning when to stop based on context length and evidence quality.
why it works It works because reasoning step patterns repeat even as paths grow longer. By training on short sequences but learning a stopping rule that adapts to question difficulty, the model generalizes to longer reasoning chains without direct long-path examples.
Coupling Global Context with Kinematic Evolution for Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses The model learns user preference evolution as continuous motion: capturing both steady-state preferences and velocity and acceleration of change, then blends these signals adaptively.
why it works It works because preferences don't jump randomly—they move smoothly. By modeling trajectory (position, speed, acceleration) instead of just snapshots, the system captures momentum and trends that predict better. Contrasting genuine trajectories against random noise reinforces these real patterns.
A Reproducibility Study of Metacognitive Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Chain language-model steps to retrieve, critique, and refine answers, using the model's self-reflection to decide when enough information has been gathered to answer.
why it works It works because AI language systems can critique their own reasoning when shown what they retrieved. The model learns to recognize when its critique signals sufficient information, making the stopping decision data-driven rather than fixed.
Retrieval-Augmented Contrastive Learning for Knowledge TracingSIGIR
uses Predict student performance by comparing them to other students with similar skill profiles, using natural examples from other learners as positive and negative contrasts.
why it works It works because students with similar skills develop similar patterns. Real contrasts between comparable learners are richer and more realistic than synthetic augmentations, so the model learns the actual trajectory patterns that generalize across sparse data.
Reasoning-Grounded Intent Injection for Generative RecommendationSIGIR
uses A model learns to forecast what users secretly want before they ask, by distilling hints from a powerful language model into a fast scoring function.
why it works This works because powerful reasoning can be compressed—the deep model's intuitions about hidden desires can be captured in a smaller student model through carefully chosen examples. Once compressed, the student runs fast enough to operate in real time.
Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase RedundancySIGIR
uses The model learns when a purchase signals satisfaction (the intent is done) versus hunger for more, then suppresses related items after purchase and gradually re-activates them as replenishment time nears.
why it works A purchase is fundamentally different from a click—it closes an intent, not opens one. The model learns the lifecycle of each product type by measuring time until repurchase. After purchase, suppressing related items reflects reality: someone who just bought shampoo doesn't want more shampoo ads today. Gradual re-awakening reflects the true rhythm of need.
Improving Dating Outcomes by Predicting for Conversations at HingeSIGIR
uses Models three sequential probabilities: likelihood of a like, a match given a like, and a conversation given a match, using a shared learned representation.
why it works It works because the dating journey is actually a chain of events with increasing commitment. Modeling the chain structure captures that conversations are far rarer but more meaningful than likes. Sharing numeric fingerprints lets the model learn representations that predict all three stages well.
Breaking the Relevance-Diversity Seesaw: Hierarchical LLM Reasoning with RL for Industrial Novelty RecommendationSIGIR
uses Break down novelty recommendation into stages (novelty direction, interest, list construction) and train them jointly using reinforcement learning optimized at both sequence and item levels.
why it works It works because relevance and diversity are at odds; a single reward signal cannot capture both. Decomposing into stages lets each stage specialize, and optimizing at two granularities (sequence and item) catches both the big-picture coherence and the fine-grained redundancy that simple sequence rewards miss.
Code-Based English Models Reveal Surprising Performance on Chinese QA Pair Extraction TaskSIGIR
uses Language models are adjust to transform unstructured text into structured question-answer pairs, with code-based models proving surprisingly effective on Chinese text.
why it works Language models have already learned patterns of how questions and answers relate through pretraining on billions of examples. adjust narrows this broad knowledge to the specific extraction task, and code-trained models transfer well because code and Chinese text both require precise syntactic understanding.
RecGPT-Mobile: On-Device Large Language Models for User Intent Understanding in Taobao Feed RecommendationSIGIR
uses A mobile language model learns to predict what query a user will type next based on their recent item interactions.
why it works User behavior is sequential: recent actions carry strong signal about intent. A language model trained on behavior sequences learns to complete that sequence by inferring hidden intent. Running inference on-device catches rapid intent shifts in real time, improving recency without cloud latency.
M&#178;GR: Generative User Interest Modeling via Multi-Granularity Multi-Objective CoT for Industrial RecommendationSIGIR
uses User interests are predicted through multiple refinement steps: first broad attributes like brand, then fine-grained exact items, then order-level behavior.
why it works Predicting the final answer directly is hard because intermediate steps contain rich information. Breaking prediction into a chain of refinements preserves all behavior data while giving the model intermediate waypoints to steer learning. Each step constrains the next, reducing spread of error and improving interpretability.
70 papers

Estimating chances from data

Much of the field is really estimating how likely something is — a click, a fraud, the next word — by learning those chances from mountains of past behaviour.

Why it works — the principle

It works because with enough independent observations the fraction of times something happened is a trustworthy estimate of how often it will happen again — and the more you've seen, the tighter that estimate becomes. It also means a few well-chosen random samples can stand in for a huge population, because their average reliably reflects the whole.

PerQA: A Benchmark for Temporally Sensitive Questions on Heterogeneous Personal DataWWW
uses Answers questions about personal data by aggregating events over time, where many questions require filtering by dates and summing counts or patterns.
why it works Personal data is temporal—what happened matters less than when it happened. By building aggregation and filtering directly into the question-answering task, the system learns to weight recent events differently than old ones, capturing how time shapes meaning.
VarParser: Unleashing the Neglected Power of Variables for LLM-based Log ParsingWWW
uses Parses logs by sampling and caching based on variable parts (IDs, numbers, paths), not just constant text, reducing the amount of text sent to language models.
why it works In logs, variables carry unique information—an error ID might appear once in a million logs. Focusing on variables finds the true needle-in-haystack without bloating context with repeated words. It's like searching for your car by license plate instead of color.
Revisiting Graph-Level Anomaly Detection: From Partially to Fully Unsupervised LearningWWW
uses Detects abnormal graphs by modeling uncertainty around predictions, allowing the system to down-weight ambiguous samples that might be anomalies during training.
why it works Normal training assumes the data is clean, but real data mixes normal and anomalous. By learning both a prediction and how uncertain to feel about it, you can ignore the ambiguous cases during learning, letting the system focus on clear examples of normalcy.
Understanding Strategic Platform Entry and Seller Exploration: A Stackelberg ModelWWW
uses Model when a platform will enter a market to compete with sellers, balancing its own profit against information it learns over time.
why it works The platform learns which products are profitable by watching sellers succeed. An optimal strategy must weigh the immediate profit of entering now against learning more by waiting. The math works because the best strategy trades off known profits and unknown upside in a way that maximizes what matters: total lifetime earnings.
Modeling Cascaded Delay Feedback for Online Net Conversion Rate Prediction: Benchmark, Insights and SolutionsWWW
uses Predict the net conversion rate (purchase and no refund) by modeling the two delays separately and learning patterns over time from continuous feedback.
why it works Refunds and purchases are linked but opposite: a refund only happens after a purchase. Modeling them separately captures this structure better than trying to predict the final outcome directly. Online learning works because shoppers' preferences drift, so yesterday's patterns matter less than fresh data today.
Resisting Manipulative Bots in Meme Coin Copy Trading: A Multi-Agent Approach with Chain-of-Thought ReasoningWWW
uses Use a reasoning model to estimate the probability that a copy-trade target is manipulated, combining signals across chat sentiment, trading patterns, and bot behavior.
why it works Manipulation leaves traces across multiple channels: price patterns, social signals, order timing. By combining these signals with reasoning about causality (does the price move precede sentiment, or vice versa?), you estimate the probability more accurately than any single signal allows.
EcoTune: Edge-Cloud Collaborative Model Adaptation for Budget-Constrained On-Device SLM PersonalizationWWW
uses Select the most informative user interactions for cloud annotation using a multi-armed bandit, then adjust only the most critical model layers on-device.
why it works Not all interactions teach the model equally; selecting the informative ones lets you learn from fewer labels. Similarly, not all model parameters matter for personalization; updating only critical layers saves memory and computation. Both strategies exploit sparsity in what actually drives improvement.
Exploring the Domain Sensitivity of AI Chatbots in Correcting MisinformationWWW
uses Train a chatbot to correct misinformation by learning correction strategies, then measure how well it reduces false belief across health, science, and politics domains.
why it works Testing across unrelated domains reveals whether the model learned general error-correction principles or domain-specific tricks, showing if its approach generalizes or needs retuning.
Online Rounding and Pricing Schemes for k-Rental ProblemsWWW
uses Solve the fractional allocation online, then round to integers using controlled randomness to preserve the cost guarantee.
why it works Rounding works because fractional solutions are easier to compute and remain feasible; randomized rounding spreads the fractional excess to integers while keeping expected cost unchanged.
Camel: Frame-Level Bandwidth Estimation for Low-Latency Live Streaming under Video Bitrate UndershootingWWW
uses Estimate true available bandwidth by watching frame-by-frame network feedback, then weight the sending rate and burst pattern to match the frame bursts without overflowing the network.
why it works Video frames come in irregular bursts, not smoothly, so packet-level averages lie about true capacity. Frame-level feedback sees the actual congestion pattern. By tuning send rate and burst limits to that real pattern, you avoid both underuse (waiting when you could send) and overflow (sending so fast queues back up), so stalls drop.
Energy-Efficient and Dequantization-Free Quantization of LLMs: A Spiking Neural Network Approach to Salient Value MitigationWWW
uses Reduces how much energy a language model consumes by storing only a few important numbers in full precision while storing the rest as binary counts, avoiding expensive arithmetic during use.
