uses Select negative examples strategically when training graph classifiers, choosing cases that meaningfully distinguish true relationships from false ones.
why it works A model trained on hard negative cases learns the boundary between real and missing edges more sharply than random negatives, so it generalizes better to unseen edges.
Network Dismantling via Reverse Dismantling: Static and Dynamic AlgorithmsWWW
uses Finds the cheapest set of network nodes to remove that disconnects the giant connected component; efficiently recomputes results using tree-based index structures.
why it works Reverse dismantling exploits that removing high-impact nodes first is more efficient than forward trials; tree caches intermediate results to avoid redundant recomputation.
Learning-Based Optimization of Atomic Arbitrage in Decentralized Financial SystemsWWW
uses Trains an agent via reinforcement learning to select a three-pool arbitrage path and trade size to maximize profit under real constraints like gas and latency.
why it works Exhaustive search finds true optimum but is too slow for blockchain execution; learned policies approximate quickly; reinforcement learning updates policy toward high-reward decisions.
Sharpness-Consistent Cross-Domain Recommendation for Cold-Start ItemsWWW
uses Optimize model parameters to find loss landscape minima that are flat and consistent across both cold-start and warm-start recommendation domains.
why it works It works because flat minima generalize better—small changes in data don't large changes in predictions. By forcing the loss landscape to be equally flat in both cold and warm domains, the model's learned patterns must work universally, not exploit domain-specific quirks. This shared flatness across domains naturally transfers knowledge from warm to cold items.
Orthogonal Meta-learning Boosted Bayesian Optimization for Uncertain Multi-Objective RecommendationWWW
uses Optimize multiple competing recommendation objectives (accuracy, diversity, fairness) per user by learning which objectives matter to each person and their uncertain relationships.
why it works It works because users rarely want one thing only—accuracy without diversity feels robotic; fairness without accuracy feels unfair to them. By tuning objectives per person and capturing uncertainty in how they interact, the system adapts to real preferences. Using orthogonal meta-learning exploits shared patterns across users to speed convergence while keeping objectives from fighting each other.
Inference Cost Attacks for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Craft malicious documents that are semantically similar to user queries yet maximize words consumption during inference.
why it works The attack works by poisoning retrieval so the model fetches long, complex documents; optimizing document words directly targets the resource bottleneck. Learning agents can discover which phrases trigger maximum words explosion.
Automating Computational Reproducibility in Social Science: Comparing Prompt-Based and Agent-Based ApproachesWWW
uses Test whether AI repair systems can match ground-truth output by iteratively applying fixes until code execution succeeds.
why it works Repairs work by exploiting the structure of common failures: missing dependencies, path issues, logic gaps. A system that learns these patterns can address each type. Success requires output equivalence, not just execution.
Rethinking Graph Generalization through the Lens of Sharpness-Aware MinimizationWWW
uses Train networks in regions where small input changes cause small output changes, measured by the flatness of the loss landscape.
why it works Sharp valleys predict poor generalization: a network tuned to a narrow optimum breaks when data shifts slightly. Flat minima are stable—small perturbations barely change the loss, so the network generalizes.
DARA: Few-shot Budget Allocation in Online Advertising via In-Context Decision Making with RL-Finetuned LLMsWWW
uses Optimizes how to split a budget across ad placements to maximize winning impressions, learns from just a few examples by reasoning first then refining based on feedback.
why it works It works because you can reason about budget trade-offs roughly without needing historical data, then feedback on your choices tells you exactly where you guessed wrong, letting you tune just the parts that mattered, so few examples go a long way.
LLMQuA: Practical Backdoor Injection on Large Language Model QuantizationWWW
uses Optimizes quantization parameters layer-by-layer to find settings that preserve normal words behavior while distorting weights to reprogram specific words into backdoor responses.
why it works It works because quantization naturally rounds weights—you need settings that hide the rounding from normal use but exploit it for attack. By learning what words pairs look similar and different in normal behavior, you find settings where backdoor words change but benign words don't, keeping the attack invisible.
LoRA-E2: Effective and Efficient Low-rank AdaptationWWW
uses Improves compact adaptation by initializing the small add-on modules matrices differently and using a better algorithm to train them, making adjust faster and more stable.
why it works Standard compact adaptation struggles when the numeric fingerprints features is huge because it spreads learning effort across many useless directions. By seeding one grid of numbers with noise scaled to the numeric fingerprints size and solving both matrices jointly rather than treating one as fixed, the method explores more meaningful directions and converges faster. This works because it balances how much each grid of numbers learns instead of letting one stay stuck.
MASI: Memory-Adaptive Inference Framework for Spiking Neural Networks on Edge DevicesWWW
uses Adapts spiking systems that learn from examples inference on phones to available memory by slicing network layers smartly, scheduling timesteps to reduce memory fragmentation, and stopping early on confident predictions.
why it works Memory on phones fluctuates unpredictably. By measuring available memory and adjusting which layers load, how they run, and when to quit early, the model fits what the device can hold right now while staying accurate.
SAGE: Sustainable Agent-Guided Expert-tuning for Culturally Attuned Translation in Low-Resource Southeast AsiaWWW
uses Translates text for low-resource Southeast Asian languages by using a learning agent to select high-quality, culturally relevant training examples instead of training on all noisy data.
why it works Translation to low-resource languages fails on massive noisy data because culture-specific meaning gets drowned out. By training a selection agent to recognize which examples preserve cultural intent, then adjust on those few high-signal examples, the model learns precise, culturally grounded translation without carbon-intensive brute-force training.
Temporal Challenges in Data-Driven Scenario-Building for Climate-Neutral CitiesWWW
uses Simulating urban systems forward in time to find which policy changes reduce emissions most effectively.
why it works It works because running a simulation from today through future years with each proposed policy lets you see which ones actually cause the outcomes you want (lower emissions, better livability), rather than guessing.
ICL-Evader: Zero-Query Black-Box Evasion Attacks on In-Context Learning and Their DefensesWWW
uses Craft adversarial examples by exploiting how models process in-context prompts, then train defenses to harden prompts against these attacks.
why it works It works because the attacks expose real failure modes in how models handle context: they don't integrate examples rationally, can be distracted by structure, and prioritize later examples over earlier ones. Defenses mitigate these modes by fixing how prompts are constructed.
Intelli-Planner: Towards Customized Urban Planning via Large Language Model Empowered Reinforcement LearningWWW
uses Reinforce planning decisions that maximize satisfaction across stakeholders by learning a policy that maps land data and preferences to layouts.
why it works Reinforcement learning finds actions that yield high rewards through repeated trial and error. Language models provide structured reasoning about what actions look reasonable, which guides the search toward good decisions faster than random exploration alone.
WAB: Overcoming Memory, Network, and Security Walls in Native Agentic Browsers with WebAssemblyWWW
uses Runs agent code inside a WebAssembly sandbox that pre-fetches context into fast memory, batches multiple actions into single round-trips, and prevents unsafe operations through isolation.
why it works It works because WebAssembly creates a walled-off playground: isolation stops malicious prompts from escaping, batching reduces network delays (many small round-trips become one big one), and loading context on demand means you only keep hot data in fast memory.
SkyCL: Swift Continuous Learning with Kinship-Awareness for Multi-Drone Video Analytics under Drastic DriftWWW
uses Detects when drone video changes drastically and retrains the model on fresh video, then reuses or adapts past models based on how similar they were to current performance.
why it works It works because when camera angles or lighting shift abruptly, old patterns no longer match new images. By noticing that shift and quickly retraining on recent frames, you keep the model current. Reusing past models that faced similar shifts saves retraining time.
Beyond Fine-Tuning: The Present and Future of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning in Vision TransformersWWW
uses Surveys efficient methods to adapt image classification models by updating only small subsets of parameters rather than retraining the entire network.
why it works It works because large pretrained models already know how to see and recognize countless patterns. You only need to steer them toward your specific task, not rebuild them. By modifying just a few carefully chosen parameters or adding lightweight small add-on modules, you get task-specific performance without recomputing millions of weight updates.
Alzo: Auto-Tuning with Reinforcement Learning for DAG-based BlockchainsWWW
uses Auto-tune a blockchain's performance by learning which parameter settings maximize throughput and minimize latency at each stage of the consensus protocol, adjusting continuously as workload changes.
why it works It works because performance metrics are differentiable with respect to parameter settings: adjusting one knob causes measurable change in throughput or latency. Hierarchical learning lets different stages optimize their own metrics then coordinate, finding compound improvements without manual trial-and-error.
Smaller but Better: Plasticity-Preserving Continual Learning for Embedded AIWWW
uses Prunes network capacity while carefully preserving the ability to learn new tasks by expanding capacity temporarily at task boundaries then re-pruning.
why it works It works because the capacity to adapt depends on having room to store new patterns; by expanding at critical moments when learning new material and re-pruning afterward, the model keeps only essential connections while staying flexible enough to absorb new knowledge.
Breaking the Scalability Barrier in Constrained Graph-Based Networked Control via Decision-Focused LearningWWW
uses Learn actions for deciding production and transport on graphs by imitating expert decisions while respecting capacity limits.
why it works It works because expert demonstrations already encode which decisions respect constraints while maximizing profit. By learning to imitate those decisions, the system avoids the hardness of solving the optimization from scratch and inherits correctness from the examples.
Tuning Qwen2.5-VL to Improve Its Web Interaction SkillsWWW
uses Improve a vision-language model's web clicking accuracy by teaching it to verify element location and state after each action instead of assuming success.
why it works It works because vision errors compound: if the model guesses wrong about where an element is, the next action fails predictably. By inserting verification after each step—explicit checking of whether the action succeeded—the model catches and corrects errors before they cascade.
Wiseswap: Elastic Datacenter Network-Aware Disaggregated Memory for Multi-Tenant CloudWWW
uses Routes data traffic through datacenter paths that have the least congestion and measures latency in real time to choose which memory locations to use and when to prioritize requests.
why it works It works because latency is directly measurable, and once you know which paths are slow, you can steer traffic to avoid them. Since different requests have different urgency, prioritizing the critical ones first while using the fast paths for all traffic minimizes the worst delays anyone experiences.
Mitigating Cumulative Privacy Risk in Continual Information Sharing: A Dynamic Stackelberg Game ApproachWWW
uses Model a user's privacy-sharing decisions over time as a game where both user and attacker learn from each other, optimize the user's strategy to minimize cumulative risk.
why it works It works because privacy leaks grow over time—each disclosure helps an attacker build a better profile, so you can't treat each choice as independent. Modeling it as a game lets you find the point where the user's best strategy and the attacker's best response meet, and then the user can follow that path downhill to minimize total damage.
R2NS: Recall and Re-ranking of Negative Samples for Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Trains recommendation systems by progressively showing them harder negative items to contrast with liked items, improving discernment over time.
why it works It works because differences teach better than agreement. Easy negatives teach the model nothing new. By gradually introducing harder contrasts, the model stretches its boundaries without breaking—each stage builds on learning from the previous harder-than-before examples.
Orchestration-Free Customer Service Automation: A Privacy-Preserving and Flowchart-Guided FrameworkWWW
uses Learns procedural flowcharts from service conversations and uses them to guide small models through customer service tasks step-by-step.
why it works It works because flowcharts reduce ambiguity—each step tells the model exactly what decision to make next. Small models can follow clear instructions when they would fail at open-ended generation. The flowchart extracted from real conversations captures the expert path.
How Quantum Period Finding Breaks Rivest Shamir Adleman AlgorithmsWWW
uses Emulates quantum computation step by step to show how quantum algorithms can find the repeating pattern in the RSA encryption system, breaking it.
why it works It works because RSA depends on a hidden repeating pattern that is hard to find classically but quantum algorithms can find it. By tracking exactly how quantum gates manipulate the state to uncover periodicity, we see that quantum processes exploit mathematical structure that classical methods cannot touch.
Breath: Adaptive Protection Boundary in FEC Encoding for Mobile Real-Time Video StreamingWWW
uses Dynamically adjust how many redundant copies of video frames to send based on network loss patterns.
why it works Burst losses happen at frame scale but smooth out across frames; changing protection per frame group matches the natural granularity of loss, so redundancy aligns to where it actually prevents playback delay.
Feedback Control for Small Budget Campaigns in AdvertisingWWW
uses Adjust ad spend rate during an auction using feedback from actual spending to stay close to budget target.
why it works Simple feedback loops stabilize under-paced spending; watching actual versus target spend and adjusting direction converges to balanced allocation without expensive retraining.
BIND: A Bidirectionally Aligned Next-token Denoising Framework for Fast and Lightweight Deobfuscation of Harmful Web TextWWW
uses Correct obfuscated harmful text by aligning characters bidirectionally and using a specialized focus to fix each position, trained to handle visual tricks and emoji substitution.
why it works Works because obfuscation exploits character-level confusion (is that zero or oh? is that L or I?) and words boundaries. Bidirectional alignment and character-level focus let the small model fix these tricks precisely without the latency of large auto-regressive models, while handling out-of-vocabulary symbols naturally.
CEAT: Context-Emotion Adversarial Training Framework for Robust Emotion-Driven Fraud DetectionWWW
uses Train fraud detection robust to emotional manipulation by adversarially injecting realistic noise into emotion signals during training, drawn from actual patterns in user behavior.
why it works Works because adversaries can subtly modulate facial expressions, voice tone, and word choice to mimic honesty while committing fraud. Training against realistic emotional perturbations teaches the model to ignore emotion-based tricks and rely on deeper behavioral patterns that fraudsters cannot easily fake.
ReFuGe: Feature Generation for Prediction Tasks on Relational Databases with LLM AgentsWWW
uses Generates relational features through schema reasoning and iterative validation, filtering infeasible combinations before testing.
why it works It works because the feature space is huge but sparse. Agents prune impossibilities early using schema knowledge, then empirically validate survivors—this combination avoids testing billions of invalid features.
AFE-Master: Enhancing LLM-Driven Autonomous Feature Engineering with Domain-Specific Language Parsing and Guided Local SearchWWW
uses Uses a language model to construct features expressed in a domain-specific language, then searches locally for small edits to features that reduce prediction error while preserving semantic structure.
why it works Domain-specific languages encode valid transformation rules, so editing within that language guarantees features remain interpretable. Local search with small steps converges reliably because you can evaluate each tiny change's effect before committing, avoiding getting stuck far from good solutions.
XLingLearn: Balancing Alignment and Robustness for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual TransferWSDM
uses Improve language transfer by pushing apart overly clustered word meanings and aligning how languages weight their focus, reducing error on unseen data.
why it works It works because languages encode meaning differently—spreading them apart in the space prevents one language from drowning out others. Consistent focus across languages makes the learned space robust to noisy or missing data.
Adaptive Continual Learning with User-Incremental Forward Compatibility for Meta-Augmented Cold-Start RecommendersWSDM
uses Learn a recommendation model on few new-user examples that also remembers old patterns, avoiding forgetting or mixing up what different users like.
why it works It works because you can keep important past knowledge separate from new knowledge by replaying examples, and you can update carefully by checking that old users still stay satisfied.
APPNet: Automatic Feature Partitioning-Based Parameter Personalized Network for Conversion Prediction in E-commerceWSDM
uses Automatically partition features into groups, then use one group to adjust network weights while the other predicts purchase likelihood.
why it works It works because different users follow different decision patterns. By identifying which features naturally group users together, you can tune the prediction model separately for each group, reducing error for each rather than forcing one model to work for everyone.
ReToP: Learning to Rewrite Electronic Health Records for Clinical PredictionWSDM
uses Rewrite medical records using language models trained specifically to improve downstream predictions by focusing on clinically relevant rewrites.
why it works It works because medical records are incomplete and contain irrelevant details. By training the rewriter end-to-end with the predictor, guided by which rewrites actually improve decisions, the model learns to amplify what matters and suppress noise, improving clinical performance over generic improvements.
Diffusion Models for Risk-Aware Portfolio OptimizationWSDM
uses Sample candidate portfolios from a learned distribution, then use a diffusion process with risk guidance to iteratively improve portfolios toward a user's specified risk tolerance.
why it works It works because portfolio quality and risk are linked: better portfolios tend to exist where risk matches preference. Diffusion allows direct sampling instead of forecasting entire time series. Risk guidance steers the cleanup process toward portfolios matching the user's appetite, so you get diverse, realistic options fast.
Bi-Level Optimization for Generative Recommendation: Bridging Tokenization and GenerationSIGIR
uses Optimize a tokenizer (item encoder) and a recommender jointly: the recommender learns to rank items given words, while the tokenizer learns which words make the recommender's job easiest.
why it works It works because item words and the recommender depend on each other—words chosen by the optimizer should help the recommender rank well. Solving both simultaneously prevents the tokenizer from generating words that are cheap to compute but useless for ranking.
From Interference to Stability: Adversarial Reliability Correction for Video Moment Retrieval with Relevance FeedbackSIGIR
uses Minimize prediction errors on video moment retrieval by actively testing the model under adversarial interference and learning to suppress unreliable predictions.
why it works It works because errors due to confusing similar moments are the real risk. By adversarially amplifying interference during training, you force the model to learn robust features that distinguish true relevance from distraction. Testing stability under these worst cases predicts which decisions will hold up in practice.
DLLM-Searcher: Adapting Diffusion Language Model for Efficient Search AgentsSIGIR
uses Train a language model to reason and call tools with parallel decoding, improve it via preference learning, then reuse intermediate reasoning steps across multiple tool calls.
why it works It works because the model can generate multiple candidate reasoning paths in parallel instead of one at a time, then select the best trajectory. Preference learning tunes the model to favor reasoning that leads to correct tool calls, and reusing steps amortizes computation.
ZIPBid: Hierarchical Zero-shot Incremental Spend Planning for Auto-biddingSIGIR
uses Plans daily advertising budgets using an AI system that reads campaign content, then adjusts individual bid prices hourly to stay on budget.
why it works It works because planning and control work together: a high-level plan from understanding campaign content gives long-term direction, while hourly adjustments adjust to follow it despite unpredictable customer activity.
PrepRet: Automated Data Preparation Pipeline Selection for Neural RetrievalSIGIR
uses Learn which data preprocessing steps to use by optimizing retrieval performance end-to-end, treating step selection as a differentiable choice.
why it works It works because good preprocessing depends on the retrieval model and dataset, so there's no universal best pipeline. By directly optimizing which steps to use based on retrieval errors, the system finds the combination that actually helps this specific model and data.
Efficient Query Region Expansion and Decomposition based Spatial Range Query AlgorithmSIGIR
uses Divide a geographic query region into blocks aligned with a grid so that each block perfectly matches the database's spatial index, minimizing extra unwanted lookups.
why it works When query borders align with index boundaries, the database can fetch entire blocks without any overlap; misaligned borders force the database to fetch blocks and then discard boundary points.
LearnDCG: End-to-End Joint Optimization of Ranker and Loss in Neural RankingSIGIR
uses Learn the gain values and temperature for ranking accuracy by treating NDCG itself as a learnable function, optimizing it end-to-end with the ranker.
why it works Standard surrogate losses are rigid—they don't adapt to your data. By making the NDCG formula itself learnable, you let the model discover what gain and discount values actually work for your relevance patterns. The model learns to match its data instead of forcing data to match a hand-designed formula.
SAGE: Solver-Aligned Guided ExplorationSIGIR
uses Train a small search model via reinforcement learning to pick which code snippets matter for a solver, using feedback on whether retrieved code actually helps patch generation.
why it works It works because you're optimizing directly against what the solver needs: code that leads to a working patch. Learning from successful vs failed retrieval attempts builds a searcher that knows what actually matters downstream.
Negotiating the Punchline: Contextual Meme Understanding via Discrete Semantic Energy MinimizationSIGIR
uses Treat meme interpretation as minimizing semantic inconsistency: iteratively compute inconsistency scores, then refine explanations by following the slope of that score downward.
why it works A good interpretation is one where all the clues—image, text, context—reinforce each other. By quantifying how much they clash (semantic energy) and stepping downhill in that landscape, you find interpretations where everything fits together.
SkillForge: Forging Domain-Specific, Self-Evolving Agent Skills in Cloud Technical SupportSIGIR
uses Creates specialized agent skills by grounding them in support documents, then automatically detects failures and rewrites skills to fix the underlying problems.
why it works It works because grounding skills in a knowledge base ensures they align with real requirements from the start. Failure analysis traces execution errors back to skill flaws. This feedback loop iteratively removes one class of defects per cycle, improving skill quality.
STAR: Staged Training with Aligned Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Faceted Distillation for Interpretable E-commerce RelevanceSIGIR
uses Train a teacher model with rewards that penalize ranking errors, then copy its reasoning logic to a smaller model that can run in production.
why it works It works because optimizing explicitly for ranking accuracy forces the teacher to learn what actually matters for relevance judgments. Copying this optimized logic to a smaller model preserves the learned priorities, so the compact version still makes sound decisions despite having less capacity.
Learning to Trust: Dynamic Utilization of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for E-commerce Search RelevanceSIGIR
uses Train the model to learn from comparing outcomes when using external context versus not using it, so it knows when external knowledge helps.
why it works It works because the comparison is direct evidence. By seeing which approach (parametric only or with context) produces better results on specific queries, the model learns a reliable signal about context trustworthiness. This learned discrimination is better than any fixed rule.
Learning to Summarize for Search Relevance with Reinforcement LearningSIGIR
uses Generate product summaries by training the model to maximize downstream relevance scores, which are computed after ranking, so summaries are optimized for the real goal.
why it works It works because the summary is now optimized for the actual objective: making products rank higher. Intermediate representations (summaries) that are aligned with final outcomes produce better results than optimizing them in isolation. The reward signal flows directly from the ranking goal back to summary generation.
40 papers

Learning from examples and comparison

When the rule connecting input to output is too tangled to write down, you show the system many examples — or many pairs of what is similar and what is different — and let it settle on a rule that reproduces them.

Why it works — the principle

It works because of a bargain between simplicity and coverage: when the true pattern is far simpler than the data and the examples cover the territory, a rule forced to fit them all has little room left to be wrong on new cases. Learning by comparison works because 'pull similar things together, push different ones apart' is enough to recover the hidden structure without anyone labelling it.

COMA: A Collaborative Multi-Role Agent Framework for Automated Lesson Plan GenerationWWW
uses Generate lesson plans by orchestrating multiple agents with complementary expertise who iteratively refine structure, content, and pedagogy.
why it works Lesson planning requires multiple types of knowledge: structure (flow), content (curriculum details), and method (what actually teaches). Each agent type learns one specialization; iteration lets them correct each other, producing better results than any single agent because diverse perspectives catch errors the others miss.
BaiJia: An Open Role-Playing Platform of Chinese Historical CharactersWWW
uses Train language models on historical character biographies to generate authentic role-playing dialogue.
why it works Character behavior patterns exist in historical texts; learning these patterns allows models to predict plausible responses consistent with documented lives.
TabTune: A Unified Library for Inference and Fine-Tuning Tabular Foundation ModelsWWW
uses Standardize preprocessing and evaluation across multiple foundation models on structured tabular data.
why it works Different models use different formats; unifying them reveals which algorithm genuinely works best on a given task by removing implementation noise.
Collaborative LLM Agents for End-to-End Software DevelopmentWWW
uses Teach agents to plan, code, test, and review by having them learn from examples, feedback, and tool outputs, building up reliable workflows instead of one-shot generation.
why it works This works because software is brittle: a single pass rarely produces working code. Learning from examples of what works (working code, passing tests, good reviews) teaches the model patterns of reliability—trial, feedback, and refinement.
Out-of-distribution Generalized Generative AIWWW
uses Train image and language models to understand and generate across many modalities, then adapt them to new, unseen distributions by learning from new data without forgetting old knowledge.
why it works This works because generalization comes from learning stable patterns that transfer: if you train on broad data and then adapt carefully, the model reuses what it learned rather than restarting from scratch.
LLM-Powered Structurer: Normalizing Natural Language to Information Delivery Specification for Industrial Data ExchangeWWW
uses Using a language model to translate a person's informal description of what information they need into formal machine-readable construction-industry data format.
why it works It works because language models have learned from billions of examples how human descriptions map to formal specifications—they can generalize the pattern from simple requests to complex ones without anyone manually writing all the rules.
Lang2Plan: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent System for Building Layout PlanningWWW
uses Decompose natural language instructions into simpler sub-tasks using multiple agents, then generate realistic 3D layouts from the refined plan.
why it works Complex language is hard to interpret in one pass. Breaking it into smaller sub-problems lets each agent focus on something simpler and reason about partial results. Robustness comes from agents catching and correcting errors before they compound into the final design.
Semi-supervised Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models on Text-Attributed GraphsWWW
uses adjust a language model on labeled node examples and unlabeled neighbors iteratively, using the model's predictions on unlabeled nodes to generate new training examples without expert annotation.
why it works This works because graph edges encode genuine correlation—if two nodes connect, they're likely similar in the task you're solving. Self-training leverages this structure: the model's early predictions on unlabeled neighbors provide noisy but correlated training signal, especially when those neighbors live near confident labeled nodes. Multiple iterations refine the signal by forcing the model to learn from nodes whose neighborhood structure matches labeled examples, so errors stay local rather than spreading.
AdVersa: Adversarially-Robust and Practical Ad and Tracker Blocking in the WildWWW
uses Detect ads and trackers using learned features from code and URL that resist adversarial perturbation; maintain accuracy over time using low-cost pseudo-labeling without human re-labeling.
why it works This works because adversaries try small perturbations (a few URL characters) hoping the model fails, but hidden code/URL features are harder to twist than raw text—the model learns invariant patterns. Pseudo-labeling for maintenance works because most ads remain ads; high-confidence predictions on new data stay correct, so retraining on predictions alone captures drift without expert overhead. Learning from perturbation-resistant features + comparison of predicted vs actual labels keeps the system robust and economical long-term.
(Mis-)Informed Consent: Predatory Apps and the Exploitation of Populations with Limited LiteracyWWW
uses Measures how well apps disclose and explain permissions to low-literacy users, then tests if language model summaries and visual aids can bridge the comprehension gap.
why it works It works because clear explanations that match how people actually understand language create better informed decisions. Simpler summaries and pictures bypass the jargon barrier that lets apps hide their true data requests.
coTherapist: A Behavior-Aligned Small Language Model Framework to Support Mental Healthcare ExpertsWWW
uses adjust a small model on therapy examples so it learns to respond with therapist-like empathy and clinical accuracy.
why it works Therapist behavior is consistent and learnable: certain responses to certain situations reliably help. When you show a model many examples of good therapeutic responses alongside the situations they answer, it learns the mapping from situation to response. Adding retrieval (looking up relevant clinical knowledge) grounds responses in fact.
Beyond Class Boundaries: Federated Visual Primitive Sharing with Text-Guided AdaptationWWW
uses Devices share reusable visual patterns instead of complete class features, allowing personalized adaptation with less communication.
why it works Decomposing class features into common building blocks decouples sharing from class count; personalization works because blocks combine differently per device.
Glasses: Enabling Fast Environment-aware Few-Shot Learning via Device-Cloud CollaborationWWW
uses Uses a small number of labeled examples and one unlabeled image of the target environment to adjust a pre-trained model's internal weights so it performs better on new tasks in that specific setting.
why it works It works because a pre-trained model already knows general visual patterns; you only need to adjust its internal settings to match your specific environment. With even one environment image to guide adaptation, the cloud can calculate small weight adjustments that eliminate environment mismatch without retraining from scratch.
The 2nd Workshop on Social Science Meets Web Data: Reproducible and Reusable Computational Approaches (R2CASS)WWW
uses Establishes shared methods and practices for researchers to reproduce computational social science findings from digital behavioral data.
why it works It works because reproducibility requires learning from past examples: seeing what methods worked in starting guess studies teaches you which practices, templates, and tools actually produce trustworthy results that others can verify and reuse.
CompTox Ontology: Leveraging Knowledge Graphs for PFAS Monitoring and Decision-MakingWWW
uses Organizes chemical compounds hierarchically with their identifiers and properties to enable reliable lookup and comparison of harmful substances.
why it works It works because chemical compounds have inherent structure: compounds with similar structures behave similarly. By organizing them hierarchically according to what chemists know about their properties, lookups become consistent and new data about unknown compounds can be reasoned from known relatives.
Pattern Discovery with Wide-Lens Analysis and Sharp-Focus ValidationWWW
uses Zooms out to find clusters of similar patterns in unstructured data, then zooms in to verify which patterns are real and build consistent categories.
why it works It works because pattern discovery has two parts: finding candidates (wide view) and confirming they are consistent (close inspection). Cycling between these discovers what actually recurs in data without needing ground truth labels. Rough candidates guide where to look closely; detailed validation confirms which candidates truly repeat.
Class-Domain Incremental Learning on Graphs via Disentangled Knowledge DistillationWWW
uses Split node features into task-specific patterns and task-agnostic background noise, then teach new classes while protecting old knowledge.
why it works Separating signal from noise lets the model learn what truly changes between tasks versus what is stable; distilling old knowledge preserves learned patterns, preventing the model from erasing starting guess insights when new classes arrive.
Hierarchical Prompt Contrastive Learning for Weakly Supervised Histopathology SegmentationWWW
uses Learn to segment tissue regions by comparing image features to text descriptions and category prompts at multiple levels.
why it works Text prompts ground visual features to semantic meaning; comparing multi-layer features to those prompts forces the model to align images with concepts it understands, and hierarchy lets it learn both fine detail and broad category at once.
RaDAR: Relation-aware Diffusion-Asymmetric Graph Contrastive Learning for RecommendationWWW
uses Generate diverse views of user-item interaction graphs using both generative models and learned edge refinement, then train by comparing views.
why it works Random perturbations destroy critical signals; generating views smartly with both global structure and relation-aware edge weights preserves semantic meaning, so comparing them teaches robust user-item relationships even under sparse data.
Adaptive Contrastive Learning in Sequential Recommendation based on Perturbation and Restoration NetworksWWW
uses Learn to adapt how you perturb and restore user sequences for comparison so augmentation preserves user intent.
why it works Hard-coded perturbations destroy the sequences users actually care about; learning what noise preserves meaning ensures augmented views still capture real preference patterns, so contrastive learning finds stable user interest structure.
PAGE: Progressive Anomaly Generation Network for Semi-supervised Graph Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Generate artificial anomalies by step-wise corruption of node attributes and connections, then train to separate real anomalies from progressively degraded normal nodes.
why it works Works because anomalies of different severity levels exist in the real world, so training on a spectrum from mild to extreme makes the model recognize subtle deviations that a single-step method would miss. The progressive constraint forces learned scores to rank corruption levels properly.
MMTableBench: A Multi-level Multimodal Benchmark for Reasoning and Layout Complexity in Table QAWWW
uses Test whether question answerers understand both the visual layout of tables and the logical steps needed to answer questions about them.
why it works By varying layout complexity and reasoning steps independently across benchmarks, you can measure which skills the model actually has versus which ones hide because the task was too easy or too hard on both features at once.
STIndex: A Context-Aware Multi-Dimensional Spatiotemporal Information Extraction SystemWWW
uses Extract and organize information from news and documents by grounding it to specific times and places, with language models filling in the structure.
why it works Space and time are universal anchors; anchoring all extracted facts to where and when they occurred aligns information that would otherwise be scattered, making downstream tasks like search and reasoning far more reliable.
SHIELD: A Framework for Online Conversational AI System for Self-Regulated Learning at Emergency Communications CentersWSDM
uses Train an AI to simulate emergency calls by comparing trainee responses against right and wrong actions, then flag when they drift from good practice.
why it works It works because learning by contrast—seeing what trainees did versus what experts would do—tells the AI which moves matter for good performance. Real-time nudges exploit this difference signal to steer learning.
Understanding and Modeling Heterogeneous Search BehaviorSIGIR
uses Extract hidden search features from how different demographic groups formulate queries and interact, then use those features to explain and predict query behavior.
why it works It works because demographic differences in search are not random; they reflect underlying strategies and preferences. By finding the hidden features that separate behavior, you capture the true drivers rather than confusing correlation with cause, enabling fair comparison across groups.
An Eye Tracking Study: Are AI Overviews Changing Search Behavior?SIGIR
uses Track where people's eyes look on search result pages when generative summaries appear above traditional blue links, measuring engagement to understand changing focus.
why it works It works because eye tracking directly reveals where focus flows. Comparing gaze distribution when generative content is present versus absent isolates its causal effect on search behavior, avoiding self-report bias.
One-for-All Community Search on Unseen GraphsSIGIR
uses Learn a single graph representation model on source graphs that generalizes to unseen target graphs by aligning features across domains and using diffusion-based refinement.
why it works It works because you train on multiple source graphs to see many graph styles, then the alignment step learns to translate between any graph's features. The diffusion refinement smooths out distribution shifts, so the function learned from training generalizes even when it encounters new graph structures.
SNBot: Modeling Self-Neighborhood Representation Discrepancy for Social Bot DetectionSIGIR
uses Detect social bots by learning to distinguish between a node's core identity and what its neighborhood looks like, rather than assuming they should match.
why it works It works because real users and bots differ in how their declared attributes relate to their social surroundings. By explicitly modeling this gap rather than smoothing it away, you preserve the discriminative signal: genuine accounts have neighborhoods that reflect them, while bots exhibit systematic misalignment.
NERBench-Chhattisgarh: A Multi-Family NER Dataset for Low-Resource Indic LanguagesSIGIR
uses Train multilingual models to recognize named entities in seven under-resourced tribal languages by learning shared features across related languages.
why it works It works because languages that share structure or script also share patterns in how entities are named, and by training on related languages together, the model learns features that transfer even when training data for any single language is tiny.
DeepResearch-9K: A Challenging Benchmark Dataset of Deep-Research AgentSIGIR
uses Learns to find answers by practicing on chains of reasoning, starting with weak examples then improving through reward signals.
why it works It works because good answers build on good intermediate steps; practicing on real reasoning paths teaches the system which intermediate steps actually lead to correct answers.
IIRSim Studio: A Dashboard for User SimulationSIGIR
uses Builds a visual workshop where users design and run experiments simulating how people search, then share and reproduce their setup.
why it works It works because reproducibility requires capturing every choice; when all setup choices are explicit and versioned, the same experiment always gives the same outcome, enabling trust and reuse.
Mine over Yours: How Authorship Biases Evaluation in Generative Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Ask participants to rate information they created themselves versus identical information framed as someone else's creation.
why it works When you create something, you understand the effort and reasoning behind it, making it feel more credible and higher quality. This bias toward self-created work is cognitive—your own reasoning feels trustworthy even when the output is the same, because you know it came from your intent.
uses Test two agent personas—one that mirrors user preferences back and one that offers social guidance—and measure their effect on shopping engagement.
why it works Interaction style shapes how users think. A mirroring agent helps users clarify their own preferences by reflecting them back; a peer agent creates social trust that relaxes scrutiny. Different conversation frames activate different cognitive modes, showing that how the system talks changes how users reason.
Beyond Unimodal Perspectives: Generative Retrieval with Multimodal SemanticsSIGIR
uses Generate item identifiers using text and images together by aligning semantic meanings across both modalities so they pull toward shared concepts.
why it works It works because objects truly are multimodal—a chair looks and sounds a certain way. By forcing the text and image representations to be close to each other (alignment), you teach the model that they are the same thing, making both modalities contribute to one consistent identity.
Domain-Specific Reranking: When is Adaptation Worth the Cost?SIGIR
uses A model trained on a few hundred labeled examples within a specialized domain performs as well as models trained on much larger domain-adaptive pretraining.
why it works It works because generic pretraining teaches broad patterns but adjust on domain examples teaches the specific distinctions that matter. When domain data is scarce, adjust focus beats pretraining breadth because the model concentrates on exactly what the domain needs.
RAPO: Reason-Aware Preference Optimization for Factual Table Question Answering over Structured DataSIGIR
uses Align an answer-generating system to produce factually correct responses by learning from examples where correct and incorrect answers are annotated with their reasoning.
why it works It works because understanding why an answer is right or wrong teaches the system the causal structure of the data. Standard preference learning ignores this reasoning, missing the underlying principles. Reason-aware alignment uses these explanations to generalize better to unseen queries.
TRACE: Term-level Reasoning And Chain-of-thought Enhanced distillation for E-commerce Multi-modal Relevance LearningSIGIR
uses Train the model to reason about which query terms are satisfied by text versus images, step by step, then teach a fast model to replicate this term-aware reasoning.
why it works It works because decomposing reasoning into term-level steps grounds the model's logic in concrete query parts. This prevents the model from relying on spurious correlations. When you transfer step-by-step reasoning to a smaller model, you preserve the interpretable logic that made the larger model reliable.
Labadain Chat: A Conversational Agent for the Tetun LanguageSIGIR
uses Adjust a general-purpose language model to Tetun by teaching it language-specific patterns through prompting.
why it works It works because language models are flexible functions that adjust their outputs based on training examples and instructions; showing the model Tetun patterns teaches it to recognize and produce the language correctly.
Building Foundations for Information Retrieval in Extremely Low-Resource Ethnic Languages: Evidence from TanzaniaSIGIR
uses Learn to translate between low-resource ethnic languages and Kiswahili using parallel sentences and speech recordings.
why it works It works because function learning from examples captures the systematic correspondence between languages: when you see enough pairs of sentences in both languages expressing the same meaning, the function naturally learns which words and phrases map to each other, enabling translation without hand-crafted rules.
User Search Behavior and Knowledge Effects in Hybrid Search EnvironmentSIGIR
uses Learn to predict search behavior patterns from eye-tracking and interaction data, conditioned on user knowledge level and cognitive processing ability.
why it works It works because cognitive level and knowledge determine how users process information: an expert scans differently than a novice, and focus reveal understanding. Modeling these patterns from data automatically learns how knowledge and cognition shape behavior without manual encoding.
Connecting the dots

Different problems, the same few guarantees

Line the ideas up and the surprise is how few there are, and how each rests on a plain guarantee. Ranking works because only order matters. Similarity works because meaning becomes distance. Estimating chances works because averages of enough observations don't lie. Spreading across a network works because neighbours are alike. Minimising error works because a slope always points the way down. Different problems, the same handful of reasons to trust the answer.

And one idea now runs through all the others: learning the rule from examples. But look closely and it doesn't replace the older math — it rides on it. A learned recommender still turns meaning into nearness and still ranks by a score; a learned language system still estimates chances and focuses on what's relevant. The 2026 story isn't that data mining stopped being mathematical — it's that a learned layer now sits on the same small, well-understood toolkit the field has always trusted.

Every good answer this field gives is one of a few mathematical questions in disguise — what's nearest, what ranks highest, how likely, what actually causes it — and each is trusted for a reason you can state in a sentence. Know the few reasons and the whole field stops being magic.

Each paper's core mathematical idea and the reason it works were read from its abstract by a language model, named from a fixed plain vocabulary; the framing of each idea is written from first principles.
